AI Memory

Building an LLM brain

Sources checked to22 November 2026
Labs rerun to23 November 2026
Written By Jeremy SchoemakerAuthor of AiBook

How to read this book

Build memory that an agent based on a large language model (LLM) can read and update. Entry points: Chapter 00 for the memory loop, 01 for flat files, 17 to evaluate, secure and operate memory, 18 to compare architectures, 20 for one assistant's six stages.

Three kinds of chapter

Architecture chapters, 01–14. Each has a summary, a strip showing maturity, setup effort and running cost, and nine sections: What it is, How it works, Good for and not for, Use cases, Numbers, Setup walkthrough, Gotchas, Verdict and Sources.

Essay chapters, 00 and 15–19. They cover memory basics, history, research, security, evaluation and operations, architecture selection and a field report. Each keeps the summary and Sources list. Strip fields vary by topic; setup and cost ratings are omitted. Read these chapters in any order.

Case studies, 20–23. These designs use only self-hosted models: one assistant in six memory stages, then a painter, a doctor's office and an international homebuilder. The last three have a full-page "What does what" map. These reference designs offer no legal, compliance, tax or clinical advice.

Running the Setup walkthroughs

Use disposable service instances, such as temporary databases without real data. Most walkthroughs refuse an existing working folder, mark created items with a run token (random string) and clean up only matching items. Some short walkthroughs use fixed names; keep those disposable too.

For a named file longer than eight lines, the chapter prints a one-line pointer that links to it. In the PDF edition, files are attached (Attachments panel, a paperclip icon) and are in the companion repository, whose address Appendix B prints. Labels such as ch09-code05 mean Chapter 09, fifth named file; the repository README maps labels to files. Source links appear under sources/ in the repository.

Walkthroughs carry these labels:

TestedRun in November 2026 using listed versions and linked files where pointers replace code.
From docs, not runAdapted from documentation, not run.

Appendix A, Glossary. Defines memory terminology and abbreviations, with chapter pointers; terms are also defined at first use. Appendix B, Code files. Indexes code files by label and path.

Editorial ratings

Setup effort (colored dots): 1 is edit files on one machine; 3 is one database or service to run; 5 is several services plus model hosting.
Running cost (dark dots): count only what memory adds over the same agent without it. 1 adds no service or hardware, though compute/storage charges may grow; 3 is one managed service or small virtual machine; 5 is several paid managed services or an added accelerator.

Ratings are editorial judgments, not measurements or budgets; cost dots compare added infrastructure. Even numbers fall between anchors. Architecture strips and Chapter 18 share these dots; essay strips omit them. Resolve ties using existing infrastructure, hosting limits and Chapter 18.

Basics · Chapter 00

00

Memory basics: four kinds, one loop

Memory supplies context, saves facts during or after a turn, or changes model weights.

Reading time

About 20 minutes

Assumes

You have called a chat model API

You get

A shared vocabulary, three design questions, a quick-pick table and sizing formulas

Best for

Anyone choosing a design.

Why a model needs memory

The context window limits input and output per request: text and, on some models, images or audio. Fixed weights retain training knowledge, but recalling a past conversation requires the harness (the program running the model) to supply it again.

Memory supplies information or preserves what a turn produced, during it or afterwards: text, records or weight changes. Anthropic calls curating the tokens available at inference time context engineering;1 in this book's terms that is mostly the read path. Claude Code loads instruction files "at the start of every conversation".2

This book judges each design by what reaches the window, its cost in calls, tokens and time, and how it scales with users, memories and concurrent agents.

A bigger window does not replace memory. A 2023 study found lower accuracy for facts in mid-context, even on long-input models.3 Chroma tested 18 models in 2025 and found reliability falls as input grows, even on trivial tasks.4 Sending more input at a fixed token rate costs more, even with prompt caching (discounted reuse of a repeated prefix).5

The four kinds of memory

The CoALA paper splits a language agent's memory into working, episodic, semantic and procedural kinds.6 The "Usually held in" column is this book's mapping.

The four kinds: examples, usual homes and lifetimes

KindWhat it holds, with an exampleUsually held inLasts
WorkingThe live conversation, tool results or scratchpad. Example: the three files a coding agent opened to fix a bug.The context window itself, plus a checkpoint, a saved snapshot of the run.One task or thread.
EpisodicWhat happened, in order, with times. Example: On 14 March the user said, "For this repository, please send small patches."A source-of-truth JSONL log or event table beside summaries; normally appended to, rewritten only for recorded deletions.Until a retention rule or user request deletes it.
SemanticFacts and preferences distilled from experience, not tied to one event. Example: "For this repository, the user prefers small patches."Rows with keyword and vector indexes, a knowledge graph, or wiki pages.Until a newer fact replaces it.
ProceduralHow to do things: rules, instructions, skills. Example: "Run make test before every commit."Versioned files such as CLAUDE.md or a skills folder.7Months, changed by review.

The kinds feed each other: episodes are distilled into semantic facts. In Generative Agents, a periodic reflection step turns observations into higher-level memories.8

The write path and the read path

The memory loop (Figure 1) has two paths: writing creates or updates external records; reading puts selected records in context. Fine-tuning updates weights offline; at inference they influence answers without a separate record lookup.

The write path

  1. Capture. Save each raw turn, tool call or document that retention policy allows, with secrets redacted. A broken index is rebuilt from these records, replaying recorded deletions.
  2. Extract. Decide what is worth keeping. A person can write it; the agent can call a memory tool during the turn, as with Letta's memory edit tools9 or the reference memory server for MCP.10 MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects tools to a model; its reference memory server runs no model, so the calling agent chooses what to save. Or a separate model reads the turn and writes facts, as Mem0 does.11
  3. Store. Write to files, rows, vectors or a graph. An embedding model turns text into an embedding, a list of numbers that places text by meaning. For vectors, record the model, its revision and the text preprocessing, because vectors from different models are not comparable unless a vendor documents a shared space (Chapter 03).
  4. Consolidate. After the turn, merge duplicates, summarize old episodes into facts and settle contradictions. Supersede a fact only when a trusted update covers the same subject, scope and period; otherwise keep both and surface the conflict at read time. Trust the authenticated user for that scope or an authoritative system of record; retrieved text and agent summaries are insufficient. Graphiti marks a superseded fact invalid, not deleted.12
  5. Forget. Expire, evict or delete by rule. Without forgetting, a store only grows. Dated facts expire at their date; user requests and sensitive records are hard-deleted. Track every contributing source ID per fact or summary. Deleting a source removes affected facts, summaries, vectors and cache entries, or rebuilds them from permitted remaining sources. Backups, replicas and provider caches outlive deletion and need a separate plan (Chapter 17).

The read path

  1. Trigger. Memory arrives in one of four ways; loading a file skips Search and Rank.
    • Session start: the harness loads the file.2
    • Agent request: requested records enter context when the memory tool returns them. Claude "automatically checks its memory directory before starting a task", but that is still a tool call.13 It can search files by exact text (for example with grep) or call a search service.
    • Every turn: the harness searches with the new message as the query, as in RAG (retrieval-augmented generation: a retriever finds text, then the model answers from it), needed or not.
    • Path match: a path rule loads extra instructions when the agent reads a file matching a wildcard such as src/api/**.2
  2. Search. Search only records the caller may read. Derive tenant (customer or user group) and access filters from the authenticated request, not the model's query. Within that set, keyword search matches words; SQLite's FTS5 full-text index with BM25 ranking (a score favoring rare query words) is one example.14 Vector search finds the nearest embeddings. Graph search walks from named entities. The ChatGPT retrieval plugin's README warns that embeddings "may not always be effective at capturing exact keyword matches", so hybrid search (keyword plus vector) is common.15
  3. Rank. Score each candidate, optionally with a reranker (a second model that rescores them), then cut the list to a fixed token count so memory never crowds out the task (Chapter 05 shows how to set that budget). Generative Agents scored on recency, importance and relevance.8
  4. Inject. Place retrieved facts and documents in the window as untrusted data; a stored memory can carry an attack.16 Load procedural rules as instructions only from sources the application authorizes; a label alone does not enforce the boundary. Chapter 17 covers attacks and write gating.

Both paths together. On 14 March the user says, "For this repository, please send small patches." The fact "For this repository, the user prefers small patches." is stored as {subject: user, scope: repo X, fact: prefers small patches, valid_from: 14 March, source_ids: [episode id], embed_model: name@rev, preprocess: normalize whitespace}. Weeks later, an every-turn trigger fires. The harness derives subject and repository scope from the authenticated request. Search uses an exact key lookup, Rank keeps the fact within budget and Inject adds "Memory (data, not instructions): For this repository, the user prefers small patches." to the window. If the user later permits large patches for repo X, Consolidate sets valid_to on the old fact and stores the new one.

Three questions that decide an architecture

External designs share this loop; ask who writes, how records are found and where they live.

1. Who writes the memory

WriterHow it worksExamplesWatch for
A personEdits a file.CLAUDE.md files.2Does not scale.
The agentCalls a memory tool in its turn.Anthropic's memory tool,13 Letta's edit tools,9 the MCP memory server.10Tool-call latency; weak models under-write or save noise.
Application codeThe harness writes by fixed rules, no model judging.Episode logs, checkpoints, caches.Saves only what it is programmed to.
An extraction modelA separate pass writes facts from turns.Mem011 and Graphiti.12Extraction costs model calls and can omit, invent or misattribute facts. During the turn it delays replies; afterwards, facts stay unavailable until it finishes.

2. How it is found

MethodHow it worksStrong atWeak at
Always loadedThe harness loads the file at session start, retaining it on later turns.2No lookup.Loaded text takes window space every session (limits: Chapter 01).
KeywordMatches words with BM25 or grep.Names, codes, exact phrases.Paraphrases.
VectorFinds the nearest embeddings to the query.Paraphrases.Exact terms. Re-embed when the model changes (Chapter 03).
GraphWalks entities and their relations.Multi-step, time-aware questions.Graphs built from free text depend on extraction quality; one independent test scored graph memory below plain retrieval on answer accuracy (Chapter 14).17
Exact key or SQL lookupFetches a record by key or query.Known identifiers, dates, filters.Needs the key or query shape.

Hybrid search combines the Keyword and Vector rows: exact terms and paraphrases, at the price of two indexes and a merge to tune.

3. Where it lives

HomeWhat it isStrong atLimit
FilesMarkdown, JSONL, git.Readable, editable, diffable.Without locking or merging, concurrent writers overwrite each other.
A databaseSQLite, PostgreSQL, a vector store, Redis or Valkey with persistence.Indexes, transactions; many writers on a server database (SQLite: one).Server upkeep (except SQLite); often pgvector or sqlite-vec for vectors; backups required.
A cacheMemcached, or Redis used as a cache.Speed, with expiry.Entries are evicted under memory pressure and lost on restart (Redis keeps them only with persistence), so a cache must never hold the only copy (Chapter 10).18
Learned stateNot external: modules that update model state, or internal caches trained offline.Smaller serving footprint in papers.19Research as of November 2026 (Chapter 16).20
WeightsNot external: fine-tuning changes the model's parameters.Nothing to retrieve at read time.Slow, costly updates; facts hard to trace or edit (below).

A Cartridge is an internal cache trained for one document: its authors report 38.6 times smaller serving memory than prompting with that text at matched quality. This book's small test kept the saving, not the quality (Chapter 16). Weights lack fact-level provenance and are hard to edit;21 this book infers similar risks for learned state.

Most systems combine answers. CLAUDE.md is the pure case: person-written, always loaded, in files.2 Mem0 has an extraction model write to a database, found by hybrid search (Chapter 13).11,22 Letta mixes always-in-context blocks with an agent that searches archival memory.9

Quick pick: a starting stack for seven situations

For tasks confined to one session, a window plus checkpoint suffices. Otherwise exclude stacks that fail deployment, isolation or audit needs, then pick below. Rows combine; Chapter 18 has the full flow.

Your situationStart withRead
A coding agent that forgets build and naming rules, or loses its plan when the context resets.Plain files under version control: a short CLAUDE.md for build and naming rules2 and a task file with the plan and next action, reloaded on resume. For shared work, add a task graph recording dependencies between work items (Chapter 01).01, then 17
A personal assistant that should remember one user's preferences for months.Load a small preference file as data. With known scope, fetch rows by user and scope. Consider extraction for free-form turns and semantic search when the lookup key is unknown.13, 03, 05
A support bot with many customers, facts that change over time, and a need to audit.Start with PostgreSQL: dated fact rows and per-tenant isolation (Chapter 08). Research notes or a large document tree to browse.An LLM-maintained wiki (Markdown pages a model keeps current), or a file tree with a model-written summary per folder (Chapter 02).02, 05
A team on a major cloud that will not run a store.A managed cloud memory service, such as Google Memory Bank or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory: the vendor extracts, stores and searches. Check data residency and export first.13, 17
Many agents or users write at once.PostgreSQL or another transactional server database: check versions on update (optimistic locking); re-read and retry within a bound on conflict, then surface persistent conflicts. Separately test concurrent updates to one fact and refusal of cross-tenant reads.08, 17; 11 if the store supports conditional updates

Prompt caching and answer caching (reusing a stored answer when request, permissions and state all match; Chapter 10) cut cost but do not track changing user facts; both complement a memory store.

Sizing reference: bytes, index overhead and calls

Estimate storage and model requests; chapters give measurements. Decimal units: 1 GB = one billion bytes.

FormatSize per scalarBytes per vector (d dimensions)
float324 bytesd x 4. A vector of 1,024 scalars takes 4,096 bytes (Chapter 03), and one of 1,536 scalars takes 6,144 bytes.
float16, bfloat162 bytesd x 2, half of float32 (used for multimodal page embeddings in Chapter 04).
int81 byted x 1, 4 times smaller than float32 (Chapter 03).
binary1 bitceil(d / 8), 32 times smaller than float32 (Chapter 03).

Raw bytes = vectors x dimensions x bytes/scalar. At float32: 1,000,000 x 768 x 4 = 3.072 GB (Chapter 13); 100,000 x 384 x 4 = 153.6 MB (Chapter 05). In PostgreSQL, pgvector vector(d) takes d x 4 + 8 bytes: 1,544 at 384 dimensions.23 Add text, rows, replicas and indexes to these vector sizes.

Index overhead. Overhead varies across stores (Chapter 09 measures one case). Load a sample; measure memory and disk before and after indexing, then divide by vector count. Repeat at several times that size: overhead shifts with index parameters, page fill and fragmentation.

  • Model requests per write = embedding + chat-model requests. Editing an unembedded file needs none (Chapter 01). Count extraction and consolidation per batch, plus triggered embeddings (Chapter 06).
  • Model requests per read = uncached query embeddings + rewriting/search-loop model requests + reranker requests. Count answer generation separately per turn. Exact lookups need none (Chapters 09 and 10; known-entity graph walks in Chapter 14).
  • Tokens = calls x tokens per call, input and output separately. Example: 2,000 chat input, 200 chat output and 200 embedding tokens, tracked separately. See Chapters 13 and 22.
  • Cost, with separate per-million input, output and embedding rates, = (2,000 x input rate + 200 x output rate + 200 x embedding rate) / 1,000,000. Hypothetical rates of $1, $5 and $0.02 per million respectively give $0.003004. Check current prices (Chapters 03 and 10).24,25
  • Time per read = latency along the sequential critical path; parallel calls contribute their slowest latency. Measure p50 and p95 (median and 95th percentile).

Part A

Files and text

The simplest memory is a folder of text files. This part covers files the agent reads directly, task memory for coding agents, and wikis and context databases that a model keeps tidy.

  • 01Flat-file Markdown memory
  • 02The LLM-maintained wiki

Part A · Chapter 01

01

Flat-file Markdown memory

The agent's memory is a folder of plain text files that it reads at session start or opens when needed.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

1 of 5

Running cost

1 of 5

Best for

One developer or a small team with short, stable facts worth a human reading.

What it is

Flat-file memory is a notes folder for an AI agent. A developer writes the build command and naming rules into a repository Markdown file, and the agent reads it instead of being told each session.

No database or embedding model is needed. Anthropic's memory tool documentation describes its storage as "a directory of memory files" that your application stores as it likes.1 Anyone can edit or delete a file; Letta, an agent framework, calls them "simple, universal primitives that both humans and agents can work with using familiar tools".2

Terms new in this chapter

Frontmatter
A block of settings between two --- lines at the top of a Markdown file.
Hook
A script the harness or git runs on an event such as session end or commit.
Worktree
A git feature that checks out a branch in its own folder, so agents can work in parallel.
Item (Beads)
One entry in the Beads task graph: title, status, owner and links to the items blocking it.
Dolt
A SQL database with git-style commits, branches and remotes.

System prompt and RAG are defined in the terms box of Chapter 00, and harness in its first paragraph.

How it works

Two loading models cover almost every tool. In the first, the harness loads the file at session start. Claude Code delivers CLAUDE.md as a user message after the system prompt, loading it "at the start of every conversation".3

In the second, the agent reads files when needed: only an index or file tree stays in view. Anthropic's memory tool works this way: "Claude automatically checks its memory directory before starting a task", then views files under /memories.1

Letta's Context Repositories combine both: the file tree is always in the system prompt, each file has a frontmatter description, and system/ files always load fully.2

OpenClawPlain Markdown in the agent workspace: MEMORY.md for long-term facts, optional USER.md, dated notes in memory/. MEMORY.md loads at session start; today's and yesterday's notes load on a new session.13Self-run agent gateway; MIT.14Flat files for a personal assistant.
GitHub Copilot MemoryFacts the agent writes, not files in your repository. Repository facts are shared and cite code; user preferences follow a person.Hosted by GitHub; paid plans.15Hosted, code-cited memory; not if memory must live in your repository.

Where flat files stop: task state for coding agents

Shared task state, notes about changing code and reusable procedures need extensions to plain notes.

A coding agent needs to know what is left, what blocks what and who has taken which item. A Markdown list can record owners and blockers; a task graph computes ready items and lets an agent claim one atomically. Beads calls itself memory for coding agents that "replaces messy markdown plans with a dependency-aware graph".8

Items occupy a Dolt database under .beads/, with hash-based ids like tasks-dvc (project prefix plus a short hash) that avoid merge collisions. A link says one item blocks another.8 Claims assign work atomically; expired leases need explicit reclaim. Part 3 shows how another session or machine continues the plan.

A framework checkpoint (LangGraph, Chapter 13) saves a run for resumption.16 Beads keeps the plan outside runs for continuation by any agent, anywhere.

Code-linked freshness: notes about code that notice the code changed

“send() never retries” becomes wrong when retries are added, yet the model trusts it. Record the file, symbol and commit supporting each fact; check before use. GitHub Copilot Memory cites code locations for each fact and checks them against the current branch before use; GitHub reports no significant added latency in testing; its docs warn the check can err.15,17 Loom (vendor claim, not checked), an Apache-2.0 ClickHouse tool announced on 13 November 2026, follows a renamed function, flags a note when the function is rewritten, and never rewrites a note itself.18

MEX's README says its code checks cannot tell whether a note still means the right thing; meaning-based checks are future work.10

In plain files, put three frontmatter fields: file and commit are required, and symbol helps whoever reviews a flag. Part 1 step 3 flags notes whose cited file changed since the recorded commit (committed, staged or unstaged),19 or when the file or the commit is missing. Unlike MEX, it only reports. It skips notes without code-link fields, such as repository conventions; review those on a schedule. A rename shows as stale, and any edit to a cited file triggers review. For a valid code link, silence means git found no difference in the index or working tree. It does not validate the fact: retry behavior might have moved into a dependency. Before trusting a flagged note, test the cited behavior and inspect its dependencies; update the fields or delete the note.

Skills: who writes the procedure

A skill is a Markdown file of instructions. Only its description stays in context and the body loads when the skill is invoked, so write the description as a trigger; long procedures cost little until used.20

KindExampleControl point
Human-writtenA person writes SKILL.md in Claude Code.20The author, in version control.
Agent-written, reviewedThe agent proposes; a person or test approves. A pattern, no product checked.Approval, versions, revocation.
Agent-written, automaticmemU 0.11.0-beta.3. The agent chooses to do nothing, patch a skill or create one, and memU indexes it for any connected agent.21No approval step in the README. Beta, not run.

Automatic reuse is the riskiest row: a bad or poisoned procedure is reused unseen (Chapter 17). Default to human-written skills in version control; allow agent-written ones only behind a review or test gate.

Good for and not for

Why teams start with flat files

  • Grep is a real retriever. The Pragmatic Engineer's write-up of an interview with Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, reports that local vector databases and recursive model-based indexing lost to model-driven glob and grep.22 A newsletter anecdote, not a benchmark.
  • Git history comes free. Letta's repositories "are git-backed, so every change to memory is automatically versioned".2

Good for

  • One developer or one small team, working in one repository or with one agent.
  • Short, stable facts people will read: build commands, conventions, preferences.
  • Portability: AGENTS.md is read by several tools, and Markdown notes move between tools with little rework.
  • A few thousand lines across on-demand notes (a rule of thumb, not measured; the lab chooses a separate 200-note threshold); always-loaded files near 200 lines; the MEMORY.md index within its 200-line, 25KB cap.

Not for

  • Many users or agents writing at once and needing isolation. Use a database with access controls.
  • Facts that change over time ("was true until March") or need contradiction handling (Chapter 14).
  • Memory that an index plus grep can no longer navigate reliably.
  • Semantic search over large collections. Letta's archival memory, described as “semantically searchable”, is an alternative.23
  • Task state that several agents claim and resume. Use a task graph such as Beads (in server mode; embedded mode has one writer, see Gotchas).

Use cases

1Solo developer, one repository

Situation
A developer retypes build/test commands and naming rules into each Claude Code session. The API rules matter only when the agent edits src/api.
Why it fits
CLAUDE.md loads at the start of every conversation, so facts arrive with no retrieval step.3 A rule in .claude/rules/ with a paths: field loads only when a matching file is read.3
Pair with
Git for history, an untracked CLAUDE.local.md for personal preferences,3 and /context all to see what loaded.

2Team that mixes coding tools

Situation
A small team shares one repository. Some use Claude Code and some Cursor, and conventions drift as each tool reads its own file.
Why it fits
AGENTS.md is an open format, and its site reports 60k+ open-source projects using it (vendor claim, not checked).4
Pair with
Share conventions in AGENTS.md; keep tool-specific files. Add @AGENTS.md to CLAUDE.md (Claude Code @path import syntax) to load the same file.3

3Your own agent with a notebook between sessions

Situation
You are building an agent on the Anthropic API and want findings to carry between runs, with no database.
Why it fits
The memory tool gives the model a /memories directory it checks before a task; your code picks the storage. The Python SDK ships BetaLocalFilesystemMemoryTool for a local folder (Part 2).1
Pair with
A request handler that rejects paths outside /memories.1

4Coding agent that resumes on another machine

Situation
A developer switches between laptop and desktop mid-feature; the next session needs completed, blocked and pending work.
Why it fits
Beads keeps the plan as a dependency graph and syncs it through the git remote.8 Tested in Part 3: after bd dolt push to a local bare remote, a clone running bd bootstrap reported only “Write login tests” in bd ready.
Pair with
CLAUDE.md for conventions, and one writer per database in embedded mode (see Gotchas).8

Scope and scale

QuestionAnswer
Cost per writeA hand edit needs no model call. In the API loop, the client runs the requested operations; continuing after their results takes another model turn.1 Storage is kilobytes.
Cost per readAlways-loaded files cost input tokens on every model turn. For ASCII English, assuming roughly four characters per token and decimal KB, 25KB is about 6,250 tokens; the line limit may bind first, so count your own index. An on-demand read adds a tool call and the file's tokens afterward.
What breaks firstFor Claude Code auto memory, the index load cap: about 200 one-line entries fit.3 Other tools hit their own context or navigation limits. With several writers there is no isolation or locking (see Gotchas).

Parts 1 and 2 share a terminal and LAB; Part 3 uses another terminal. Part 1. Flat files for Claude Code

  1. Create the files (in $LAB/repo)

    Keep CLAUDE.md short. docs/memory/INDEX.md is a project index, not the auto memory MEMORY.md. The paths: list limits a rule to matching files, and a rule file without it is always loaded.3 INDEX.md link text tells the agent when to open each note.

    bashTested
    mkdir -p .claude/rules docs/memory/decisions
echo "CLAUDE.local.md" >> .gitignore
cat > CLAUDE.md <<'EOF'
## Memory
Before a design decision, read docs/memory/INDEX.md and grep docs/memory for the topic.
EOF
cat > .claude/rules/api.md <<'EOF'
---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
---

# API rules
- All endpoints validate input.
- Error shape: { "code": string, "message": string }.
EOF
cat > docs/memory/decisions/2026-11-20-flat-files.md <<'EOF'
---
type: decision
---

Decision: flat files until >200 stable notes or >1 writer.
Reason: one person keeps these notes and INDEX.md finds each by name.
Revisit if notes are missed.
EOF
cat > docs/memory/INDEX.md <<'EOF'
- [flat files](decisions/2026-11-20-flat-files.md) - why files, not a DB
EOF

Cite the decision note." It should open the linked note.

    claude codeFrom docs, not run

  3. Check a code-linked note

    Add a source file and a note recording its file, symbol and commit.

    bashTested
    mkdir -p src/net && echo "export function send() {}" > src/net/send.ts
git add src && git commit -qm "feat: add send"
cat > docs/memory/send-retries.md <<EOF
---
file: src/net/send.ts
symbol: send
commit: $(git rev-parse HEAD)
---
send() never retries
EOF

    Save this as check_notes.sh and run bash check_notes.sh from the repository root or a session-start hook. Use unquoted values between opening and closing --- lines at the top.

    bashch01-code01 · check_notes.sh33 lines · in this PDF and the companion repositoryTested

    The clean note prints nothing; changing src/net/send.ts adds a STALE line:

    textTested output
    $ bash check_notes.sh
$ echo "// retry" >> src/net/send.ts && bash check_notes.sh
STALE docs/memory/send-retries.md: changed since recorded commit

    STALE is a report, not an exit status. For CI, use flags=$(bash check_notes.sh) && [ -z "$flags" ]: script errors or flags fail the job.

    Inspect and test flagged code. If the note remains true, commit the code, record that hash in the note and rerun. If reverting the code, rerun; the flag should clear. Commit the note separately. Keep cited commits reachable; amend, rebase or squash can invalidate them in clones.

    Separate edge-case suite, not walkthrough files: rerun 23 November 2026, one note per case. Clean notes, omitted/body-only symbol, CRLF, trailing spaces, duplicate keys and empty folders printed nothing.

    CaseSTALE message
    Blank file, missing commit, symbol onlymissing file or commit field
    Unavailable commitcommit unavailable
    Missing path or directory at commitpath absent at recorded commit
    Renamed filepath missing from working tree
    Committed, nested, staged, unstaged; staged then reverted in working treechanged since recorded commit
    Unclosed frontmatterunclosed frontmatter

cat >> docs/memory/INDEX.md <<'EOF'

EOF

Gotchas

Gotcha: caps truncate and conflicts persist

Auto memory loads only the "first 200 lines or 25KB" of its index. If the index is over the limit, the write succeeds, but Claude Code returns an error telling Claude to rewrite it.3 Put detail in topic files. Contradictions persist too: "If two instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily."3

Gotcha: two writers can lose data

Tested: this book reproduced a lost update when two writers read the same old file and replaced it without locking. A controlled schedule proves possibility, not frequency; the test is in the companion repository, benchmarks/stores. Inside the repository, use one writer per checkout, or one branch and worktree each, commit edits and review the merge; git cannot recover an uncommitted edit overwritten in a shared checkout. Auto memory is not protected this way: all worktrees share one folder outside the repository, so run one writing session per repository at a time or turn it off in parallel worktrees. Have every cooperating writer lock the same lock file before reading and hold it through replacement; that prevents lost updates. Write a temporary file beside the target and rename it over the target so readers see no partial file. Neither prevents contradictions.

Beads' default embedded mode (the database runs inside bd) has one writer; several agents need server mode (a separate Dolt server; documented, not tested).8 Divergent pushes were not tested: run bd dolt pull before each session, bd dolt push after it, and do not work on both machines between syncs.

Gotcha: cloned memory is untrusted input

Before the first run, review the instructions your harness can load from a cloned repository, including imports and path-scoped rules, as you would a build script (Chapter 17: memory poisoning).

Open questions

  • Letta's default block limit: the documentation gives the unit (characters) and examples, not a default.7
  • Devin Local per-file size caps: the official page states none.6

Verdict

Verdict: start here

A few Markdown files, a short index and git give memory that people can read, review and move between tools, with no service to run.1,2 Keep CLAUDE.md to 200 lines or fewer and the auto memory index within its 200-line, 25KB cap. Add a task graph such as Beads to share a plan across sessions or machines (run bd reclaim to recover expired claims), and code-linked fields for notes about code that changes.

Move on when several users or writers need isolation (Chapter 08), facts need dates or contradiction handling (Chapter 14), you would rather have the model maintain cross-linked pages than curate by hand (Chapter 02), or an index plus grep misses paraphrased facts (Chapter 05, with embeddings from Chapter 03). Worked example: Chapter 21 keeps a painter's owner-edited procedures as Markdown files beside one SQLite file.

Part A · Chapter 02

02

The LLM-maintained wiki

An agent compiles raw sources into linked Markdown pages, maintaining knowledge across questions.

Maturity

Prototype

Setup effort

2 of 5

Running cost

3 of 5

Best for

One person or small team building lasting, reviewed knowledge on one domain.

What it is

An LLM-maintained wiki is a git repository of Markdown pages an agent maintains from sources. A person reads and reviews it.

Andrej Karpathy described the pattern in a gist titled "LLM Wiki", created on 4 April 2026. It is an "idea file" for an agent such as Claude Code or Codex.1 It contains no code.1

Chapter 01's flat files hold notes. A wiki maintains source-derived claims with cross-references and contradictions. Retrieval over raw chunks (Chapters 03 and 05) rebuilds those links for every question. Two families follow: agent-written Markdown wikis and context databases (OpenViking), which retain files and summarize directories.

Terms new in this chapter

Schema
A file such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md specifying page format and ingest, query and lint steps.
Ingest, query, lint
The three loops: add a source, ask a question, check the wiki's health. Lint is a structural script on every commit plus periodic agent semantic lint.
L0, L1, L2
Three detail levels in a context database: a short abstract (about 256 characters by default), a longer overview (about 4,000 characters), and the original files.

BM25 (keyword ranking), embeddings, vector search and reranking are defined in Chapter 00 and the glossary.

How it works

The gist defines immutable raw sources, an LLM-written wiki (summaries, entity and concept pages, cross-references, overview), and a schema specifying page structure and workflows, its key configuration file.1

Two files anchor three loops. index.md is the catalog the agent reads first, one line per page; log.md is append-only, with a prefix grep can find, such as ## [2026-04-02] ingest | Title.1 During ingest, the agent reads a source, summarizes it, updates the index and related pages; the gist says one source may touch 10 to 15 pages.1 In query, the agent follows index entries to pages and answers with citations. A query writes nothing; keeping an answer counts as ingest, with branching, lint and review. In lint, checks look for contradictions, stale claims, orphans and missing cross-references. The walkthrough tests structural lint; semantic lint is specified but untested.1

Searching a wiki

The gist reports an index serving about 100 sources and hundreds of pages without embeddings.1 Beyond that, add search in this order:

  1. Keep index.md while it finds the right pages on recurring test questions; add search if it recovers missed pages at acceptable cost.
  2. Add rg (ripgrep, exact text) or qmd search (BM25 keyword ranking, no model; qmd is a local search tool) when you know the words.
  3. Add qmd query when you do not: it combines BM25, vector search and LLM reranking, all on your machine, and qmd has a CLI and an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server.2

A vector index over both raw/ and wiki/ can rank generated pages above human-written sources (embedding retrievers show this bias; see Numbers), so check that raw quotes still surface.

The second family: context databases

A context database retains files and adds two model-written directory summaries. OpenViking, an open-source project from Volcengine, presents knowledge, memory and skills as one virtual filesystem under viking://, with ls, read and grep to scan summaries before files.3

L0 lives in a hidden .abstract.md file, L1 in .overview.md, and L2 is the original file, read only when needed. Imported files get wrapper directories and thus directory summaries (Walkthrough, step 8).4 The server needs an embedding model and a summary model, from providers such as Ollama. The summary model uses the vlm (vision-language model) key even when it is text-only.5 The ov client offers ov read for files or summary URIs, ov find for embedded-query vector search over a target directory’s L0/L1/L2 records with optional reranking, and ov search for LLM query planning from session context.6

ProductWhat it storesRun, license, versionPick it when

Good for and not for

Good for

  • One person or small team researching one domain over weeks, such as due diligence.1
  • A few hundred pages or fewer, with reliable index navigation.1
  • Work where every change should be reviewable in git.1
  • A large project directory that needs summaries without hand-written pages (use a context database such as OpenViking).

Not for

  • Large or fast-changing data such as tickets or logs: use retrieval over the raw data (Chapters 03 and 05).
  • Company-wide knowledge with one curator. A vendor argues the pattern does not scale to a company.11
  • Exact recall of original text. A wiki is synthesis, so keep and cite the raw sources.
  • Many writers and no human review. Use a database with access controls (Chapter 08).

Use cases

1One analyst, one research file or decision log

Situation
An investor reads 60 filings, papers and articles on one company over two months, asking what each claims and where they disagree.
Why it fits
Each document is ingested once, within the gist's scale.1 Semantic lint is untested here; its conflict-detection rate is unknown. The schema requires source tags, which structural lint can check.
Pair with
Obsidian as the viewer, raw PDFs in raw/ for exact quotes, and a person reading every diff.

2Several agents on one shared wiki

Situation
Coding and research agents overwrite each other's wording in one knowledge base; their flat memory files scatter and duplicate facts.
Why it fits
Schema and lint give agents shared rules; flat files become an immutable compilation inbox. One home-lab wiki works this way, but its backlog was about four fifths uncompiled (Numbers). It fits only while review keeps pace: cap agents or sources to what the merger can review.
Pair with
Per-agent branches, pre-commit lint, backlog counts and a human merger. Every ingest appends to index.md and log.md, so the second of two parallel branches conflicts there: rebase each branch on main first.

3A large project directory for a coding agent

Situation
A team keeps a few thousand files of API docs, design notes and runbooks. Grep finds the words but not the directory, and nobody will hand-write a wiki of it all.
Why it fits
A context database summarizes each directory at import, so the agent reads an L0 or L1 to pick a subtree, scopes find to it and reads L2 for the hit.3,6
Pair with
A capable summary model, a test that re-import skips unchanged files, and a review of the summaries (see Gotchas).

The retriever-bias studies above cover web-style corpora, so applying them to a wiki is inference.

Scope and scale

QuestionAnswer for an LLM application
JobReplaces re-retrieval with a short index and a few cited pages, so context holds compiled text, not raw chunks.
Cost per writeAn ingest reads one source, rewriting up to 10 to 15 pages.1 Write estimate, 40-line index: 5,000 source tokens, a 1,000-token index (about 40 lines) and 10 pages of 700 tokens yield about 13,000 tokens in, 7,000 out for full rewrites. OpenViking made 17 records; step 7 measures re-import times. Model-call counts were not measured.
Cost per readWiki reads need no embedding or reranking model; budget separately for agent selection and answer turns. Read estimate, 300-line index: 300 lines × about 25 tokens plus 3 × 700-token pages yield about 9,600 tokens in. qmd query runs local models (61.7 seconds for expansion on the first CPU query, measured here in step 4). OpenViking find embeds the query and can rerank results; search also calls an LLM to plan queries.
StorageMarkdown and git history, kilobytes per page. qmd adds a SQLite index and about 2.2 GB of GGUF files (a local-model format). OpenViking adds a server, a vector index and two Ollama models (about 1.6 GB here).
GrowthMore agents mean more branches and a person merging; when volume outruns review, the backlog builds.
Breaks first, then moveAt 300 index lines the index alone is about 7,500 tokens and the read about 9,600, so the limit is finding the right line, not fitting it. Then add qmd, or move to retrieval over the raw data (see the Verdict).

Setup walkthrough

Steps 1 to 4 build and search a wiki (schema, lint, git hook). Rerun: 23 November 2026, after the research cutoff; Ubuntu (32-thread shared consumer CPU), git 2.53.0, ripgrep 15.2.0, Node 24.22.3, npm 11.19.1 and qmd 2.9.0, plus uv, Docker, curl and sudo. Steps 5 to 8 import three files: OpenViking 0.5.5, containerized Ollama 0.40.16, Python 3.12.16, models nomic-embed-text and qwen3:1.7b (digest prefixes 0a109f422b47 and 8f68893c685c), also on CPU. Semantic lint remains untested; see AGENTS.md.

Copy chapter files from the companion repository outside the lab, retaining bin/wiki-lint, and run bash lab.sh there. By default only wiki and ripgrep run; enable WITH_QMD=1 and WITH_OPENVIKING=1 beforehand. Step 6 replaces ov.conf placeholder __LAB__ with the lab path.

qmd, npm, uv, OpenViking and XDG state share one lab folder; step 9 deletes it and owned containers. Outside remain the Ollama image and machine-wide model lock (gpu filename), which serializes either opt-in. An existing-folder refusal creates nothing. The exit trap checks ownership after success or failure. Defect: even wiki-only cleanup inspects Docker by name and invokes sudo; an unrelated same-name container can block cleanup. It should track only a successfully created container ID and remove wiki-only files unprivileged (repair not tested).

Gotchas

Gotcha: repeated rewrites corrupt documents

DELEGATE-52 found agentic tool use did not reduce long-workflow editing corruption; larger documents, longer interactions and distractor files worsened it.12 Repeated wiki rewrites resemble that workload (inference; wikis were not tested). Review every agent rewrite. Structural lint catches missing index lines and broken links, not dropped caveats. Keep raw sources immutable and review diffs against them, applying step 2’s changed-claim checks and [UNVERIFIED] rule. Human review is the tested control; semantic-lint detection is unmeasured.

Gotcha: the compile backlog

Maintenance shifts effort from notes to schema and lint.1 Count un-ingested sources and unreviewed ingest branches. If either grows, stop sources or narrow scope until ingest and review catch up.

Gotcha: generated summaries can be wrong

The 1.7B abstract omitted feedback.md despite full sampling (step 8). The decisions overview invented Postgres reasons ("performance, scalability, and the existing infrastructure") and an invalid link, viking://input_sample_f1, rejected by the server. The file gives SKIP LOCKED, team size, volume and a revisit threshold, not those invented reasons. Summaries varied; retrieval found the files. Use a stronger summary model (Chapter 06); abstracts are pointers. Spot-check L0/L1 for three known files: passing summaries invent no facts or links.4

Gotcha: summaries can be sampled and pending

OpenViking’s default sample covers 32 direct children (semantic.overview_sample_limit).4 Above that limit, parent overviews lag until pending changes reach 10% of entries (semantic.freshness_refresh_ratio); no timed refresh is promised.4 Read raw .overview.md (step 8); ov abstract and search previews hide metadata. Positive pending_child_changes means lag; positive unsampled_entries means skipped children, requiring direct reads. The three-file lab cannot test sampling.

Unverified: open questions

  • Where cross-linking pays. A vendor says 100 to 200 notes, as "community calibration"; the post gives no measurement.18
  • Whether the OpenViking gains on LoCoMo (a long-conversation memory benchmark, see the glossary) hold outside the maintainers' evaluation. They report 80 to 83% for three agents versus 24 to 57% on built-in memory, using Volcengine’s Doubao models. Not reproduced here; the local test used a 1.7B model.3
  • The obsidian-llm-wiki retrieval claim. Its README compares Personalized PageRank with nearest-neighbor retrieval on a private vault, not a public benchmark. Its scoring denominator is unspecified.9

Verdict

Verdict: a good second step after flat files

Pick a wiki when one person or small team maintains a few hundred pages of lasting domain knowledge with diff review and lint. Linked, dated, source-cited pages remain readable and revertible without retrieval infrastructure.1 Evaluate a context database when index navigation fails recurring questions and you can run a server. Untested large-directory overviews require checks at every level. The tested 1.7B model failed (Gotchas). Before adopting, check a stronger model (Chapter 06) and time unchanged/edited re-imports on your corpus.

Add qmd when the index misses pages on recurring test questions, retrieval over the raw data (Chapters 03 and 05) when the data is large or changes fast, and a database with access controls (Chapter 08) when many writers need isolation. Skip the wiki if you cannot keep up the lint and review loop.

B

Part B

Vectors and retrieval

Search by meaning turns text and images into vectors. This part covers the embedding models and the retrieval techniques that decide what the agent finds.

  • 03Text embeddings
  • 04Multimodal embeddings
  • 05Retrieval techniques

Part B · Chapter 03

03

Text embeddings

A model turns text into numbers so a program can find it by meaning.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

2 of 5

Running cost

1 of 5

Best for

Anyone whose agent must find notes by meaning, on a CPU-only box or through a hosted API.

What it is

An embedding is a model-computed number list for finding notes by meaning: a search for "the tax thing from March" can land on a note that says "quarterly filing", although the two share no words.

Similar meanings point in similar directions; the program compares texts by their angle (cosine similarity; a smaller angle scores higher).

The list is a vector; dimensions count its entries: 1,024 dimensions means 1,024 numbers per text. The two smallest models tested, bge-small-en-v1.5 (bge-small below) and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (MiniLM below), return 384, and the largest Qwen3-Embedding model returns 4,096.1

The model neither answers nor remembers; the vector store holds memory (Part D). Images: Chapter 04.

Terms new in this chapter

MTEB
An embedding benchmark suite with several versions.
nDCG@10
Normalized discounted cumulative gain at 10 rewards ranking relevant results near the top. Scores here are the usual 0 to 1 value times 100.
Matryoshka (MRL)
Training that makes a vector’s first k numbers usable alone.
Scalar and binary quantization (of stored vectors)
Shrinking vectors with 8-bit integers or single bits.
Prefix
A short instruction placed before the text, which some models expect on queries, documents or both.

How it works

Save each chunk beside its embedding. Recall it by embedding the question with the same model and fetching the nearest vectors. Most models read the whole text at once: each token reflects words before and after it. They pool (combine) token vectors, usually by averaging; the model card specifies how. Some, such as Qwen3-Embedding, read left to right and take the last token's vector, which has seen the whole input. Servers may ask for a pooling mode (step 5).

Chunk at paragraph or heading boundaries near 300 tokens to balance precision and prompt cost, or at the model’s lower context limit; MiniLM truncates at 256 tokens. Overlap only when sentences often cross a boundary. Record chunking and token limits as corpus metadata.

Dense, sparse and multi-vector

Almost every model here is dense. BGE-M3 can produce all three kinds.2

KindWhat is stored per textWhat it is good at
DenseOne fixed-length floating-point vector.Meaning matching by nearest-neighbor search, usually cosine. Smaller than multi-vector storage.
SparseA weight for each vocabulary term the text uses. Size depends on non-zero term count and index encoding.A learned keyword index; rare exact terms still match.2
Multi-vectorOne vector per token. Each query token is scored against its best-matching document token and the scores are summed (late interaction, MaxSim).Better recall on long, detailed queries. At equal dimensions and precision per vector, storage grows roughly with the token count.2

pgvector 0.8.7 stores a dense vector in 4d + 8 bytes and a sparse vector in 8n + 16 bytes, where d is the dimension count and n the number of non-zero weights. At d = 1024, a sparse vector is smaller for n ≤ 510 non-zeros (8n + 16 < 4104; equal at 511). With 100 non-zeros it takes 816 bytes against 4,104. Sizes exclude table and index overhead.3

Matryoshka truncation

Matryoshka lets you keep 256 of 1,024 dimensions at a small quality cost. Jina v5 small supports sizes spanning 32 to 1,024; use a listed size.5 The EmbeddingGemma 2 card reports its MTEB English score falling from 68.46 at 768 dimensions to 67.78 at 256 (0.68 points lost for a third of the size) and to 65.68 at 128.7 Tested: on these three tasks, cutting EmbeddingGemma 2 from 768 to 256 dimensions cost 2.36 nDCG@10 points (95% interval 1.78 to 2.97): a mean of 60.73 fell to 58.37. The published figure averages the whole English suite.

Code will slice any vector, so cut only a model trained for it, to card-listed sizes; re-normalize afterwards.

int8 and binary quantization

Scalar int8 keeps one byte per number and binary keeps one bit. Jina says its v5 vectors survive binary quantization.5 Recall loss depends on the model and data; this book has no measurement of it. Compare float32 and quantized retrieval on identical held-out questions and corpus. Count answering notes in the top k chunks your agent reads; accept only tolerable loss. Top-10 overlap shows changed rankings but is not the acceptance test. With binary, fetch 10 times more candidates (an unsourced starting estimate; measure) and rescore with float32 or int8 vectors. Fit int8 ranges per dimension on a representative sample, save them with a calibration ID and reuse them for every later write; changing them means requantizing.

Vector bytes for a 1,024-dimension model (decimal MB and GB, no index overhead; method in the Chapter 00 sizing reference):

FormatBytes per vector8,000 vectors1,000,000 vectors
float32, 1,024 dimensions4,09632.8 MB4.1 GB
int8, 1,024 dimensions1,0248.2 MB1.0 GB
binary, 1,024 dimensions1281.0 MB128 MB
int8, cut to 256 dimensions2562.0 MB256 MB

Query and document prefixes

Asymmetric models embed questions and passages differently. Omitting a prefix silently lowers quality. Ollama's documentation does not say it adds one, so add it in separate query and document functions.23

  • Qwen3-Embedding expects a task instruction on the query side. Its card says instructions typically add 1 to 5 points and recommends writing them in English.1
  • The EmbeddingGemma 2 card says omitting its prefix still works but lowers precision, and that prefixes apply to text only.7

When vectors can and cannot be compared

Compare matching models, revisions and preprocessing. Separate coordinate systems remain incomparable despite equal dimensions. bge-small-en-v1.5 and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 both return 384 dimensions, so a store takes either, yet the walkthrough scored one sentence across both at 0.2608, a plausible number with no meaning.

Two exceptions apply. A model trained with distinct query and document prefixes expects that difference: use each prefix as its card specifies (see Query and document prefixes).1,7 Two vendors also document shared family spaces:

  • Voyage states that all embeddings from its 4 series are compatible, so a large model can index and a lighter one answer queries.12
  • Cohere states that embed-v5.0-pro and embed-v5.0-fast share one space, and recommends indexing with Pro and querying with Fast.17

For shared families, record the space identity and models separately; this lab checks one model. Otherwise treat the model name, revision, prefix, cut length (Matryoshka dimensions kept), quantization and, for int8, the calibration ID as one identity recorded beside every vector. Search quantized vectors only with the scoring the store documents for that format: for binary vectors (one bit per dimension; step 6), Hamming distance (counting differing bits), never float cosine on the packed bytes.

Re-indexing

The identity identifies stale vectors. A supported Matryoshka cut needs no model call on saved full-precision vectors: slice, re-normalize and rebuild the store's index. Otherwise, changed spaces or document preprocessing require re-embedding every chunk. A change to the query instruction alone leaves stored vectors valid: version it and retest retrieval. To re-embed:

  1. Build a second index; preserve the old one.
  2. Embed every chunk again at the first ingest's cost: 1 billion tokens is about $20 on text-embedding-3-small and about $130 on text-embedding-3-large.15,16 For a local model the cost is wall-clock time.
  3. Pause writes before backfilling, or use a snapshot and replay writes, edits and deletions through a recorded cutover point. Check coverage, compare real questions on both indexes, switch reads and retain the old index. During the rollback window, apply writes, edits and deletes to both with their respective encoders, or log changes and catch up the old index before reverting. A deprecated hosted model forces it.

Picks by situation

Good for and not for

Good for

  • Finding a note by its meaning when the question shares no words with it.
  • Checking a new memory against stored ones before writing, to avoid duplicates.
  • A corpus of thousands of chunks on a CPU-only machine.

Not for

  • Exact strings such as error codes: use a keyword or sparse index (Chapter 05).
  • Choosing the current fact by similarity alone: filter on validity dates or a superseded flag first (Chapter 14).
  • A commercial product built on a non-commercial license, or a setup that cannot record the model identity next to each vector.

Use cases

1 8,000 blog passages on a mini PC

Situation
A writer searches eight years of posts: 8,000 passages on a CPU-only PC.
Why it fits
At 1,024 dimensions, vectors fit in memory: 32.8 MB float32 or 8.2 MB int8. Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B embedded 6 short notes in 1.17 seconds on 4 CPUs (Numbers): about 26 minutes for 8,000; real passages are far longer, so plan for hours (estimate) and time 200 first.
Pair with
SQLite or pgvector for storage (Chapters 12 and 08), and a reranker from Chapter 05.

2 Personal notes search

Situation
A few thousand personal Markdown notes need meaning-based search, as in the opening filing example.
Why it fits
MiniLM returns 384 numbers per chunk with a few sentence-transformers lines.10
Pair with
Chapter 01 flat files for the notes, and grep for exact words.

3 Deduplicate memories before writing

Situation
An agent saves "User lives in Paris", then "The user is based in Paris". Near copies accumulate.
Why it fits
Embed each new memory and find its nearest neighbor (one call per write). Before merging, check entity, claim, polarity and time, since "User no longer lives in Paris" is a near match to keep. Set the threshold on labeled pairs; the walkthrough's question-to-note scores (0.7480 and 0.6636) only show that related text stays well below 1.0.
Pair with
A memory framework (Chapter 13) and a small model that decides merge or keep (Chapter 06).

4 Support docs in several languages

Situation
A team keeps help articles in English, Spanish and Japanese, and users ask in any of them.
Why it fits
Qwen3-Embedding has multilingual MTEB scores; BGE-M3 also offers sparse output.1,2 One index holds all languages; cross-lingual retrieval (Japanese questions finding English articles) remains untested. Check your pairs.
Pair with
Hybrid search with a keyword index, from Chapter 05.

Numbers

Sources were checked through 22 November 2026; the walkthrough reran on 23 November 2026. Timings are single observations on a shared 32-thread CPU (containers limited to 2 or 4 CPUs, no GPU), including local HTTP overhead. Larger models need a RAM and latency check on the target CPU.

Tested: three English tasks (SciFact, NFCorpus, ArguAna; 2,029 queries/model) ran on an 8 GB NVIDIA GPU: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, Jina v5 small, Harrier 270M and 0.6B, EmbeddingGemma 2, BGE-M3 and bge-small. Of 21 model-task pairs, 19 have published scores; 18 lie within the local 95% interval (resample queries; recompute task means). The exception is Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B on ArguAna (69.15 locally, 70.97 published). Harness: benchmarks/mteb. A Mac run (benchmarks/mteb-large; Apple M3 Ultra, 96 GB) used Qwen3-Embedding-4B at 8-bit and the 8B at 4-bit weights, which may shift scores. Five of six published scores lie within intervals; 8B/ArguAna differs: 74.37 locally (1,406 queries, 95% interval 72.89 to 75.88) against 76.85 published. Harrier 27B was skipped for time, so its 74.3 was not reproduced. Intervals describe query variability, not repeat runs.

GPU and Mac encoding throughput was not isolated by the benchmark harness; no sourced speed figure was found.

Measurements made for this chapter (scores and prices above)

FigureWhat it measuresEvidence
153,600, 38,400, 4,800 bytes100 vectors of 384 dimensions as float32, int8 and packed binary, confirming the ratios.Measured once
373.1 texts per secondtext-embeddings-inference (TEI, Hugging Face's embedding server) cpu-1.9, bge-small-en-v1.5, 100 short synthetic texts in 0.268 s, 2 CPUs, shared host.Measured once

Scope and scale

Vectors cost no context tokens; only retrieved chunks do. A write is one embedding pass per chunk, with no generation call; a read is one pass plus the tokens of the top results: five chunks of 300 tokens add about 1,500 prompt tokens (estimate).

No source gives a maximum count for scanning every vector (brute-force search). Check scan latency against your read budget and embedding throughput against your write rate.

  • Scan latency. Storage grows linearly (Chapter 00 sizing reference). At 1,024 dimensions, 10,000 memories take 41 MB as float32 and 100 such users take 4.1 GB, a million vectors. At an assumed 10 GB/s, reading an isolated 41 MB user partition takes at least about 4 ms; reading all 4.1 GB takes at least 0.41 s (estimates). Time the actual filtered query, including scoring.
  • Embedding throughput. Ten agents writing 20 chunks per second need 200 sustained. Measured: 373.1 texts per second (bge-small, 2 CPUs) and about 5.1 per second (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B through Ollama, 4 CPUs), both on short texts; 300-token chunks will be slower. Replay your own chunk lengths.

Move to a store with an index (Chapters 08 or 11) when a scan misses your latency budget, to Chapter 05 when exact terms matter, and to Chapter 14 when facts change.

Setup walkthrough

Requires Linux, Bash, Docker, curl, GNU coreutils and Python venv; macOS needs a Linux VM. Steps 1 to 3 build a stored search with Ollama. Steps 4 to 7 are optional: TEI, llama.cpp, quantization and an EmbeddingGemma 2 precision check. The 23 November 2026 rerun used the shared host above, with Docker, Ollama 0.40.16 (0.40.17 was published on 10 November 2026), TEI image cpu-1.9, llama.cpp image server-b12464, sentence-transformers 6.3.0 and Python 3.14.4. Timings are observations.29

Gotchas

  • EmbeddingGemma 2: avoid float16 (Local models).
  • A missing prefix can silently lower precision (Query and document prefixes).
  • Equal dimensions do not make cross-model cosine meaningful (When vectors can and cannot be compared).
  • TEI defaults to at most 32 texts per request (step 4).

Gotcha: the context claim differs by source

The Qwen3-Embedding card gives 32,768 tokens; Ollama’s 4b tag differs at 40K (0.6b shows 32K).1,25 Count prefixed tokens; obey documented and server limits. Test retrieval before relying on extensions.

Unverified: open questions

  • Current MTEB No. 1 and GPU/Mac speed.
  • Cohere embed-v5.0 and official embed-v4.0 prices; EmbeddingGemma 300M license (gated card).

Verdict

Verdict: small, local, labeled

Follow Picks by situation: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B handles occasional writes, about 5.1 short notes per second on 4 CPUs.1,25 For throughput or tight storage, test bge-small’s held-out recall. Record vector identity; check recall before int8 (Chapter 17).

For multilingual GPU work, time 200 representative chunks before choosing 4B/8B; GPU throughput remains unmeasured. Add keyword search and a reranker for exact terms (Chapter 05). Chapters 21 to 23 use 1,024-dimensional Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B notes for a painter, doctor’s office and homebuilder.

Part B · Chapter 04

04

Multimodal embeddings

Shared vectors let a sentence find a picture across text, images, screenshots and video.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

3 of 5

Running cost

3 of 5

Best for

Agents that must find screenshots, photos, slides or video from a text description.

What it is

Multimodal models embed text, images, screenshots, video and sometimes audio in shared vectors (Chapter 03). Similar meanings sit close across forms.

Qwen3-VL-Embedding, released in January 2026, accepts "text, images, screenshots, and videos, as well as inputs containing a mixture of these modalities".1,2 Google's Gemini Embedding 2 maps "text, images, video, audio, and documents" into one space.3

Terms new in this chapter

Modality
An input type: text, image, video or audio.
Modality gap
Matching text and image vectors in separate regions.
Multi-vector
Many vectors per item (Chapter 03), here per page patch (small image tile). MaxSim sums query tokens’ best patch scores.
Backbone
Pretrained core. Adapters add weights, sometimes separately licensed.
Interleaved
Text and images mixed in one input.
nDCG@5
Normalized discounted cumulative gain at five: relevance versus the ideal top five; 0 to 100 here (Chapter 05).
bfloat16
Two-byte float with float32's exponent range and fewer precision bits. float16: same bytes, narrower range. Stored-vector precision is independent (Chapter 03).

How it works

On write, embed items and save vectors and paths. On read, embed the question, search, optionally rerank and pass matching originals to the model.

One vector or many per page

Single-vector models compress pages into one vector; ColPali and ColQwen2 keep one vector per patch. The ColPali authors call this "ColBERT-style multi-vector representations" and introduced ViDoRe (visual document retrieval) to argue that embedding page images beats indexing text from optical character recognition (OCR), which can lose the link between a chart label and its bar.8,9 Storage is the cost. ColQwen2 caps a page at 768 visual patches8 of 128 numbers each, plus a few special text-token vectors; its card shows an example page with 755 vectors.8 The table sizes one million pages in float16 (two bytes per number).

Worked storage arithmetic, before any index overhead

LayoutArithmeticPer pageOne million (decimal GB)
Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B, 4096 numbers4096 x 2 bytes8,192 B8.2 GB
Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, 2048 numbers2048 x 2 bytes4,096 B4.1 GB
Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, 512 numbers512 x 2 bytes1,024 B1.0 GB
ColQwen2, 768 patches768 x 128 x 2 bytes196,608 B196.6 GB

At 768 vectors per page, illustrative multi-vector storage is 24 times the 8B single vector and 48 times the 2B one. The 2B model truncates anywhere from 64 to 2048 numbers; no source reports quality at 512.1 Qdrant supports multi-vector MaxSim scoring since v1.10.0;21 Chapter 11 gives the recipe.

The reranker that pairs with it

Reranking adds one model pass per query/candidate pair. Qwen3-VL-Reranker (2B and 8B) takes mixed text and image pairs.4 Re-score a few dozen candidates on GPU; on CPU, skip reranking or cap it at three to five (about 13 seconds per screenshot pair below). ViDoRe V3 reports gains from text rerankers;22 only vendor tables measure visual reranking,4 so require better top-five hits on your queries (Chapter 05).

One backbone, and the modality gap

CLIP-style models train separate text and image encoders to place matching captions and images near each other; Qwen3-VL-Embedding uses one backbone.4 Whether the gap in two-encoder models20 also appears in this model is unmeasured. A gap could favor captions over matching screenshots. Test whether the top five change before mixing them in one index.

The alternative: caption first

Caption on write for editable text embeddings (Chapter 03), adding a generation call. Retrieval sees only captioned details.

Separate caption collections use their own embedder. Merge ranks (Chapter 05); scores across embedding spaces are incomparable.

The 50-query test

  1. Test five layouts on identical items: images only (multimodal embedder), captions only (text embedder), rank fusion over those separate collections, one mixed index using the multimodal embedder for images, captions and queries deduplicated by item id, and one vector encoding image plus caption jointly.
  2. Write 50 requests before seeing captions. Record target ids for exact lookup; for descriptive search, pool candidates and judge relevance blind to route.
  3. Fetch five distinct item ids per route; count requests with targets or relevant items among them.
  4. Report paired wins/losses. Prefer simplicity unless the alternative answers about five more of the same 50 requests correctly within the top five. This deployment margin is not a significance test.

Good for and not for

Good for

  • Search boxes where people describe an image, a slide or a moment in words.
  • Content whose meaning is visual: screenshots, charts, slides, photos with no useful text.
  • A picture plus a line describing it, stored as one vector; if the text is unrelated, embed the image alone (Use case 2).
  • Local-first: Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B has open weights; about 4 GB in bfloat16 (2B parameters x 2 bytes; computed, not measured).1
  • Documents where OCR loses the layout: on ViDoRe V3's tested datasets, visual retrievers beat its textual baselines.22

Not for

  • A text-first collection: a text embedder scores higher on text (Chapter 03).1
  • Millions of pages without a multi-vector budget: 196.6 GB per million pages in float16.
  • Speech inside video: Gemini Embedding 2 ignores the audio track, so send it separately (see Gotchas).3
  • Tracking where objects are over time: an image embedding finds a matching view, not a position. Extract positions into structured records for spatial tracking.

Use cases

1Screenshot memory for a computer-use agent

Situation
A computer-use agent seeks a failed-deploy screen outside its context window.
Why it fits
Qwen3-VL-Embedding retrieves screenshots. Save timestamps, tasks and last actions with images; retrieve past states by text intent instead of replaying history.1 Neither the model card nor the paper tests agent screenshot tasks.
Pair with
Task/window filters and reranking. Re-observe before acting: retrieved screens show past state.

2A social feed where each post is a picture and one line

Situation
An assistant searches a million posts for "dog on a beach at sunset", but the post text is an unrelated joke.
Why it fits
Qwen3-VL-Embedding can fuse text and image into one vector, but the joke would pull it away from "dog on a beach". Embed the image alone, and add the fused vector only if the 50-query test shows a clear gain over image-only.1
Pair with
A separate text embedding of the line for text-only queries, merged as in Chapter 05.

3Slide and PDF search without OCR

Situation
An LLM answers from thousands of slide decks, but OCR scrambles chart labels and text retrieval misses pages.
Why it fits
ColQwen2 embeds page images. ViDoRe V3 reports stronger visual retrieval on its tested datasets.22 At 768 vectors, a 200-page deck needs about 39 MB before indexing.
Pair with
A reranker. For slow scoring, shortlist before MaxSim with one Qwen3-VL-Embedding vector per page. For limited storage, keep only those vectors and rerank originals with Qwen3-VL-Reranker-2B; measure latency.

4A laptop archive that stays offline

Situation
An offline laptop assistant searches 10,000 field photos and voice notes.
Why it fits
EmbeddingGemma 2 supports all these inputs locally. The 440M parameters (text and images) or 740M (all modalities) take about 0.88 GB or 1.48 GB of bfloat16 weights before runtime memory, or about 1.76 GB or 2.96 GB in float32. Computed from the card; EmbeddingGemma 2 was not run.11
Pair with
Local files and SQLite (Chapter 12), a 768-number vector per item, and date/project filters. Test recall on real photos and speech before choosing a smaller vector.

5Finding a moment in a video

Situation
Search hour-long screen recordings for "the part where the error dialog appears".
Why it fits
Gemini Embedding 2 samples at most 32 frames per video.3 Size clips, up to 120 seconds, for the shortest event to catch; shorter clips give denser sampling. Sampling all 32 frames averages one per 3.75 seconds for 120-second clips (30 clips an hour), one per second for 32-second clips (about 113 clips an hour). Neither guarantees catching brief dialogs. Store start times.
Pair with
The audio track, embedded as audio on its own (see Gotchas).3

Own measurement

Tested here: ViDoRe V3 subset (318 English queries, 1,110 pages), not MMEB-V2 or ViDoRe V2, not comparable with vendor figures, including Nomic Embed Multimodal 7B's 58.8. nDCG@5 was 58.77 (95% bootstrap interval over queries, 55.39 to 62.20) for Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B and 55.17 (51.64 to 58.74) for Nomic Embed Multimodal 7B. Both used 4-bit weights (compressed; Chapter 06), which may lower scores. Paired difference: 3.60 points (95% paired bootstrap interval 1.00 to 6.19, 10,000 resamples of shared query ids), so Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B scored higher here. A separate bfloat16 2B run scored 54.98 (51.36 to 58.55) on this subset; runtime and precision differ. Companion: benchmarks/mteb-large/vidore.py; the folder also holds text-embedding runs.

Scope and scale

Keep paths current; replace or delete vectors with originals, and re-embed the collection when changing models. The answer model sees selected images or clips; its resolution and frame policy set token costs.4

  • Per write: one embedding pass per item, no generation call. Per read: one query embedding plus one pair-scoring pass per reranked candidate (Chapter 00).
  • Storage: raw float16 sizes follow the table above (method in Chapter 00). Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B in float16 needs 4.1 GB for 100 users at 10,000 memories each, before originals, payloads and indexes.
  • Memory: budget about 4 GB of bfloat16 weights per independently loaded Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B. For shared instances, measure peak memory at intended concurrency.

Benchmark real page sizes and concurrency; full-page GPU memory and latency are unmeasured. Use captions if visuals add little (Chapter 03), fewer reranking candidates for latency (Chapter 05), or a dedicated vector store for index RAM (Chapter 11). No source gives an item-count cutoff.

Setup walkthrough

Create three PNGs, embed them and a query, store vectors in Qdrant, filter, rerank and return the original filename. Start a child Bash shell; paste shell blocks in order (or source setup.sh) to preserve directories and exports. Failed commands stop it. Needs Linux x86-64, Docker 29.1.3, uv 0.13.9, Git, curl, GNU time (/usr/bin/time), internet, about 16 GB disk and 4 GB free RAM; Google Chrome for optional screenshot timing. Public models; authentication optional.

Lab verification (run date unrecorded; not verified against the 22 November 2026 research cutoff) on an x86-64 CPU (32 logical CPUs, 8 PyTorch threads), bfloat16, CUDA disabled. Versions: Python 3.12.16, PyTorch 2.8.0, torchvision 0.23.0, Transformers 4.57.1, qwen-vl-utils 0.0.14, SciPy 1.18.1, Pillow 11.3.0, accelerate 1.10.1, huggingface-hub 0.36.2, Qdrant 1.15.4 and client 1.15.1. Synthetic plumbing test; document recall and agent usefulness untested. Checkpoints and helpers pinned.4

Gotchas

Gotcha: pgvector index limits

pgvector indexes up to 2,000 numbers per vector, or 4,000 with its two-byte halfvec type (Chapter 08). Use halfvec for 2048 or 3072; truncate 4096.

Gotcha: Gemini Embedding 2 media and page caps

For frame density and clip length, see Use case 5. In Gemini Embedding 2, "Audio tracks are not processed in video files".3 A 40-page deck must be split at 6 pages per request.3

Gotcha: hosted availability varies

Alibaba Model Studio Qwen models are region-bound with separate keys.19 Pinecone (November 2026) says Gemini Embedding 2 "is only offered as a text model today" in its integration, though its native API takes images.25 Check the surface you call.

Gotcha: EmbeddingGemma 2 precision

Run EmbeddingGemma 2 in bfloat16 where supported and float32 otherwise (Chapter 03); the card warns that float16 can produce NaNs.11 Check finite vectors and known query/item pairs before indexing.

Verdict

Verdict: one small model, then measure

Pick it when remembered content is visual: screenshots, photos, slides, short video. Start with Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B. The walkthrough checks plumbing. For latency decisions, time identical queries, candidates and caps end to end in fresh and resident processes. The ViDoRe V3 subset scored 54.98 for 2B versus 58.77 for 8B; precision and runtime differed. Run the 50-query test. Choose CPU, GPU or hosted against a preset latency/cost budget using warm real screenshots; include hosted network time and reranking. Use a page model such as ColQwen2 for slides and scans. If weights exceed local memory, consider hosted inference (Gemini Embedding 2 for audio or PDF) only if the originals may leave the device. Offline, test EmbeddingGemma 2 (card claims; not run here).1,8,11,24

Use captions and a text embedder (Chapter 03) for word-focused queries or when captions keep needed details. For audits, retain originals and provenance; captions are inspection aids, not proof. If patch vectors exceed budget, try one visual vector per page with reranking (Use case 3). Store vectors in pgvector (see Gotchas and Chapter 08) or a dedicated vector store (Chapter 11), and merge text results (Chapter 05). Worked example: Chapter 23; page multi-vectors: Chapter 11.

Part B · Chapter 05

05

Retrieval techniques

Retrieval turns a question into a short ranked list of stored notes: scope, search two ways, merge, rerank, then measure.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

2 of 5

Running cost

2 of 5

Best for

Anyone whose memory store is too big for the prompt.

What it is

Retrieval picks the few saved notes that fit an assistant's prompt from thousands stored.

Each search returns n; merging yields N distinct candidates; a reranker orders them and the top k enter the prompt. Anthropic uses N=150 and k=20.1 Set k from the context budget; those figures illustrate one operating point.

Terms new in this chapter

Candidate pool
Distinct first-stage results; N cannot exceed summed search limits: 2n for two searches of n each.
Reranker (cross-encoder)
Scores question and chunk jointly, per pair at query time, unlike stored-vector comparison. Apply it only to the pool; sorting scores is reranking.
Recall@k
The share of known-correct notes in the top k results.
MRR
Mean reciprocal rank: average 1/rank of each question's first correct result; 0 for no hit within the evaluated list.
RRF
Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Merges lists by rank alone.
MMR
Maximal Marginal Relevance. Balances relevance against similarity to chosen results.
HyDE
Hypothetical Document Embeddings. An LLM drafts a plausible answer, which is embedded and searched instead of, or alongside, the question.
Average precision
Sum precision at correct results' ranks, divide by the known-correct count, then average across questions for mean average precision (MAP). Early hits score higher.

BM25 (keyword ranking) is defined in Chapter 00/glossary. Agentic search is iterative, model-directed retrieval through tools.

How it works

Build the golden set

A golden set pairs questions with answering note IDs. Test exact IDs, semantic matching through paraphrases sharing no words, and multi-answer recall through two-note questions. Compare identical questions:

  • recall@k, measured on the pool as well as the final list. Pool recall is the share found among all candidates; it caps later stages and shows whether reranking can help.
  • MRR, which rewards putting one right answer first.
  • Mean average precision (MAP), used in Numbers, rewards finding several right answers early.

With 20 equally weighted questions, one moves mean recall by up to 0.05; smaller gaps need more examples.

Techniques at a glance

Scope is mandatory before search limits (Scope before the limit). Match other failures below; RAPTOR and soft forgetting follow.

TechniqueFixesCostsAdd it when
