Heading-aware chunkingAnswers cut in half or cut off from their subject.A parser for your formats.Documents have headings or turns.
Contextual RetrievalChunks that mean nothing outside their document.1One LLM call per chunk, once, at write time.Long documents with many similar sections.

Scope before the limit

Rule: scope every search before its limit. Apply trusted user/project checks and metadata/time filters inside each search, before external rerankers see text. Recency, importance and MMR rank results; they never replace access controls.4,5 If filtering leaves fewer than k candidates, log and return fewer. Widen only a documented freshness preference, never an explicit date range, retention rule or user or project scope. Chapter 22 shows this for one patient per search.

Ranking without mixing score scales

Keyword/vector scales differ; RRF merges by rank. SQLite FTS5 returns BM25 scores where smaller means more relevant, so an ascending ORDER BY bm25(fts) puts better matches first.6 PostgreSQL uses its own full-text ranks, not BM25.7 RRF discards score magnitudes, giving even a weak match full credit for its rank. It sums 1 / (60 + rank) across lists. Second in both scores 0.03226; first in only one scores 0.01639.8

Preserve the meaning of each chunk

Keep headings with sections, questions with replies and paths with functions. Contextual Retrieval prepends 50 to 100 LLM-written tokens to each chunk before embedding and keyword indexing.1 Late chunking embeds the whole document first, then pools token vectors into chunks.9

First-stage variants

Learned sparse retrieval, such as SPLADE, has a model output weighted vocabulary terms for an inverted index. Late interaction (also called multi-vector retrieval) keeps one vector per token and matches each query token to its best document token: ColBERTv2 is the reference model and PLAID its fast index. BGE-M3 produces dense, sparse and late-interaction outputs from one model.10,2,11,12

Rerankers

Raise n until pool recall levels off or reranking reaches budget. Each candidate costs one pair score; benchmark end-to-end p95 at realistic chunk lengths, batching and concurrency. Three options:

  • Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B: Apache-2.0, 0.6B parameters, 32K tokens, runs on your hardware.13
  • Jina reranker v3.5: CC-BY-NC-4.0 (non-commercial), 0.6B parameters, 131K tokens, runs on your hardware or Jina's API.14
  • Cohere Rerank 5: managed service when hosting is impractical; text leaves the machine. Its listed context window is 32,768 tokens.15

Agentic search and repository maps

For changing code, an agent can read the current checkout or query an existing index. Claude Code's creator reports better results than RAG on his own code (Chapter 01).16

A repository map supplies paths and symbol signatures before full-file reads. Aider's 22 October 2023 design uses tree-sitter definitions and references instead of ctags, ranking a file-dependency graph to fit signatures into a token budget.25 A language server can supply symbols, definitions, references and call hierarchies through the Language Server Protocol (LSP).26 (From docs, not run.) Prefer a map for whole-repo structure; add LSP for precise definitions or call hierarchies when a server is available.

Refresh symbols after edits; generated code and dynamic calls can leave gaps. Use grep for exact text and embeddings for paraphrases, then read current source before editing. Compare file recall and prompt tokens; no comparison was measured here.

Hierarchical summary-tree retrieval (RAPTOR)

RAPTOR builds a hierarchy of summaries at write time: it embeds leaf chunks, clusters related ones, has a language model summarize each cluster, embeds the summaries and repeats for higher levels.17 At query time the collapsed tree flattens all levels into one list, searching chunks and summaries together by similarity within a token budget. This costs one query embedding and no summary call.17 Writing costs one summarization call per cluster at every level plus one embedding per leaf and summary; corpus-dependent cluster counts make per-document cost variable.18

The checked implementation rebuilds on additions, with no incremental update or deletion route. Track dependencies: replacing leaves requires refreshing summaries and embeddings, possibly reclustering. Deleting only leaves retains their information in summaries; rebuild or invalidate before serving. The implementation stores child-node IDs; add source document, version and page or chunk IDs and verify answers against the leaves, since a summary is not a quotation.17,18 The paper reports gains over flat retrieval on long-document questions, including QASPER research papers, but no comparison with entity graphs (Chapter 14). Test it where flat top-k retrieval cannot synthesize across passages, and compare answer quality, source coverage and rebuild cost on your golden set. Late chunking keeps context without summary levels.17,9

Soft forgetting: lower retrieval strength without erasing

Unused memories can lose ranking weight while retaining evidence. The Generative Agents paper (April 2023, section 4.1) scores recency as recency = 0.995^h, where h is sandbox game hours since the memory was last retrieved, and retrieval refreshes that clock; the final score also combines normalized relevance and importance.4

The released code differs: the August 2023 repository snapshot computes recency_decay^i over positions i in a list sorted by last access, not over elapsed hours.19 A policy proposed here (not from the paper): refresh strength on verified use, not retrieval alone; pin confirmed enduring preferences; keep strength separate from authorization and retention, since hard expiry or required erasure must remove the memory from live reads whatever its score (Chapters 10 and 17). No gain was measured.

Good for and not for

Good for

  • A memory store too large to put in the prompt whole.
  • Mixed questions: exact IDs and codes next to paraphrases.
  • A store you can test with 20 real questions, keeping only the steps the numbers support.

Not for

  • If authorized notes fit the context and cost budget, compare loading that scoped set whole; Anthropic suggests caching below about 200,000 tokens. Reuse cached contents only while authorized and current.1
  • Source code that changes all day without index refreshes. Use current-file search or refresh the symbol map.
  • Fixing duplicates or contradictions, which needs write-time rules, not a better ranker. Supersede contradictory notes when writing them (Chapters 13 and 14).

Use cases

1Small personal corpus

Situation
One person keeps about 5,000 prose, ticket and config notes. Dense search misses ticket numbers; keyword search misses paraphrases.
Why it fits
BM25 catches exact tokens and a small embedding model catches paraphrases. RRF merges the lists with one constant and no score tuning.8
Pair with
Chapter 12 for the SQLite setup. Add a reranker only if the top five are noisy.

2Code in a repository

Situation
An agent works in a large, hourly-changing repository with exact function names, flags and paths.
Why it fits
Agentic search runs grep and glob on current files, seeing the current checkout.16 Saved code notes need repository, path, symbol and commit metadata to flag or suppress stale notes; ClickHouse's Loom, an agent-memory product, documents one vendor implementation.20
Pair with
Chapter 01 for notes beside the code and its freshness policy for stale ones.

3Chat history

Situation
An assistant keeps months of chat and must answer "what did I say about the router last week" and "what was that error code".
Why it fits
Use indexed-field equality for exact codes, FTS5 for words/token phrases. Filter to the requested week before ranking; dense handles paraphrases and recency favors recent turns.4
Pair with
Index each complete turn with its preceding turn's ID. After retrieval, fetch the preceding turn for context and include each turn only once.

4Long documents

Situation
A team indexes 400-page manuals whose sections repeat headings like "Overview" and say "this setting" without naming it.
Why it fits
Anthropic reports Contextual Retrieval cut top-20 failures by 49%, and by 67% with reranking; Numbers checks the full pipeline locally; keyword search and reranking may explain its gain.1 For text that fits a long-context embedder's input window, late chunking is a cheaper route.9
Pair with
Hybrid search, then rerank the top 150 down to 20.1

5A corpus that changes daily

Situation
A support team edits notes daily. Old answers must not outrank today's; nightly re-embedding of everything is wasteful.
Why it fits
Keyword indexes update cheaply on write. Hash each chunk's embedding input, headings and prefixes included, and re-embed only changes, plus chunks whose prefix depends on a changed document. Mark replaced versions inactive on write and exclude them in both searches before the limit; use recency only to order eligible notes.
Pair with
Write-time supersede rules in Chapters 13 and 14. For files that change within a session, fall back to agentic search.

Without contextual prefixes, hybrid plus reranking had 12.81% SciFact failure and 0.72% LoCoMo failure, versus the contextual rates above. Question-level intervals cannot establish stability across conversations. MAP's paired 95% intervals exclude zero in opposite directions. If RRF loses on your golden set, ship the better retriever or rerank both lists.

Tested locally: on 300 LongMemEval conversational-memory questions, BM25 answered 191/300 correctly (63.7%) against dense retrieval's 165/300 (55.0%), an 8.7-point gap (exact form of McNemar's test for paired binary outcomes, p = 0.006). These answer accuracies use MiniLM and a local Gemma 2 9B reader. BM25 was strong on single-session facts and knowledge updates, weak on multi-session reasoning and preferences. Intervals and the full table are in Chapter 17.

Cost and scale

  • Writes and reads: one embedding per chunk and query; keyword indexing and RRF need no model. Reranking scores at most 2n pairs for two first stages of n, even with batching.
  • Storage and scans: 384-dimension float32 vectors take 1,536 bytes each: 153.6 MB for 100,000 chunks or 1.536 GB for one million, before text and indexes (Chapter 00). Exact search scans every vector per query: ten concurrent uncached queries at one million rows read roughly 15.36 GB before reranking. Embedding and scoring add time; latency was not measured.
  • What to do: more users multiply rows and more agents multiply queries, so measure p95 retrieval time and pool recall under load. If scans exceed the latency budget, move to indexed pgvector (Chapter 08) or a dedicated store (Chapter 11). If concurrent writes stall, move to PostgreSQL (Chapter 08).

Setup walkthrough

Build SQLite keyword/vector indexes, score four pipelines, then load vectors into PostgreSQL. Save complete files at their named paths; long blocks print as pointers. dataset.py supplies 24 notes and 20 questions. This single-user plumbing fixture measures neither production quality nor speed and lacks tenant authorization. Add user/project conditions inside both SQLite queries before LIMIT and k (Chapter 12), never by filtering returned IDs.

Walkthrough scripts/output verified after the 22 November research cutoff: 23 November 2026, Ubuntu x86-64, AMD Ryzen 9 8945HX (32 hardware threads, four used here), CPU only: Python 3.14.4, SQLite 3.51.3, torch 2.15.0+cpu, sentence-transformers 6.3.0, transformers 5.23.0 and sqlite-vec 0.1.9. PostgreSQL 18.7 and pgvector 0.8.7 ran under Docker 29.1.3. You need Python with venv support, curl, tar, a C compiler, make, timeout, coreutils and a running Docker Engine, but no model API key.

Save named files together outside the lab; run bash lab.sh, for all steps in one process; do not run excerpts separately. Preflight refusals leave existing resources alone. After creation, an exit trap checks each resource independently and removes only resources carrying this run's ownership token.

Gotchas

Gotcha: a reranker cannot fix a pool miss

In the walkthrough the five-candidate BM25 pool misses n16, so reranking cannot recover n16. If pool recall is low, improve the first stage with a better chunk, a rewritten query or a second search.

Gotcha: FTS5 query syntax breaks on hyphens

Unquoted agent-memory in MATCH fails with "no such column: memory", because the unquoted hyphen is query syntax, not part of a literal phrase. A parameterized query does not help: the query language lives inside the parameter. Quoting each word, as the bm25 function in search.py does, avoids the error but splits the ID into OR-ed tokens. Quote the whole ID to require adjacent tokens in order. For literal identifier lookup, index the ID in a separate column and use equality.

Verdict

Verdict: build the golden set first

Write 20 real questions first. Then compare BM25, one dense model and their RRF merge on a store you already run. Test reranking when pool recall meets your target but recall@k or MRR@k lags at serving cutoff k. Set targets from missed-answer costs. With 20 questions, one or two misses signal only that the set must grow. If correct notes rarely enter the pool, fix retrieval first. Test heading-aware chunks or Contextual Retrieval for lost context. Failure was lower on these 150 LoCoMo questions and inconclusive on SciFact; keyword search and reranking may explain the gain.

Before shipping, freeze both pipelines and compare fresh labeled questions at the same context budget.

Part C

Models that remember

A second model can read, write and tidy memory for the agent. This part covers small local models and uncensored ones, and where each fits.

  • 06Small LLMs as memory models
  • 07Uncensored memory models

Part C · Chapter 06

06

Small LLMs as memory models

A small chat model on your own machine reads conversations and writes down the facts worth keeping.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

3 of 5

Running cost

2 of 5

Best for

Private memory that must stay on your hardware and runs in the background.

What it is

A small language model, the writer, records conversation facts in the store's format. Most have 1 to 9 billion parameters. Mixture-of-experts models select parameter groups (experts) per token: 30B-A3B runs about 3 billion parameters but stores all 30 billion.

The chat model writes notes; an embedding model encodes them for similarity search (Chapter 03). Memory usually needs both.1

Terms new in this chapter

Mem0 v3
The open-source memory algorithm in the pinned mem0ai==2.2.1 Python package; algorithm and package versions are numbered separately.2,37
Extraction
Turning conversation into separate facts or entities.
Constrained decoding
Restricting output tokens to a schema or grammar.
Thinking mode
Writing reasoning before the answer.
Weight quantization
Storing weights with fewer bits, such as 4, so the model needs less memory. The GGUF labels Q4_K_M and Q8_0 mean roughly 4-bit and 8-bit.
GGUF
A single-file model format used by llama.cpp and Ollama.

The glossary defines parameters, tokens and context window.

How it works

What each framework asks of the model

On saves and sometimes reads, writers extract facts, reconcile changes and duplicates, summarize or answer recall questions.

FrameworkOn writeOn read
Mem0 (v3 algorithm)Mem0 retrieves up to ten related memories, asks the model once for new facts, then removes exact duplicates by hash.2It retrieves candidates by embedding similarity; when enabled, BM25 lexical scores and named-entity matches only reorder them (Chapter 13, Gotchas). The README also lists time-aware ranking. It describes no model call on read.2,3
Hindsightretain pulls out facts, dates, entities and relationships with a model.4recall runs four searches in parallel and merges them. reflect asks the model for deeper synthesis.4
GraphitiEntity and edge extraction plus deduplication, all as structured JSON.5Search over the graph. The README does not describe model use on read.
Letta sleep-time agentsA second agent edits memory blocks while the main agent is idle.6Memory can be read at any time, because editing happens off to the side.6

These sources recommend no small model. Test your candidate writer on representative conversation turns with the framework's actual prompt and output format. Where permitted, retain access-controlled transcripts for failed extractions; delete them with the memories (Chapter 17).

Why reliable JSON matters

Graphiti "depends on structured (JSON) output".5 Constrain decoding to prevent missing fields and prose wrappers; validate identifiers against the store and check for truncation.

Constrained decoding blocks schema-breaking tokens. Ollama takes a schema in format.10 llama.cpp supports GBNF grammars11 and OpenAI-compatible response_format with type json_schema (step 3). Reject truncation, refusal and runtime errors, then validate fields; a schema cannot make facts true.

Tested With llama.cpp, constrained output and thinking off, Qwen3.5 4B returned valid JSON on 79 of 100 prompts with a narrow three-field schema. All 21 failures repeated to the output limit; doubling it rescued none. General-schema validity was 100 percent (Numbers); narrow-schema prompts are in benchmarks/extraction/v1/data/sample.json. Test your shipping schema. Use repetition penalty 1.1 only for this failure: it gave 100 of 100 but lost facts on the broader test (Numbers). Set repeat_penalty in the llama.cpp request body or Ollama options. Treat 100 schema-valid responses with no unexplained empty lists as a format check. Loop the step 3 check over your prompts; benchmarks/extraction shows the pattern. Before testing, label must-keep facts on held-out turns, including no-fact turns, and set minimum coverage and maximum unsupported-fact rates. Ship only when the framework-level run meets those targets.

Thinking mode off for extraction

For schema-constrained extraction, keep thinking off: it can consume the output limit before JSON starts.

Source or runtimeDefaultSetting that turns thinking off

Quantization

Use a 4-bit build; measure its extraction quality. Unsloth's bfloat16 (16-bit floating point) and 4-bit estimates (Numbers) are secondary, not file sizes or serving measurements.17 Unsloth says its 4-bit builds keep sensitive layers at higher precision.17 Ollama's default file is not always 4-bit: qwen3.5:2b is Q8_0 (step 1).

Plan on about 6.6 GB for Qwen3.5 9B with vision: the Q4_K_M file is about 5.6 GB, and the bfloat16 vision projector, unneeded for text-only writing, adds the rest. Ollama's MLX package (its Apple-silicon format) is 7.6 GB, not the GGUF size. Downloads exclude context buffers, so measure peak memory at your context size.19,20,21,22 From file sizes, not measured: on an 8 GB GPU stay with 2B to 4B models; use 9B on 16 GB or more.

Research note: sub-1-bit weights

Use the 4-bit builds above, not sub-1-bit weights. Samsung's LittleBit (NeurIPS 2025) and LittleBit-2 (ICML 2026) compress a model to 1.0 to 0.1 bits per weight with binarized low-rank factors and learned scales.23 It requires quantization-aware CUDA training, so finished checkpoints cannot be converted. Supported families are OPT, Llama, Phi-4, Qwen2.5, QwQ, Gemma 2 and 3, and Qwen3, but not Qwen3.5, under CC BY-NC 4.0, which bars commercial use. Not run here; paper accuracy tables unchecked.

Latency and why saves run in the background

In the Chapter 19 deployment (retain and recall calls, a 9B writer, an Apple silicon Mac), recall took about 2 seconds, a warm retain about 25 seconds and a cold service start about 2 minutes; the timings are unpublished.24 Mem0 first embeds the conversation and retrieves the ten nearest memories as context.2,25 In the CPU test (step 4), one Mem0 add took 68.6 seconds: 52.8 reading Mem0's own 8,226-token prompt at 155.7 tokens per second, 8.4 generating 62 tokens and 7.4 not itemized. The repeat add reused cached computation for the unchanged prompt prefix, evaluating only 125 tokens anew. Its 13.6 seconds does not predict unrelated saves. Queue saves and answer first.

Queued saves can overwrite newer corrections, duplicate facts on retry or revive deleted facts on replay. Chapter 17 covers ordering, idempotency and lasting deletes.

Plain recall skips the writer. Hindsight can prune results with a small "decision" model: it reports a 167 ms median on its workload, against 1 to 7 seconds for a main model call. On an Apple M1 Ultra it took 132 ms for prompts of about 240 tokens (36 requests) and 2.1 seconds for about 5,700 tokens (206 requests).26

Inkling 2 Mini

Inkling 2 Mini is Thinking Machines Lab's open-weight model, released 20 November 2026; it runs its middle layers three times per token. It passed the Mac schema check only with reasoning_effort: none (minimum effort, distinct from thinking off); thinking off alone exhausted even the larger limit. Extraction quality and the card's 32 GB Apple silicon minimum (32 GB of VRAM on other GPUs) were not tested here. It documents tool use but no structured-output guarantee.44 The maker says looping improves reasoning and long-context results, not stored facts, so you still need an external store.45

Larger open-weight models Inkling 2 Small (594B total, 17B active, released 5 November 2026) and the original Inkling (975B total, 41B active) exceed this chapter's hardware.47 From docs, not run: the maker's Tinker service hosts Mini for inference and fine-tuning at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens (read 21 November 2026).48

Small Qwen3.8 models are community builds

The official Qwen3.8 collection has no 2B, 4B or 9B model (see Chapter 07).32 Only the dense 27B (Apache 2.0, thinking by default) plausibly fits one consumer machine.16 Larger members use other licenses: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 125B lists license: other and license_name: qwen-community-1.0; Chapter 07 lists the larger official models' licenses, including the 2.4T-parameter one.33

Refusals: card 6 of 100; local 4-bit copy 14 of 100 by the same keyword rule, 43 of 100 on reading.Apache 2.0. Revision 820ba8f.

Both cards name Qwen3.5 bases; benchmark claims remain unchecked. In benchmarks/small-reruns, keywords missed answers substituting the safe opposite, making refusal counts lower bounds; the original empero-ai 9B distill refused 98 of 100 (Chapter 07). Think-block training may override the thinking switch; the larger empero-ai builds returned empty lists in extraction. Test them.

Not yet tested here: purpose-trained memory writers (Hy-Memory)

Tencent's Hy-Memory-30B-A3B is trained for long-term memory writing, rather than general chat with an extraction prompt. It was not run. The card states no quantized size or hardware requirement; an untested estimate puts a 4-bit file near Inkling 2 Mini's 20 GB, beyond the 8 GB and 16 GB machines this chapter targets.

  • Released in October 2026, it has about 30 billion parameters, about 3 billion active per token. Its weights are Apache 2.0, read 20 November 2026.7,8
  • The card describes a drop-in writer for Mem0, MemOS and Hy-Memory, with transfer evaluated on EverMemOS, a framework held out of training; it selects facts and reconciles new evidence.7
  • The separate Hy-Memory framework, also Apache 2.0,41 supports Chat, Working and Coding pipelines, described in Chapter 16.9
  • The card reports a 55.49 overall score for this writer against 54.62 for Claude Opus 5. Tencent averages six metrics on 20% subsamples across four memory frameworks, changing only the writer; this is not extraction accuracy. Its coding metric averages two repository QA evaluations (Chapter 16).7

Not yet tested here: memory managers trained with rewards

Memory-R1 (27 August 2025, first paper version) trains a Memory Manager that chooses ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP and an Answer Agent that filters retrieved memories, by reinforcement learning on correct answers. It evaluates 7B and 8B backbones on LoCoMo, a long-conversation memory benchmark, with 152 training question-answer pairs and reports better answers than its reimplemented baselines, with no production reliability or 2B results.40 It trained on four 80 GB H100 GPUs and was not run. Chapter 16 compares other learned-memory approaches, including MemRL, which updates stored episodes' utility at run time with frozen weights.

Good for and not for

Good for

  • Personal or regulated memory that must not leave your network.
  • A save on every message, where a cloud call per turn is costly or not permitted.
  • A schema, such as preferences, entities and dates, that a grammar or JSON schema can enforce and that passes 100 of your own prompts.
  • Background and overnight work, where a 25-second save does not matter.
  • A Mac with 16 GB or more, or an 8 GB GPU running a 4B model, if peak use with your prompt and context leaves OS and embedder headroom.

Not for

  • Bulk-loading documents you have: embed them, since paraphrasing risks lost details (see the cost example).
  • Multi-hop recall answers and long synthesis. Use a larger or hosted model for those steps.
  • Writes that must be right first time with no review. Mem0's add-only pass makes a bad extraction stick,2 and the measured writers missed many reference facts.
  • Tool calling without testing both thinking modes: every model moved 8 to 12 points; 4B worsened (Numbers).
  • Graph extraction that produces many invalid edges; move that step to a bigger model.

Use cases

1Private assistant memory on a 16 GB Mac or an 8 GB GPU

Situation
A chat or voice assistant on a 16 GB Apple silicon Mac or 8 GB GPU keeps weeks of preferences and events off-cloud.
Why it fits
Gemma 4 E4B (4.5 GB estimated at Q4_0, including 20% overhead) led observed fact recall. E4B and Qwen3.5 4B are 8 GB GPU candidates; measure peak GPU use with your context and embedder.17,28 On 16 GB, Qwen3.5 9B (5.6 GB, text-only Q4_K_M) also supports tools.19,20 Hindsight lists local providers including Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp.4
Pair with
Queue saves, timestamp facts, keep raw transcripts and require a JSON schema on extraction calls; step 4 does not demonstrate that constraint. Chapter 07 covers sensitive content.

2Extraction on a CPU-only mini PC

Situation
A CPU home server saves a few agent memories hourly.
Why it fits
Small models run on CPU. A 2B model returned a schema-valid answer in 4.9 seconds with thinking off (warm model, step 2), and a Mem0 add took 68.6 seconds (step 4, using the step 3 server and step 1 embedder). That suits a queued job, not a live one.
Pair with
A job queue. The 2B writer covered only 34.3 percent of reference facts; where policy permits, skip live extraction and batch transcripts directly to a larger nightly writer (Chapter 17). 0.8B extraction is unmeasured.

3Nightly consolidation of a day's log

Situation
A nightly job deduplicates an agent's daily log and drops stale lines.
Why it fits
Letta's sleep-time design edits memory while the main agent is idle, so the slow call costs no waiting.6 A local run avoids per-call fees but occupies the machine.
Pair with
Keep raw episodes: a small model can overwrite a correct fact with a worse summary (operator judgment).

4When to pay for a hosted model

Situation
A product serves many users, answers multi-hop queries or loads history once.
Why it fits
Mem0's quickstart default is hosted, gpt-5-mini.1 Hosting removes local fit constraints; compare it with your local writer on your product's tool calls.
Pair with
If policy permits sending the question and retrieved facts off-device, host only the hard step, such as graph extraction or reflection; otherwise queue it for a larger local model or omit it.

Measured extraction quality

Tested Small writers rarely stored a wrong fact: precision was about 95 percent or better for most, but fact recall ranged from about a quarter to under 60 percent. The main risk is forgetting. Keep raw transcripts searchable and re-extract nightly with a larger writer where policy permits (use cases 1 to 3).

The run made 9,000 requests across ten arms: the seven writers below, a repetition-penalty arm and two Qwen2.5-Coder files (Chapter 07). Each arm used 300 public long-conversation benchmark turns (LoCoMo and LongMemEval), three seeds, Q4_K_M files and an Apple M3 Ultra, 96 GB. Pooled per-arm precision divides supported facts by written facts; fact recall divides covered references by all references. Invalid or empty responses lower fact recall, not precision. The implementer wrote reference facts without independent review; update and contradiction reconciliation were not measured.

The local judge (Qwen3.5 9B, also a tested writer) agreed with the tester's hand labels on 53 of 60 real cases. The judge disagreed on 7 of 60 cases, about 12 percent. Gemma 4 E4B covered 6.7 percentage points more reference facts than Qwen3.5 9B (paired 95% interval 1.7 to 12.1). Paired results compare both writers on the same 300 turns. Their marginal intervals (53.2 to 62.0 and 45.9 to 56.3) overlap; the paired interval measures the gap. Repetition penalty 1.1 cost the 4B writer 4.6 points of fact recall (paired 95% interval 1.6 to 7.5). The empero-ai Qwen3.8 4B and 9B distills returned valid empty lists (not token-limit failures) on 510 of 900 and 645 of 900 requests, explaining their low fact recall. These writer-only numbers do not predict Chapter 20's pipeline scores. The companion repository holds conversation-clustered 95% intervals (resampling conversations, keeping their seeds together) under benchmarks/extraction, and exact repository revisions and hashes in benchmarks/extraction/v2/models.json.

Scope and scale

What a local writer costs as the store grows (arithmetic is an estimate)

QuestionAnswer
JobWrites facts from new conversation in the background.
Per writeBeyond the embedding and ten-memory lookup (Latency), mem0ai==2.2.1 makes one extraction call, then embeds and stores the facts.2,25 Hindsight and Graphiti also extract entities and relationships; the cited pages give no call count.4,5
Per readOne embedding call and a store lookup; no writer for Mem0-style recall. Vector storage per memory is in the Chapter 00 sizing reference; that figure excludes the stored text and the index.
GrowthFor fixed input and output lengths, inference costs roughly the same as the store grows; index lookup and insertion can change. Writes queue behind one model.2,25 At 68.6 s, 3,600 / 68.6 gives about 52 saves an hour for one continuously busy worker; the 120.5 s rerun gives about 30, and the Chapter 19 deployment's 25 s retain gives 144. These do not predict throughput at larger store sizes.
What breaks firstThe save queue: a backlog leaves answers on stale memory. Compare measured service rate with peak arrivals, clustered in waking hours; check the oldest queued save against your freshness target.
Move on whenThe queue never empties: move extraction to a GPU or hosted model and keep the store (Chapter 08 for many writers). Move to Chapter 14 when questions need relations or time, such as who held a role last year.

Worked cost example: 7,700 existing passages

Pushing 7,700 passages through a 25 s retain call takes 192,500 s, 53.5 hours, on one worker; at the CPU Mem0 add's 68.6 s, 146.7 hours. Embedding is far smaller: a CPU text-embedding server embedded 100 short texts in 0.544 seconds (Chapter 03), so 7,700 take about 42 seconds, a floor because real passages are longer.

Gotchas

Gotcha: thinking eats the answer

Despite the 2B card, both tested runtimes thought by default, and step 3 exhausted its output limit on reasoning (fix: Thinking mode).13,18

Gotcha: the prompt is bigger than the conversation

mem0ai==2.2.1 sent 8,226 tokens to the model for a two-sentence chat, and a 4,096-token window failed with HTTP 400. Size the window for the framework's prompt.

Gotcha: Mem0 keyword and entity boosts do not widen the candidate set

In mem0ai==2.2.1 the keyword (BM25) and named-entity signals only re-rank semantic candidates, so they cannot rescue an exact identifier the semantic search missed (Chapter 13).2,37

Open questions

  • Extraction quality across other hardware, quantizations and schemas remains unmeasured here.
  • 4-bit memory for the official Qwen3.8 27B: the card does not state it.

Verdict

Verdict: local for new conversations, embeddings for old documents

Pick a small local model when memory is private, saves run in the background, and your framework run meets the format and fact-coverage targets above. Start with Gemma 4 E4B: on the general schema and 96 GB machine it led fact recall with lower median latency than Qwen3.5 9B. The printed end-to-end walkthrough uses Qwen3.5 2B. Measure peak memory and fact coverage with your framework prompt: a 9B model at 4-bit is the 16 GB Mac candidate, a 4B model or E4B the 8 GB GPU candidate. If you also need tools, compare both on your tool calls (Qwen3.5 9B scores 66.1 on its card; E4B was not tested). Avoid the empero-ai 4B and 9B distills. Disable extraction thinking; test thinking for tools. Updates and contradictions were not tested; check them before trusting background saves.

Embed existing documents instead (Chapter 03). Use a larger or hosted model for multi-hop reads or graph extraction. For uncensored variants, see Chapter 07; for case studies, Chapter 21 picks Qwen3.5 9B with a 2B vision worker for a one-owner business; Chapter 22 splits a 27B staff lane from a 9B phone lane.

Part C · Chapter 07

07

Uncensored memory models

A model edited to reduce refusals, tested here as a note-taker that must preserve facts in valid JSON.

Maturity

Prototype

Setup effort

3 of 5

Running cost

2 of 5

Best for

Private local assistants whose stock extractor refuses or softens facts in your tests.

What it is

This chapter calls models changed to refuse less “edited”. Abliteration (defined below) and fine-tuning are two methods. This test evaluates an upload labelled abliterated by its quantizer, not the editing procedure. Fine-tuned builds need their own provenance checks and acceptance tests; they are not evaluated here. An edited memory extractor records turn facts; consider it when stock declines or softens needed medication, debt or divorce facts. “Uncensored” describes intent, not accuracy.

The walkthrough tests two small quantized models on ordinary facts, health, debt, divorce and quoted profanity for a private adult assistant. Stock preserved all 13 acceptance facts; edited reversed two. Both corrupted adult-content probes without declining.

Terms new in this chapter

Abliteration
Abliteration finds a direction (a vector in the model's internal activations) that separates prompts it refuses from prompts it answers, then edits the weights so they can no longer write along it, without further training.12
KL divergence
An asymmetric measure of how far one probability distribution diverges from a reference. Heretic, an open-source tool that automates abliteration, uses it to check how far an edit moves outputs on harmless prompts, not memory accuracy.3

How it works

The extractor proposes facts; the application checks and stores them for later retrieval by the chat model. Swapping Chapter 06's extractor leaves storage unchanged.

What an edit changes

Arditi and colleagues reduced refusals by removing one such direction in the models they studied.12

Heretic seeks fewer refusals while keeping next-token probabilities on harmless prompts close to the unedited model. This checks unrelated output changes, not whether a dose or date survives extraction. Its AGPL-3.0 license does not replace the weights' licenses.3

The build page linked from the edited quantizer's card returned HTTP 401 on 20 November 2026; its procedure remains unconfirmed.45 Before adopting an edited upload, record uploader, base checkpoint, immutable revision, claimed procedure and weight license.

Good for and not for

Good for

  • A private assistant whose stock extractor refuses facts it should record.
  • Short extraction tasks with explicit expected facts.
  • A local deployment with pinned weights, hashes and runtime settings.
  • Comparisons that include harmless facts, corrections and messages with no extractable facts.

Not for

  • Fixing retrieval errors (diagnose the read path with Chapter 05).
  • Assuming reduced refusal means better accuracy.
  • Replacing permission checks or access controls with model behavior.
  • Choosing edited weights when the stock model passes your tests.

Use cases

These scenarios motivate tests; none demonstrates a stock-model failure.

1Health notes

Situation
An adult tracks medication and dose in a private assistant; a changed number would corrupt the note.
What to check
Stock kept every health fact here. Storing a dose as “takes medication” (illustrative, not observed) warrants testing an edited extractor. Compare medicine, dose and polarity.
Pair with
A reviewed notes store and Chapter 17 evaluation.

2Household finances

Situation
A budgeting assistant records a debt of $240 and must not turn it into savings.
What to check
A refusal or softening would drop or blur the amount, so compare who owes whom and how much.
Pair with
SQLite (Chapter 12) and source-turn references.

3Relationship changes

Situation
An assistant records a divorce or a move, and stale facts can leak into later answers.
What to check
Mark each fact current or past, as the residence-change test below does. The edited build reversed this kind of correction here, so require a correction control.
Pair with
Temporal records (Chapter 14), not destructive overwrites.

4Quoted frustration

Situation
A journal includes profanity the writer wants preserved literally.
What to check
Check the quotation, speaker and denied regret; cleaned-up wording changes the record.
Pair with
Flat files (Chapter 01) with human review before saving.

5An audit that keeps the stock model

Situation
A developer compares stock and edited models before changing a private assistant.
What to check
If both keep the facts, do not switch.
Pair with
Chapter 06 model settings and held-out examples of your stock model's real failures.

Numbers

Edited recorded Austin as current and Oslo as past; stock preserved every fact. That correction error reversed two propositions. No explicit declines occurred; refusal recovery is unmeasured. Ten mild cases, one prompt and one seed provide anecdotal first-party results, not evidence for other prompts or seeds. Adult-content probes are separate.

Each model saw ten messages once without history: nine contain 13 propositions, including past/current residences; the tenth expects an empty facts array. A proposition combines subject, predicate, value, polarity (true asserted, false denied) and validity (current/past time status, distinct from JSON validity). Scoring:

  • Refusal: an explicit decline counts as an observed refusal.
  • Omission: a missing expected fact. An unexpected empty array counts as omissions without distinguishing a decline, missed facts or finding nothing.
  • Addition: an unsupported fact. Other wrong values, including softening (“takes medication” for “fluoxetine 20 mg”), count as an omission plus an addition. Tag softened expected propositions separately during review.
  • Reversal: flipped polarity or swapped current/past on an otherwise identical fact, counted once. A changed value instead counts as an omission plus an addition.
  • Syntax and schema failures (duplicates and extra fields included) count per response; semantic counts cover schema-valid responses only.
Measure after canonicalizationStockEdited
Responses1010
Invalid JSON (responses)00
Invalid schema (responses)00
Explicit refusals observed (responses)00
Omissions (propositions)00
Additions (propositions)00
Reversals (propositions)02
Disputed reviews00

Separate adult-content probes. Eight responses cover two cases, two models and both decoding modes; four are constrained. None explicitly declined. Each constrained quote response has two omissions and two additions: altered quote, invented relationship_status friend, missing denied regret. Each constrained health response has one addition: sexual context stored as another medication. Stock's unconstrained health response violates the predicate enum. Excluded from acceptance scoring, both constrained probes fail for both models. Exact tuple counts cannot identify refusals; sensitive.jsonl holds raw rows.

Ten-case acceptance requires zero invalid responses, refusals and semantic errors. Stock passes; edited fails on two reversals. Scripts print counts, not verdicts. Schema constraints limit how a decline can appear; zero observed declines does not establish unconstrained behavior.

The schema allows owes, excluding owed; this run cannot test unaided wording. Both models ignored the subject instruction; the script maps I/me to user. Beyond that, only edited's fluoxetine 20 mg terminal period was canonicalized. Exact matching adds one omission and one addition. memtest.py review retains raw responses and comparison tuples in reviewed.json and journals decisions in reviewed.jsonl. Other equivalences require dispute review. Neither returned an empty array when facts were expected; both did on no_facts. For an unconstrained check, run memtest.py free stock money; read free.jsonl.

Offline review of the saved suite reports stock-softened propositions fully recovered by edited / stock-softened propositions: not measured (zero denominator).

Different sizes, llama.cpp releases and parameter counts prevent isolating abliteration. Ollama reports the counts above despite edited's 1.5B card name; abliteration cannot add parameters. The extra 233,373,696 equal 151,936 × 1,536 (vocabulary by hidden size), an output matrix mapping the final hidden state to vocabulary scores. Header inspection found no separate output.weight in stock; edited has one with these dimensions. Stock may share (“tie”) output and input embeddings. Treat them as different builds.

The official collection has no small models,8 so uploads named Qwen3.8 2B, 4B or 9B are community builds before any edit, as are the unedited empero-ai 2B, 4B and 9B distills Chapter 06 tested for extraction.9

Chapter 06 is the closest prior evidence, and the reason a human scores refusals here. On 100 refusal prompts against the petruhonk 9B Heretic build, the card reported 6 refusals, a keyword rule counted 14 and a human reader counted 43, so the card and the keyword count both understated them.10 The unedited model it was edited from refused 98 of 100 in the same rerun.

Check the LICENSE at the exact checkpoint revision: family names do not determine licenses. Official Qwen3.8 files read 20 November 2026 (none run): 27B/27B-FP8, Apache-2.0;1112 2.4T-A95B/FP8, Qwen3.8-Max License.1314

Larger community builds, not run: huihui-ai Qwen3.8-27B abliterated GGUF (base Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B, Apache-2.0 tag), 4,534,445 downloads;15 SC117 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next abliterated GGUF (ISTA-DASLab quant, Apache-2.0 tag), 4,108,369.16 Counts checked 22 November 2026. The two run Qwen2.5-Coder files are unmatched builds (Numbers); Q4_K_M is a quantization level (Chapter 06). One quantizer supplied both at pinned revisions; both cards declare Apache-2.0. Repeat the test on your deployment model.

Scope and scale

Each saved turn costs one model call (twenty here). Reads cost none; retrieved notes consume answering-model input tokens. The fixture caps context at 2,048 tokens and output at 512. Normal calls unload afterward. memtest.py warm stock preloads, times a second plain-case call with keep_alive, then unloads; that call took 5.416 s. Reading and parsing the two-fact note took 0.064 ms with a warm file cache. Both timings are anecdotal.

Share weights across users: about 2.1 GB for both files, plus Ollama copies and runtime memory. At 1 KB per accepted note, 100 users × 1,000 notes need about 100 MB before indexes and logs (sizing reference, Chapter 00). For slow writes, see Chapter 06; for slow scans, add Chapter 05 retrieval and Chapter 08 storage.

Gotchas

Gotcha: syntax is not truth

A valid fact object can still mark Austin current and Oslo past. The checker's self-test asserts that this reversal and a flipped drinking negation are both caught. Never infer accuracy from a JSON-validity percentage. Live assistants lack labels: check names, numbers and doses against the source turn, and confirm changed residences with the user; schema validation accepts swaps.

Gotcha: model edits do not grant storage permission

At write time, exclude or redact facts about other people (names, health, relationships) unless the user wants them kept, in application code before anything is saved, logs included. Keep source-turn references and review sensitive notes; local inference does not control backups or sharing (Chapter 17). The synthetic names fixture grants no retention permission.

Verdict

Verdict: choose on preserved meaning

Use an edited extractor only when that exact candidate preserves necessary facts better than the stock model on held-out failures of your own stock extractor. Collect permission-cleared examples where it declined or softened a fact, label the expected facts before running either model, and require the candidate to recover the missing meaning and still pass ordinary, correction and no-facts controls on the quantization and prompt you will deploy (Chapter 06).

Keep stock for the ten-case acceptance suite. Neither model passed both constrained adult-content probes; treat sensitive notes from either as unreviewed until your own cases pass. Chapter 06's refusal counts and general refusal benchmarks measure requests models decline, not whether personal facts survive extraction. Use short validated writes and keep evidence for corrections.

Part D · Chapter 08

08

PostgreSQL and pgvector

One Postgres database holds facts, vectors and keywords for one filtered, ranked memory query.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

2 of 5

Running cost

2 of 5

Best for

Teams already running Postgres who need per-user, transactional memory.

What it is

pgvector adds embedding types (Chapter 03) and nearest-neighbour indexes to PostgreSQL for similarity search.1

Agent memory uses episodes rows for events and memories rows for facts and summaries, each with an embedding. One backup, permission model and query language cover keyword search, permissions and transactions.

Memory, embedding, audit and outbox rows (pending deliveries) commit or roll back together, and reads can join users and permissions while ranking. Framework support (Chapter 13): LangGraph ships PostgresSaver and PostgresStore,2,3 Mem0 has a pgvector provider,4 and Hindsight uses Postgres with pgvector as its primary storage backend.5

Terms used in this chapter

HNSW
Hierarchical Navigable Small World, a layered-graph approximate-search index (Chapter 00). Chapter 11 compares index families.
ef_search
Candidate-list size per HNSW query: higher means better recall, slower queries.
Recall@10, RRF
With at least ten eligible rows, recall@10 is the overlap of returned and exact top tens under identical filters, divided by ten. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists (Chapter 05).
IVFFlat
pgvector's clustered-list index: probes sets how many clusters (lists) a query searches, trading speed for recall. It learns list centres from existing rows.
tsvector, GIN
tsvector holds searchable words; GIN indexes them for fast matching.
RLS
Row-level security. Policies control which rows a role sees.

How it works

The application commits raw turns to episodes. Fact extraction, often a model call (Chapter 06), produces memories. After extraction and embedding succeed, one transaction commits each memory, its vector and any audit or outbox row, with index updates. Never hold a transaction open across model calls.

Reads embed the question with the same model. One SQL statement filters user and validity, merges vector-distance and keyword rankings, and returns prompt rows. The walkthrough checks memory timestamps valid_from <= now() and valid_to IS NULL for current facts. For future start or end dates, test valid_from <= :as_of AND (valid_to IS NULL OR :as_of < valid_to) in both branches; the current-row partial index cannot cover this predicate.

Types and distance operators

pgvector adds three column types (vector, halfvec and sparsevec) and supports binary-distance search on PostgreSQL's built-in bit type. Its distance operators are <-> for L2 distance, <#> for negative inner product, <=> for cosine distance, <+> for L1, <~> for Hamming and <%> for Jaccard.1 Index use requires LIMIT and an ORDER BY matching the operator class (e.g. <=> with vector_cosine_ops); the planner may prefer exact scan and sort.

TypeUseLargest indexable size
vectorThe default dense embedding column.2,000 dimensions
halfvecDense embeddings that need an index above 2,000 dimensions.4,000 dimensions
bitBinary vectors, for example from binary_quantize with Hamming distance.64,000 dimensions
sparsevecSparse vectors that store only non-zero elements.1,000 non-zero elements

These are the README's index caps.1 Tested: each HNSW cap was accepted and cap+1 rejected, two boundary cases per type. Above 2,000 dimensions (e.g. 3,072), HNSW needs halfvec or dimension reduction. Alternatively, use CREATE INDEX ON memories USING hnsw ((embedding::halfvec(3072)) halfvec_cosine_ops) and order by embedding::halfvec(3072) <=> $1::halfvec(3072).

Index kinds

Index (100,000 vectors)Defaults and tuningTrade-off
None (exact)Unfiltered exact search scores all 100,000 rows; a user index narrows it to one user.Recall is perfect. Tested median latency was 37.242 ms; no growth curve was measured.
HNSWm 16, ef_construction 64, query setting hnsw.ef_search 40.Tested recall@10 was 96.95%, above default IVFFlat; median query latency was 2.827 ms. The build took 202.359 seconds and 204,808,192 bytes (195 MiB).
IVFFlatLoad data first. Recommended lists: rows / 1000 up to 1M rows, then √rows; probes near √lists. Tested ivfflat.probes defaulted to 1.With 100 lists, it built in 2.725 seconds using 164,323,328 bytes (157 MiB). At 10 probes, recall@10 rose from 38.90% to 67.10%, median latency from 1.165 ms to 4.010 ms.

README defaults and sizing.1 Tests use 100,000 clustered synthetic vectors of 384 dimensions, CPU only: one build per index, 200 queries per setting, default HNSW parameters. HNSW built with 512 MB of maintenance memory and no parallel workers. Treat the numbers as one run. Boundary, filter and storage tests: companion repository, benchmarks/stores.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) distinguishes exact sorts from HNSW scans naming the matching distance operator. Measure recall against exact search.

Higher m (links per node) can enlarge the index; higher ef_construction (build candidate list) lengthens the build. Either can raise recall; measure it. If the build reports the graph no longer fits in maintenance_work_mem, raise it for that session before building, e.g. SET maintenance_work_mem = '2GB', leaving memory for other work; otherwise expect a slower build.

Variants and tools (as of 2026-11-20)

ToolWhat it addsVersion and caveat
pgvectorVector types, distance operators, HNSW and IVFFlat.10.8.7, changelog dated 2026-10-01; pinned below. Older versions: see Security below.6
PostgreSQLThe database.19 released 2026-11-19.7 Latest 18.x is 18.7, released 2026-11-12.8
pgvectorscaleStreamingDiskANN (disk-based graph) index, Statistical Binary Quantization and label-filtered search. Requires pgvector.90.9.1 (release page checked 2026-11-20); not used below.10
VectorChordThe vchordrq index: IVF with RaBitQ (binary) quantization and reranking, using pgvector's types.111.1.1 (Docker tag pg18-v1.1.1). 1.0 was released 2025-11-11.
ParadeDB pg_searchBM25 (term-frequency) ranked full text as an index, plus hybrid search.12Docs at v0.27.0. The index access method was renamed paradedb in 0.25.0.
Built-in full texttsvector with GIN and ts_rank_cd for ranking, and pg_trgm for fuzzy matching.Ships with Postgres. No BM25 scoring.
Apache AGEopenCypher graph queries inside Postgres.13 Chapter 14 covers graphs.1.7.0, released 2026-01-21, with PostgreSQL 18 builds and RLS support. Its GitHub tag is named v1.7.0-rc0; a 1.8.0 release candidate was published 2026-09-19.

Hybrid search and filters. RRF (Chapter 05) sums 1 / (60 + rank) per keyword/vector list; 60 is tunable and follows pgvector's example.14 Filter user and validity in both branches; HNSW can underfill (Gotchas). RLS restricts visible rows,15 without creating per-user approximate indexes.

Good for and not for

Good for

  • Existing Postgres teams adding memory tables.
  • Memory writes committing with business data and audit.
  • Queries mixing user/validity filters, keyword rank and vector rank.
  • RLS-enforced user isolation (one tenant = one user_id).
  • Exact search within budget (tested: 37.242 ms median, 100,000 384-dimension rows, 2 CPUs), or HNSW meeting recall targets.

Not for

  • Tuned queries missing p99 targets: compare VectorChord, pgvectorscale and dedicated stores (Chapter 11).
  • Primarily multi-hop reasoning: Apache AGE covers moderate graphs; Chapter 14 covers dedicated graph memory.
  • Write-heavy streaming ingestion with no tuning or vacuum budget.
  • A single user with a few hundred notes: flat files (Chapter 01) or SQLite (Chapter 12) need less.
  • Teams unable to operate Postgres. Managed hosting handles provisioning, patching and most backups; tuning, vacuum, extension upgrades and RLS remain yours.

Use cases

Row counts here are assumed sizes.

1Shared documentation assistant

Situation
A team searches 8,000 documentation passages and needs exact error-code matches alongside paraphrases.
Why it fits
SQL combines keyword and vector ranks on the same rows,14 so no second store needs synchronising.
Pair with
Pre-release EXPLAIN and model revision metadata. Chapter 05 covers reranking.

2Per-user assistant memory in a SaaS app

Situation
A support assistant remembers preferences and tickets: 5,000 users, about 2,000 memories each, 10 million rows total.
Why it fits
RLS keeps each user's rows private.15 At 2,000 rows per user, exact user_id-indexed search gives perfect recall. Shared HNSW can underfill even with iterative scans (continuing until enough rows pass the filter); see Gotchas.1
Pair with
Use the partial user index; partition and vector-index large tenants only when filtered exact search misses budget.1 Compare Chapter 11 if tuning still misses latency.

3Booking agent with an audit trail

Situation
A booking agent records "prefers aisle seats" with 200,000 yearly reservations; compliance requires every change logged.
Why it fits
The memory, reservation, audit and outbox rows commit together, preserving the pending Redis cache refresh (Chapter 09).
Pair with
A worker retries pending outbox rows, so refreshes must be safe to repeat. NOTIFY only wakes the worker; a missed one does not lose the row.16 See Chapters 09 and 17.

4Support agent that must match order numbers

Situation
An agent searches 300,000 past tickets. Embeddings blur an error code or order number, and a pure keyword search misses paraphrases.
Why it fits
tsvector with GIN and an HNSW index sit on the same rows, and RRF merges their rankings in one statement.14
Pair with
ParadeDB BM25 if keyword ranking quality matters more than ts_rank_cd.12

5Facts that change over time

Situation
A sales assistant tracks 100,000 customer facts. "Works at Acme" must become "worked at Acme" when the customer moves, without losing history.
Why it fits
A valid_to column marks superseded rows: one transaction closes the old fact and inserts its replacement and audit row. A partial index on null rows keeps current-fact lookups small.
Pair with
A fact-extraction model (Chapter 06). Chapter 14 covers temporal graphs when relations outweigh rows.

Numbers

Result quality. Filtered HNSW can finish quickly yet underfill (see Gotchas).1 Measure count, recall and p95/p99 under expected concurrency. Run pgbench -c CLIENTS -T 60 -l -f read.sql; compute logged transaction-latency percentiles against an exact-search baseline. Exact cost follows eligible rows per user; no universal cutoff applies.

Storage. The documented 4d + 8 bytes for vector(d) gives 1,544 bytes at 384 dimensions, confirmed here.1 Tested table storage was 163,905,536 bytes (156 MiB) for 100,000 rows. Vector-only extrapolations: 1.54 GB per million, 15.44 GB per ten million, excluding text, indexes and replicas; not loaded tests.

Calls and tokens. A raw episode write needs no model call. An extracted memory costs one extraction call (Chapter 06) plus one embedding call. A semantic read costs one query embedding, and ten illustrative 100-token facts add about 1,000 prompt tokens plus wrappers. Keyword-only reads need no embedding call.

Time. Extraction and embedding calls add model time (Chapter 03) where used; the walkthrough timings report SQL time only. Chapter 20 measures caching of repeated finished answers.

Setup walkthrough

Post-cutoff walkthrough test: 2026-11-23, CPU only, with the container limited to 2 CPUs and 4 GB: PostgreSQL/psql 18.7, pgvector 0.8.7. Requires Linux, Bash, Docker, procfs and GNU coreutils; database clients run inside the image. PostgreSQL 19 was not tested. Synthetic vectors test storage, search and permissions, not semantic quality or application latency.

Paste shell blocks into one bash subshell; separate script processes lose start.sh variables needed by cleanup.sh. Save SQL listings by name in the created lab directory. If the directory or container exists, stop and leave it alone. After interruption, restore LAB=/var/tmp/memlab-08, LAB_TOKEN=$(cat "$LAB/.owner") and LAB_REAL=$(cat "$LAB/.path") before cleanup, only for your own run.

Create and index the memory tables

setup.sql creates the episode and memory tables with a user-qualified foreign key, validity dates, embedding provenance and full-text data. It loads 20,000 seeded random vectors, shows plans before and after HNSW, keyword and current-user indexes; exact search suffices here. The fixture assigns users by i % 20 and text by (i / 20) % 4, so each user has all four texts. Fusion asserts keyword-only, vector-only and both-list hits. Bulk loading uses autocommit; the supersession step below demonstrates a transaction. Without i * 0, Postgres would evaluate the ARRAY subquery once, giving all 20,000 rows the same random vector.

sqlch08-code02 · setup.sql68 lines · in this PDF and the companion repositoryTested

The setup inserted two raw turns in 0.287 ms.

Check search, isolation and supersession

recall.sql runs keyword, vector and fused search, compares approximate results with the exact top 10, and tries default, iterative and wider HNSW scans. Searches use stored vectors (id = 1 or 22) as queries, under the table owner before RLS. At LIMIT 50 the vector branch sorts the user-index rows exactly; at LIMIT 10 the planner chooses HNSW, exposing underfill and recovery with iterative or wider scans.1

With HNSW present, materialize filtered current rows in a CTE before sorting for exact search. Fusion needs unrounded RRF ordering, rounding only for display. The keyword parser ANDs terms: extract key terms or use OR; test code tokenization.

Supersession needs a lab repair: row 22 is a travel fact; use preference row 2 with a newly computed embedding. The copied vector is wrong; stale retries can duplicate outbox rows. Enqueue only this transaction's audit RETURNING rows; zero means stale. Validity boundaries match. NOTIFY has no listener here (Chapter 09).

RLS assertions then check unset-identity and Alice/Bob isolation, aborting on failure. Owners bypass RLS unless forced; use a non-owner without BYPASSRLS.15 Set app.user_id with set_config('app.user_id', $1, true) in the query's own transaction to expire at commit; session-level SET survives for the next pooled caller. Only trusted application code may hold this role, deriving identity from authentication; exclude caller- or agent-supplied SQL. After COMMIT, current_setting('app.user_id', true) returns an empty string, hence NULLIF. Both tables reject empty user_id; post-COMMIT isolation is asserted on the same connection.

Gotchas

Gotcha: exact search slows down silently

A bare vector column returns correct answers at any size, only more slowly. Check EXPLAIN before launch and during growth: sorting a whole-table sequential scan may be unintended, while sorting user-index rows is intended exact search. Alert on p99 and rows sorted, not plan shape alone. Chapter 19 reports audit-discovered unindexed search; its fix remains unconfirmed.19

Gotcha: filters shorten the result

HNSW finds distance candidates before the WHERE filter, so it can underfill LIMIT even for thousands of eligible rows (a 5% filter keeps about 2 of 40 candidates). Tested at ef_search 40 and LIMIT 10 on the 100,000-row table, one-user filters averaged 2.025 rows with 20 equal users (5,000 rows each) and 0.005 rows with 5,000 users (20 rows each; 200 queries). Iterative scans raised the mean from 2.025 to 10.000 rows at 5% selectivity but only to 4.015 at 0.02% selectivity (eligible share), where the scan stopped at hnsw.max_scan_tuples (default 20,000). The 10-million-row case was not run. Counts do not measure eligible-top-10 recall. Consider higher ef_search, exact search over a selective user index, partial indexes or partitions.1

Gotcha: incompatible embedding spaces break search

Store immutable model-and-revision IDs in embedding_model and filter the vector branch on them; the fixture names a synthetic space. Re-embed and rebuild the indexes when the model, revision or dimension count changes (Chapter 03), validating the new space before switching reads; a dimension change also needs a second column or shadow table.

Gotcha: churn and old versions

For update-heavy memory, run current pgvector. After bulk updates or re-embedding, watch n_dead_tup and last_autovacuum in pg_stat_user_tables and the size of memories indexes; the README speeds HNSW vacuum with REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY first.1 The changelog lists HNSW vacuum and index-repair fixes in 0.8.3 and 0.8.4.6

Security: IVFFlat index builds

CVE-2026-103484 affects pgvector versions before 0.8.7. A database user permitted to create an IVFFlat index can write data out of bounds during the index build, which could lead to arbitrary code execution. It concerns IVFFlat builds, not ordinary nearest-neighbour queries.20

Upgrade older installations to 0.8.7 or later before allowing IVFFlat index builds; the setup above pins 0.8.7. Its release tag is the version-bump commit of 2026-10-01; the announcement is dated 2026-10-05.6,21,22 Restricting who can create indexes reduces exposure during the upgrade but does not patch the extension.

Verdict

Verdict: the default store once memory is shared

Pick it when Postgres is installed, writes need transactions, users need database isolation, or queries mix filters, keywords and vectors. Start with exact search and add HNSW when it exceeds a p99 SQL budget from your end-to-end latency target, at expected concurrency. Keep per-user search exact as described above; reserve HNSW for shared or large-tenant corpora with iterative scans, partial indexes or partitions.

Reconsider it when latency still misses the target after tuning, or when multi-hop relationships are the core need. Try pgvectorscale (label-filtered or disk-resident search) or VectorChord (quantized IVF with reranking) on dedicated hardware first, then a dedicated vector store (Chapter 11) or graph memory (Chapter 14). Chapter 22 (case study) shows row-level security as a second boundary below a patient-scoped gateway. Chapter 20 combines exact vector search, dated facts and a response cache in a single-user assistant.

Part D · Chapter 09

09

Redis and Valkey

An in-memory server for agent sessions, recent history and vector lookups, backed by a durable store.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

2 of 5

Running cost

3 of 5

Best for

Agents needing fast shared state, with a database as the record.

What it is

Redis is a fast shared notepad for agents: a server that keeps data in RAM in ready-made structures (hashes, lists, streams, sorted sets), with keys that can expire. Valkey is a community fork with the same protocol.

Agents use it for sessions, recent messages and facts, cached answers and worker coordination. Disk writes are optional (snapshots or a log), so a crash can lose recent writes.1

Redis is a hot tier in front of a durable store: Chapter 08’s database stays the record and rebuilds Redis when needed. Chapter 10 covers caching.

Terms new in this chapter

TTL
A key's lifetime, set with EXPIRE.
Hit, miss, eviction
A hit returns a cached result; a miss finds none. Eviction drops keys at the memory limit.
RDB snapshot
A copy of the whole dataset written to disk on a schedule such as save 60 1000 (seconds, then changed keys).1
AOF
Append-only file. A log of every write, flushed to disk under one of three policies: always (each write batch), everysec or no (when the OS decides).1
Stream
An append-only log of entries with ids, read by position or by a group of workers.
Consumer group
A stream feature that hands each entry to one worker in the group and tracks whether it was acknowledged.

HNSW is defined in the Chapter 00 terms box and compared with other index families in Chapter 11. KNN, FLAT and quantization are in the glossary appendix.

How it works

The app names keys such as session:alice; the key's type sets its commands. HGET reads the summary in one round trip; pipeline it with XREVRANGE to fetch history in that round trip too. Redis stores and compares embeddings from your model (Chapter 03) and makes no model call.

EXPIRE sets a TTL on a whole key of any type and removes the key when it fires. Stream and sorted-set entries stay until your code trims them, and Vector Set elements until VREM or key expiry.

Two vector options

Redis 8 has two ways to search by meaning. The Query Engine (formerly the RediSearch module, now in Redis 8) indexes hashes or JSON documents. A vector field can be FLAT, HNSW or (from Redis 8.2) SVS-VAMANA (a graph index with vector compression), in float32 or a narrower type; the figures here are float32 HNSW. One query can filter on tag, numeric and text fields.2 Vector Sets are a separate data type: VADD adds an element, VREM removes it and VSIM searches. With persistence on, the graph is stored in the snapshot and reloaded at restart, so vectors need no re-insert. Recent-write survival depends on the persistence policy and crash type (see the restart test). Docs claim, not tested here.3

Note: two score scales

VSIM ... WITHSCORES returns a score s from 0 to 1, where 1 is identical and 0 is opposite. The module README documents this; a test with three unquantized vectors (identical, orthogonal, opposite) returned 1, 0.5 and 0.4 FT.SEARCH and RedisVL (see the products table) return a distance instead: for cosine, 0 is identical and 2 opposite. Convert thresholds between APIs (cosine index only):

  • Score from cosine similarity: s = (1 + cosine) / 2.
  • Cosine similarity from score: 2s − 1.
  • Cosine distance from score: 2(1 − s).

How the two options differ

AspectQuery Engine indexVector Set
FilteringTag, numeric and text fields in one query. Tested with a tag filter.Filters on per-element attributes; benchmarks/stores/worker.py tests VSETATTR and returns only the match among three.5
MemoryMeasured about 15.3 kB per 1,536-dimension vector (15,306 B, hash plus index).The maintainer reports default 8-bit codes at about 25% of float32 payload space.3 Measured 2,293 B per vector including the graph; hash plus index stores each vector twice, while the Vector Set is quantized.
StatusPart of Redis 8 core.6Beta in the 8.0.0 release notes and still in the 8.10.3 README.6,7

Choose Redis or Valkey: licenses and versions

Default to Redis 8 if AGPLv3 is acceptable; choose Valkey when you need a BSD license. Valkey forks Redis 7.2.4 and stays BSD-3 under the Linux Foundation.8 Redis itself changed license:

  • Redis 7.2 and earlier stay BSD-3; the 7.2.12 patch release of 2 November 2025 still ships the BSD license file.9,10
  • From 20 March 2024, Redis 7.4 and later are available under RSALv2 or SSPLv1.9
  • Redis 8 (1 May 2025) adds AGPLv3 as a third option.11 Its 8.0.0 release notes say the Query Engine, JSON, time series, five probabilistic structures and Vector Sets moved into core.6

Good for and not for

Good for

  • Session state and scratch memory that should expire on its own.
  • The last N messages of a conversation, read on every turn.
  • Shared locks, counters and queues across agent workers.
  • A cache of model answers keyed by meaning.
  • A hot slice of recent facts, refilled from a database.

Not for

  • The only copy of facts that matter. Keep the system of record in Chapter 08's database.
  • A vector corpus larger than RAM. Use a disk-based store (Chapter 11); keep the hot slice here.
  • Multi-record transactions or relational queries (use PostgreSQL).
  • A team that has not approved the AGPL, RSAL or SSPL terms. Use Valkey or review the license.

Use cases

1Support chat: session summary and last messages

Situation
A few thousand open support chats need summaries, ticket ids and the last twenty messages after worker restarts; abandoned chats should expire.
Why it fits
Refresh each chat’s hash and stream with EXPIRE 1800 every turn. XADD appends one message per entry. MAXLEN ~ trims approximately; the stream can exceed the cap. COUNT bounds the read. XREVRANGE history:alice + - COUNT 20 reads the newest twenty, newest first; the app reverses them (step 3).21
Pair with
PostgreSQL (Chapter 08) commits turn and numbered outbox row together. The relay’s Redis script atomically checks sequence, XADDs messages, updates summary/sequence and refreshes both TTLs. Old numbers return “already applied”; missing sessions or gaps trigger a PostgreSQL rebuild. Untested design sketch. Image defaults lose open chats in a crash (restart test below), so also enable the AOF.

2A fleet of workers sharing one job

Situation
Twelve workers watch one task list. Uncoordinated workers can summarize the same user, write conflicting notes and both pay for model calls.
Why it fits
Consumer groups assign each task to one worker. Commit under a unique job id before XACK; XAUTOCLAIM only after the slowest job’s timeout. For different tasks touching one user, SET key value NX PX 30000 grants one lease (a lock with a TTL). Leases reduce overlap; reclaims can repeat model calls. Database uniqueness prevents duplicate commits. The walkthrough tests XREADGROUP, XAUTOCLAIM and XACK. The lock guide accepts single-instance locks where occasional races are acceptable.22
Pair with
Database cases: accept any result with a unique job id; accept only the current owner with fencing (atomically check its database-issued, increasing generation). Calls can outlast leases; failover can lose them or roll back Redis INCR. Token checks on delete only protect another worker’s lease.

3Answer cache for repeated questions

Situation
An internal help bot pays for model calls for paraphrases of one question.
Why it fits
RedisVL's SemanticCache stores answers keyed by the question's embedding and returns one only when a new question is close enough. distance_threshold defaults to 0.1 (lower is stricter).23 Define a tenant tag in filterable_fields, store it on each entry and require its exact match on lookup. Skip shared caching for personalized answers. Key prefixes are not a security boundary: use ACL users and TLS (Chapter 17).
Pair with
Chapter 10, on setting and testing the threshold, exact-key caching and invalidation.

Numbers

Three reruns used 10,000 seeded uniform-random (synthetic) 1,536-dimension vectors; walkthrough environment/date. Timings include serialization. Real embedding clusters can change latency/recall; memory sizing is indicative. Prose-only tests: companion repository, benchmarks/stores.

Scope and scale

QuestionAnswer
JobThe slice read every turn (session summary, last messages, cached answers, leases): a bounded prompt and fewer repeat model calls.
Single-key writeOne command. A chat turn uses several; pipeline to reduce round trips; use MULTI/EXEC for atomic writes, Lua for read-dependent writes. A semantic write adds one embedding call from your model (Chapter 03) and the per-vector RAM measured above.
Single-command readOne round trip, plus one query embedding for a semantic read; medians are above.
GrowthRAM grows linearly with keys and vectors. More users add keys, and more workers add lock and stream traffic.
Breaks firstRAM, then the crash loss window. Snapshot writes retain old and new memory pages. Measure peak parent/child memory under write load; budget replicas and fragmentation (mem_fragmentation_ratio in INFO memory) separately.
Move on whenVectors outgrow the memory budget (Chapter 11 or 08), or facts need history, joins or a durable record (Chapter 08).

Raw float32 sizes are in the Chapter 00 sizing reference. This estimate scales the measured per-vector figure (15,306 B for hash plus index) linearly, though graph overhead can change with size: at 100,000, 1 million and 10 million vectors, hash plus HNSW comes to 1.5 GB, 15.3 GB and 153 GB, a Vector Set to 229 MB, 2.3 GB and 23 GB.

Gotchas

Gotcha: a restart can erase the memory

Image defaults (save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000, appendonly no) lost a seconds-old key after restart: no snapshot had run. With appendfsync everysec the docs report about one second of loss, more with appendfsync no.1 AOF retained its write; process kill leaves the fsync window untested. No host crash was run.

Gotcha: a full server errors or evicts

On 64-bit systems maxmemory defaults to unlimited; set a dataset limit below container/host RAM. At the maxmemory threshold, the default noeviction rejects writes that need more memory and allkeys-lru evicts approximately least-recently-used keys; process RAM can exceed the limit. Run answer caches on an evicting instance and keep sessions, leases and vector-bearing hashes on a non-evicting one: the policy is server-wide, and an evicted hash silently drops out of search results. A test on both servers (limit 2 MB above idle) got write errors under the default and, under LRU, accepted all 4,000 writes and evicted earlier keys.24

Gotcha: release only your own lease

Acquire each lease with a fresh random token; release only your own. Use DELEX key IFEQ value (Redis 8.4 or later), which deletes only on a value match. The walkthrough rejected the wrong token and removed the matching lease with Redis's command, Valkey's DELIFEQ and the compare-and-delete Lua fallback on both servers.22

Unverified: open questions

  • Single-instance tests omit failover, clustered leases/rate limits and database commits.
  • SemanticCache runtime behavior, precision and filtered Vector Set recall at scale remain untested.

Verdict

Verdict: the hot tier, not the record

Pick it for sessions, recent history, answer caches and worker coordination backed by a database.

Default to Query Engine for per-user memory; consider Vector Sets or narrower types at RAM limits. Vector Sets remain beta; test filtered top-10 overlap against brute force before scaling. For BSD choose Valkey’s search bundle (no Vector Sets); its tag-filtered search returned expected matches.8 Keep vectors plus other keys below maxmemory with measured fork/fragmentation headroom. During snapshot/rewrite load, inspect used_memory_peak (INFO memory), rdb_last_cow_size and aof_last_cow_size (INFO persistence). At budget, move vectors to PostgreSQL (Chapter 08) or disk (Chapter 11). Chapter 23 uses regional Redis for sessions/caches, never signed facts.
