Part D · Chapter 10

10

Memcached and the cache layer

A cache keeps recomputable answers, vectors and prefixes so an agent can reuse work.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

1 of 5

Running cost

1 of 5

Best for

Agent apps that repeat prompts, embeddings or tool calls, with a durable store behind them.

What it is

Agents repeat prompts, embeddings and document reads. A cache provides fast, disposable copies, avoiding repeat costs. Memcached stores these copies under keys, in RAM by default, until expiry or eviction.12

Keep facts elsewhere. This chapter covers Memcached, response, semantic, embedding and tool-result caches, provider prompt caching and local inference-level reuse.

Terms new in this chapter

Prompt prefix
A prompt’s start; requests share one when their first tokens match.
KV cache
Attention keys and values for a prompt, unrelated to key-value stores. Reuse skips re-reading the prefix.
Semantic cache
Matches questions by meaning, not exact text.
Cache key, authorization scope
A key names a stored value; authorization scope identifies who may reuse it.
Cache control
A provider marker or option selecting prompt blocks for reuse.
Slab class, CAS
Memcached pools similar-sized items in slab classes and evicts within each. CAS (compare-and-swap) uses a token from a versioned read; writes with stale tokens fail.
Hit, miss, TTL, eviction
A hit finds a usable entry; a miss does not. TTL limits serving time; eviction drops entries early for space (Chapter 09).

How it works

Applications manage Figure 1’s first four layers. Memcached serves exact-key lookups; semantic lookup needs a vector-capable store such as Redis. Providers or inference servers manage the last two.

The six layers

LayerWhat it stores and matches onLifetime guidance
Exact-match response cacheA finished answer keyed by hashed model, parameters, prompt, authorization scope and data version.Minutes to hours. Bump the data version on write.
Semantic cacheAn answer matched by question embedding within a distance threshold (lower is stricter). Examples: GPTCache,4 RedisVL,5 Redis,6 Amazon ElastiCache.7Short, and only after hit precision is measured.
Embedding cacheA vector, keyed by pinned model revision, preprocessing settings and text hash.Long or none. Changing any of these changes the key.
Tool-result cacheRead-only tool output keyed by tool, arguments and authorization scope.Bound the TTL by permitted staleness. Cache user-dependent reads only with authorization scope and data version in the key.
Provider prompt cacheProvider-held state for a repeated prefix, excluding answers; re-reads cost less.Anthropic’s documented default: 5-minute retention. Prices and thresholds under Numbers.8
Inference-level reuseThe engine keeps or restores prompt-prefix KV state.Until the engine evicts it or the file is deleted.

Memcached keys and defaults

Memcached stores opaque bytes under keys. set writes a value and get reads it back. It has no data structures or vector search. Keys are limited to 250 bytes, and the protocol forbids whitespace and control characters.

Hash prompts, validate keys client-side and avoid tabs/control bytes even if accepted.1

Flash, restart and expiry are cache features

  • Extstore moves colder values to flash and keeps keys and the hash table in RAM.19
  • Warm restart keeps items in a memory-mapped file, recording metadata at graceful shutdown. It requires a stable clock; missed sets/deletes during restart can leave stale entries. The cache starts empty if -m, -I, slab chunk sizes, -C (CAS) or slab reassignment differ from the previous run. Extstore is documented as incompatible.3
  • Expiry up to 2,592,000 seconds (30 days) is relative; larger values are Unix timestamps. Eviction reclaims least-recently-used items within each slab class; watch the per-class evicted counters before raising memory.12

Local servers

  • llama.cpp server: --slot-save-path plus POST /slots/{id}?action=save or restore saves or restores a slot’s KV state (one server-side conversation context).14 Saved prompts are readable; treat files as sensitive.
  • LM Studio MLX engine: loads previously seen prompt KV state from disk; see the cited configuration guide.15
  • oMLX: persists KV cache blocks to SSD; see its configuration guide (checked 20 November 2026).16
  • vLLM: reuses matching prompt-prefix KV state to cut prompt-processing work.17
  • LMCache (repository checked 20 November 2026): a self-run, Apache-2.0 layer that offloads KV state from GPU memory to CPU RAM, local disk or remote backends and shares it across requests and engines. It saves prompt-processing work, not provider billing.18

Good for and not for

Good for

  • Identical requests permitting replay: FAQ questions from, or normalised to, a fixed list. Repeating templates around changing records suit provider prompt caching.
  • Embedding the same text repeatedly: re-indexing, retries, repeated chunks.
  • Read-only tool calls repeated within a short window.
  • Cheap shared caching across app servers already running Memcached.
  • Long stable system prompts or document prefixes, through provider prompt caching.

Not for

  • Agent memory: facts about a user, decisions, task state. Use a durable store (Chapter 08; Chapter 11 for embedding retrieval).
  • Answers that depend on per-user state when the key cannot carry that scope.
  • Matching by meaning: Memcached alone has no vector search. Use RedisVL or GPTCache with strict thresholds.
  • Medical, legal or financial actions where a stale hit does harm.
  • Persistence, data structures or queue semantics. Use Redis or Valkey.

Use cases

1FAQ bot with repeated questions

Situation
A support bot pays per model call for a few hundred recurring questions through one template.
Why it fits
An exact-match response cache uses the layers-table key with fixed public scope and FAQ version as data version. Each repeat needs one get for a listed or normalised question; hashing keeps keys under the 250-byte limit.1
Pair with
A minutes-to-hours TTL; bump the data version when answers change. Skip it for questions that depend on the signed-in user.

2Re-ingesting a document library

Situation
A nightly job re-embeds all 20,000 chunks though few changed.
Why it fits
For repeatable embeddings, store vectors by text hash, pinned model revision and preprocessing settings. Only new or edited chunks need embedding (figures under Numbers).
Pair with
A vector-store index (Chapter 11). Flushing the cache forces re-embedding.

3Agent that keeps calling a read-only tool

Situation
A research agent repeatedly fetches slow or rate-limited exchange rates or documentation each hour.
Why it fits
Key tool results by tool name, arguments and authorization scope. Set TTL to accepted staleness: minutes for exchange rates, hours for documentation.
Pair with
State-dependent read keys require authorization scope and relevant data version. Keep the authoritative copy elsewhere. Never cache state-changing calls; a write must bump the changed data’s version.

4Long system prompt on a hosted model

Situation
A coding agent’s repeated long instructions and tool definitions dominate its input bill.
Why it fits
Anthropic bills a cached prefix at a fraction of base input, from 0.025x for Fable/Mythos 5.2 to 0.1x for Haiku 5.5 (per-model prices are on the pricing page).8 Memcached is not involved.
Pair with
Usage fields cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens; nonzero reads on the second call confirm reuse.

5Local agent on llama.cpp with a big prefix

Situation
A local agent reloads a large prompt each session, delaying its first answer.
Why it fits
llama.cpp can save a slot's KV state to disk and restore it, reusing a compatible prefix. Check timings.cache_n and prompt_n to confirm the reuse, and time it on your hardware.14
Pair with
Restricted permissions on the save folder.

6Pilot of a semantic cache

Situation
Support teams want paraphrased questions to share answers, but "Cancel my order" and "cancel my subscription" must not.
Why it fits
RedisVL’s SemanticCache separates near matches with a distance threshold, TTL and metadata filters.5
Pair with
Hit precision measured on real logs before launch.

Local reuse timings

Supplemental verification after the research cutoff, 23 November 2026: llama.cpp b12464, CPU only, two threads, Qwen2.5-0.5B Q4_K_M. A saved 889-token slot reused 888 tokens and processed one after restart. What a hit saves, and sizing

A cache tells the model nothing new; it saves work by layer:

  • Exact-match response cache: a hit costs one lookup and zero model calls or tokens.
  • Embedding cache: a hit makes no embedding call, a miss one.
  • Semantic cache: a lookup generally embeds the query even on a hit.5
  • Provider prompt caches and inference-level reuse: they still generate output tokens and skip only reusable input processing.17

Capacity estimate: payload RAM = users × entries/user × bytes/entry. At 1,000 users × 100 entries × 8 KiB, that is about 781 MiB, while 256 MiB item memory (-m 256) fits at most 32,768 such payloads, fewer after keys, item headers and slab rounding. All 100,000 cannot coexist; expect evictions.

Watch the stats command (get_hits, get_misses, evictions) and, per slab class, stats items: rising evictions with a falling hit rate signal a capacity problem.2

Worked example: embedding cache on a re-ingest (counts are assumed)

RunEmbedding-model callsCache hits
First ingest, 20,000 chunks20,0000
Re-ingest, 400 chunks edited40019,600
Re-ingest after switching embedding model20,0000

Re-ingest makes 98 percent fewer embedding calls; the third misses on model-revision change. Memory cost: 20,000 vectors of 1,536 float32 numbers take about 117 MiB raw, before per-item overhead (bytes per vector: Chapter 00). The walkthrough stores float32 bytes but returns original floats on misses, rounded floats on hits; its fixture hides the difference. An undersized cache drops items for re-embedding: slower, never wrong.

Gotchas

Gotcha: unsecured defaults

Authentication and TLS are off by default. Bind privately; firewall or tunnel access from untrusted hosts.

Gotcha: the cache must not be the only copy

Write the source of truth to a durable store first, so a miss is only slower, never wrong.

Gotcha: stale or cross-user answers

Include authorization scope, model, parameters, prompt and data version in every response key. Memcached cannot delete by prefix. Commit data and its version together; fill from the same snapshot under that version. New-version readers cannot hit old entries, which age out. Missing scope risks cross-user answers; missing versions risk stale advice.

Gotcha: semantic false hits

Questions that read alike can need opposite answers. Tighten the threshold (walkthrough step 3), gate by metadata, and measure hit precision on real logs first.5

Gotcha: prompt-cache misses are silent

Anthropic documents silent misses below the minimum prefix length; check usage counters. An entry is available only after the first response starts, so parallel requests on a cold prefix can all miss; start one first, then fan out.8

Gotcha: a stampede on one key

Popular-entry expiry can send many workers to the model together. Within one process, share one in-progress fill per key. Across processes, Memcached add creates a short-lived lease only if absent; only the successful caller fills. On a failed add, back off and recheck. Size the lease for slow fills, and tolerate duplicate work if one outlasts it.

Verdict

Verdict: use a cache, never as memory

Add a cache layer when prompts, texts or tool calls repeat. Count repeated requests, unchanged chunks and shared prefixes within provider retention; measure hit precision and savings per hit. Adopt layers whose savings exceed lookup, write and storage costs. Include full authorization scope in response keys. Choose Memcached for existing installations or exact-match bytes with TTLs; otherwise reuse Redis or Valkey.

For shared state or persistence choose Redis or Valkey (Chapter 09); for semantic matching choose a vector index (Chapter 11). Keep required facts durably (Chapter 08 or 11). Chapter 22 applies these keys to a regulated office: actor, patient, task, policy and data version.

Part D · Chapter 11

11

Dedicated vector stores

Searches vectors and metadata, with indexes and storage for large or multi-vector memory collections.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

2 of 5

Running cost

3 of 5

Best for

Tenants, large corpora or multi-vector pages outgrowing general databases.

What it is

A dedicated vector store is a database that finds memories by meaning. It saves each memory as an embedding (Chapter 03), text and metadata; a query vector retrieves the nearest vectors and their metadata.

General database vector columns do this too. In pgvector, a scan of every eligible vector is exact, and a query through a graph index (HNSW) or cluster index (IVFFlat) is approximate. PostgreSQL also offers ACID transactions and joins with ordinary tables (Chapter 08).1 Dedicated stores add search-focused filtering and object-storage designs.2,3 Coverage includes servers, services, embedded stores and libraries; sqlite-vec appears briefly here, fully in Chapter 12.

Terms new in this chapter

Payload
Metadata saved beside a vector, such as a user id or timestamp.
Collection, namespace
A named group of records; isolation and filtering guarantees vary by store.
MaxSim
Late-interaction models (Chapter 04) emit a vector per image patch or token. MaxSim sums each query vector's best page-vector similarity; rank pages by decreasing score.

Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes skip vectors, trading recall@k (share of true top k returned) for speed. Chapters 03 and 05 explain embeddings, quantization and hybrid ranking. User id is the examples' tenant key.

How it works

Save embedded memories, text and metadata. Embed questions, search the permitted tenant and put the top k hits into the prompt.

Index families in plain words

FamilyHow it worksWhat it trades
FlatCompares the query with every vector.Exact results, but cost grows linearly with the corpus.
IVFSplits vectors into clusters and scans only the few nearest clusters.Faster than flat, but misses neighbors in unscanned clusters.
HNSWA layered near-neighbor graph, mostly in RAM, searched by node-to-node hops (below).4Fast and accurate, but memory-hungry.
Disk graphs (DiskANN)A graph designed for SSD.5Handles data larger than RAM, with slower hops.
Scalar and product quantizationShrink each vector to fewer bits or to a short code.4Less memory, some recall lost.
Binary quantizationKeeps one bit per dimension, with full vectors on disk to rerank candidates.6Up to 32x smaller than float32, but it needs reranking to keep recall.

Milvus lists DiskANN and HNSW among its index options.5

HNSW parameters

Conventional HNSW names are M, efConstruction and efSearch. In pgvector, m limits links per node per layer (layer 0 allows twice that). Graph links add to raw-vector storage; doubling m roughly doubles this overhead. ef_construction sets the build candidate-list size (higher: better recall, slower builds). hnsw.ef_search sets the query candidate-list size (higher: generally better recall, higher cost). Qdrant calls them m, ef_construct and hnsw_ef: defaults 16, 100 and 100. pgvector defaults are m 16, ef_construction 64 and hnsw.ef_search 40. A non-iterative pgvector scan also caps returned rows at hnsw.ef_search; iterative scans (below) continue.1 Tune query breadth first (pgvector hnsw.ef_search; Qdrant hnsw_ef), measuring latency and recall@k against exact filtered search (Numbers).

Metadata filtering: before, during or after the search

Pre-filtering restricts candidates before scoring, often scanning matches directly. in-graph filtering checks predicates during traversal. post-filtering drops mismatches afterward, potentially returning fewer than k results. Chapter 08 demonstrates pgvector HNSW post-filtering. Qdrant filters in the graph, or scans exactly when few points match; check other stores separately. In Qdrant, tenant payload indexes add tenant-specific graph links. Create them before ingest; filtering improves at the cost of slower builds and larger graphs.2

In pgvector, filtering follows the index scan. If 10% of candidates match the tenant, a non-iterative scan with hnsw.ef_search = 40 returns about four matching rows on average. Set hnsw.iterative_scan to relaxed_order or strict_order (default: off) to continue until enough rows match, index exhaustion or a resource limit (hnsw.max_scan_tuples or hnsw.scan_mem_multiplier). Relaxed order may slightly misorder distances. Selective filters can still hit that limit (Numbers). Use partial indexes for a few predicates; for many tenants, consider PostgreSQL partitions, Qdrant graph filtering or store namespaces.1,2 Qdrant filters support nested AND, OR and NOT clauses.2

Hybrid search

Vector search struggles with exact names, ids and rare words. Hybrid search blends keyword rankings such as BM25 with vector rankings, usually through reciprocal-rank fusion (Chapter 05). Qdrant 1.20 documents BM25 ranking on a full-text index over stored text, so the client builds no sparse vectors; the walkthrough instead shows unfused LanceDB searches.7

Good for and not for

Do you need one at all

Stay on PostgreSQL until filtered recall or p95 misses your target, the index exceeds RAM, or multi-vector pages require reconsideration. Record exact in-tenant top-k ids and latency; if too slow, test ANN against those ids and remeasure latency. pgvector gives no switching threshold.1

Good for

  • Selective filters: tenant-scoped search prevents other tenants consuming candidate budgets. Measure recall against exact in-tenant search.
  • Corpora too large for one machine's RAM, using disk graphs, quantization or object storage.
  • Multi-vector pages: hundreds of vectors per document.
  • Hybrid keyword and vector queries in one API.
  • Teams that want a managed service for index tuning.

A server or managed store is not for

  • One user's local notes: use an embedded store (use case 1) or SQLite (Chapter 12).
  • Transactional joins with relational data: use PostgreSQL (Chapter 08).
  • Offline devices: use embedded stores (use case 5).

Index libraries return vector ids; applications must synchronize text, tenant permissions and deletes.

Use cases

1Local memory for a desktop or command-line agent

Situation
A laptop agent needs persistent semantic search over thousands of notes.
Why it fits
Chroma and LanceDB persist local directories in process; LanceDB is pre-v1.19,20 For one .db file, use dependency-free C sqlite-vec (Chapter 12; pre-v1).23 Pin versions.
Pair with
Chapter 12 for SQLite. Avoid a second daemon for one user.

2Millions of memories across many tenants

Situation
A hosted assistant serves mostly small tenants; queries must stay within their tenant.
Why it fits
Qdrant filters during the graph search;2 Numbers compares filtered recall with unequal search budgets. For RAM-resident Qdrant, share one collection; on turbopuffer and Pinecone, give each tenant a namespace, since idle namespaces sit in object storage, not RAM.3,15
Pair with
For tenant-only Qdrant, mark the tenant keyword index is_tenant; m=0 skips the global graph and payload_m=16 builds tenant-specific links. Retain a global graph for fast cross-tenant searches.26 Avoid post-filter-only designs for selective filters.

3Very large corpora

Situation
Years of cold documents exceed one machine's RAM.
Why it fits
Milvus is distributed with many index types.5 S3 Vectors suits cold tiers, and AWS says infrequent queries return in under one second (a vendor claim, not run here).27
Pair with
Quantization with full-vector reranking. Avoid single-node RAM-only HNSW at this size.

4Multi-vector pages from Chapter 04

Situation
Scanned PDFs use a late-interaction model such as ColQwen2: up to 768 visual patches plus text tokens.28
Why it fits
Qdrant supports late interaction with a MaxSim comparator (its API calls these multivectors). The walkthrough queries two stored synthetic pages.29
Pair with
Shortlist before MaxSim reranking. Budget 197 GB raw per million pages (Numbers).

5Offline or edge use

Situation
A field device or Raspberry Pi needs memory without reliable networking.
Why it fits
Milvus Lite targets laptops and edge devices with Python.21 usearch keeps a small footprint.25 sqlite-vec (Chapter 12) runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, WASM and Raspberry Pi.23
Pair with
Sync to a server later. Avoid managed-only services, which have no offline mode.

Numbers

Managed-service latency and quotas remain untested. Measure recall@k and p95/p99 (95th/99th percentile latencies).

Tested: 100,000 seeded 384-dimension vectors, 200 queries per filter, LIMIT 10, CPU only (benchmarks/stores/ch11-filter.py). Mean recall@10 is exact in-tenant top-ten ids recovered divided by ten, averaged over queries.

Configuration10%: mean rows / recall@105,000 tenants: mean rows / recall@10
pgvector, hnsw.ef_search=403.925 / 37.85%0.005 / 0.05%
strict_order, default scan limits10 / 87.15%4.115 / 28.85%

Predicate-specific partial HNSW10 / 93.95%10 / 100%

Ground truth is exact tenant-scoped PostgreSQL search; Qdrant exact=True matched all 200 queries at each filter. Qdrant used m=16, ef_construct=100, not the tenant-only layout above. Unequal search breadth (pgvector 40, Qdrant 100) prevents isolating filter placement. Qdrant may scan small tenants exactly. One build per store; no throughput claim. Shared memory/disk pressure invalidate latency comparisons; higher scan limits trade time for recall.

The selective filter has 20 rows. Default iterative limits include hnsw.max_scan_tuples=20,000. Partial indexes cover queried predicates; per-tenant maintenance was not tested. For small tenants, benchmark indexed tenant lookup with exact scoring.

Tested: in a local MongoDB Atlas container with 100,000 384-dimension vectors, CPU only, one build per mode, index files shrank 3.221x with scalar quantization and 15.680x with binary. Only unquantized files include full vectors; quantized files exclude reranking vectors, so total disk savings are smaller. Graph links do not shrink. These ratios neither measure MongoDB's RAM metric nor verify Atlas Required Memory or peak RAM.

Scope and scale

Retrieval supplies context without judging memories' truth. Latency includes embedding and store time; the walkthrough tests correctness only. Retrieving a new memory in the same turn requires searchable writes; Qdrant scripts use wait=True. Elsewhere, probe a same-tenant write then read; record time-to-visible. Beyond the turn budget, read the write store or wait explicitly.

  • Per write or read (one unbatched item): one embedding call plus an upsert or a search. Five 200-token hits add about 1,000 input tokens to the answer (estimate).
  • Capacity: see the Chapter 00 sizing reference. 1,000 users x 1,000 memories at 1536 dimensions in float32 is the 6.1 GB row above; 100,000 users need 614.4 GB, and indexes, text and replicas add more (estimates). A 16 GB RAM budget cannot hold three million such vectors uncompressed (18.432 GB); multi-vector pages hit it sooner.
  • Concurrency: 100 agents making one lookup per second need 100 searches and 100 query embeddings per second, before batching or caching.

Measure RAM-resident HNSW memory at target size and p95 at target concurrency. Measure object-backed cold and warm store p95 separately from embedding time. If recall misses its target, test filtering or search breadth; if RAM is exceeded, trial disk-backed search. No universal row threshold applies. Chapter 10's cache handles repeated lookups.

Gotchas

Gotcha: churn and traps

  • Pre-v1 components change APIs. sqlite-vec's docs site labels v0.1.10-alpha.4 but its latest GitHub release is v0.1.9: pin one.
  • LanceDB's create_fts_index is deprecated as of 0.25.0, though online examples still show it.
  • A client-supplied filter is not authentication; derive it from the authenticated tenant.

Migration and lock-in

Keep stable ids, tenant metadata, model/preprocessing revisions and embedding inputs; for scans, keep PDFs and page mappings or images alongside extracted text. Snapshot consistently, record the change-log position, load the target and compare recall@k on identical queries. Replay subsequent upserts and deletes in order; pause writes, drain the log, compare per-tenant counts, verify deleted ids are absent and switch. Keep the old store read-only until acceptance; rollback is a config change only while writes stay paused. Retain the log after writes resume. For rollback, pause writes, replay post-cutover upserts/deletes into the old store, verify catch-up and switch back. Re-embed when the model changes (Chapter 03). Milvus Lite 3.x cannot open a 2.x .db in place.21

Verdict

Verdict: use one when filters, tenants or size force it

Pick a dedicated store when PostgreSQL misses product recall and p95 targets. Budget store time within the turn; measure recall against exact filtered results. For MaxSim, shortlist densely, then trial native reranking if application reranking misses that deadline. Qdrant, Chroma and LanceDB passed toy tests; filtered recall used synthetic vectors. Weaviate structured filters, turbopuffer and Pinecone namespaces, Milvus at scale and S3 Vectors remain untested.

Avoid server stores for single-file notes (Chapter 12) or relational joins (Chapter 08). Chapter 23's homebuilder starts on pgvector, reconsidering for page multi-vectors.

Part D · Chapter 12

12

SQLite and other stores

One database holds text, keyword index and vectors rebuilt from JSONL; the survey compares other stores.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

2 of 5

Running cost

1 of 5

Best for

One desktop app or agent with searchable local memory.

What it is

A laptop assistant stores notes, a keyword index and per-note vectors in one database file. SQLite provides FTS5 keyword search; sqlite-vec adds the vec0 vector table. Both run through one in-process connection, without a server.1,2 Pick it when one user or host owns the memory.

The JSONL log is the source of truth; searches read a rebuilt SQLite index. The survey compares neighboring stores. Memory kinds (semantic, episodic, procedural) follow CoALA.3

Terms used in this chapter

JSONL
One JSON object per line; here, the append-only event log.
Materializer
Rebuilds the database from the log; materialize() builds a fresh file or in-memory index.
Supersede
A correction naming the event IDs it replaces as parents.
Tombstone
A log entry recording a deletion.
WAL
Write-ahead logging: a journal mode that lets readers continue during a write.

How it works

Write. An add transaction atomically writes a memories row, FTS5 entry and vec0 vector under one row ID, preserving crash consistency.

Read. Non-empty text merges two searches. Skip embedding and recall for blank queries: they return nothing. This fixture has no vector-only mode. FTS5 returns keyword matches ordered by BM25 (a keyword relevance score).1 vec0 returns nearest vectors (k-nearest-neighbor search, KNN; exact here) through embedding MATCH ? AND k = ?, by L2 distance (straight-line Euclidean distance; smaller is nearer). For cosine ranking, unit-normalize stored and query vectors; record preprocessing (Chapter 03).2 Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) adds 1 / (60 + rank) per list containing an item; rank 1 is best (60 is usual; see Chapter 05 for BM25 and RRF).

Log underneath. Events contain IDs, keys, operations and parent IDs; materialization rebuilds live state.

Worked example from the test. laptop:1 puts the preference "metric". laptop:2 supersedes it with "imperial", the sole live value. laptop:3 deletes the key permanently; retrying laptop:1 cannot revive it. Replay is arrival-order independent, using an explicit stack for deep histories:

EventWhat it doesRules
putCreates the first value for a key.Takes no parents.
supersedeReplaces earlier values, each named as a parent.Parents must be puts or supersedes of the same key. A supersede missing a parent waits, out of the live index.
deleteRemoves the key.Permanent: recreating the item needs a new key. Takes no parents.

Puts are ready immediately; supersedes wait until every parent is present and ready. Ready values stay live until superseded. Multiple live values are contested; rebuilds exclude them.

Log and SQLite commits are separate: acknowledged corrections and deletes leave stale search results. Block freshness-sensitive reads until a published rebuild includes the acknowledged event (Chapter 17). Without log keys or source event IDs, this fixture cannot validate search candidates against live state.

  • Conflict: supersede changes; give episodes distinct keys. To resolve contention, the app or user appends a supersede naming every live event for that key, then materializes again; only the agreed value enters search.
  • Erasure: a delete is logical; old log bytes keep the text. Protect live logs and databases with file permissions and OS full-disk encryption. Physical erasure needs retention and compaction policies covering archives, backups and derived database files and journals (Chapter 17).

Where SQLite and the other options fit

RoutePick it whenBoundary
SQLite + sqlite-vec 0.1.9You want local keyword and vector search in one file.1,2Pre-v1; pin the version. One host and writer; benchmark exact scans.
libSQL / TursoYou ship a mobile or edge app and want native vector columns.4A different engine and API; verify its sync contract.
DuckDB + vssYou analyze archived episodes in batches.Experimental; its index must fit in RAM (measured in this chapter’s Numbers section).5
MariaDB 11.8 LTS (VECTOR)You run MariaDB and need semantic recall beside tenant data.6Server administration; measure filtered recall.
Browser SQLite / wa-sqliteYou need an offline SQLite database inside a browser page.7From docs, not run; vectors unestablished. Retain exports and a server copy.

Framework checkpoints and provider conversation state resume runs, not fact stores (Chapter 13).8,9 For the earlier taxonomy, keep procedures in reviewable files and tasks in a tracker such as Beads (Chapter 01).10

Good for and not for

Good for

  • Personal disk memory for one agent or desktop app.
  • Keyword and vector search merged in application code.
  • A JSONL event log written before any other store.
  • Serialized writes owned by one host.
  • Exact scans within the query latency budget.

Not for

  • Several hosts writing one memory: use PostgreSQL (Chapter 08).
  • Network filesystems: WAL shares memory, requiring all connections on one host; network filesystems were not tested.11
  • Exact scans exceeding the query latency budget: benchmark an approximate index (Chapter 11).
  • The browser as the only copy of user memory.

Use cases

1Personal assistant on one laptop

Situation
A desktop assistant needs semantic search over one user’s notes; Markdown folders lack it.
Why it fits
One file combines FTS5 keyword and sqlite-vec vector search in Python.1,2
Pair with
The JSONL log as the source of truth and an embedding model (Chapter 03).

2Coding agent that must find exact identifiers

Situation
A coding agent recalls function names, errors and paths. Vector search blurs them; a word index misses fragments.
Why it fits
FTS5’s trigram tokenizer (walkthrough step 2) matches identifier substrings; the local check tests the feature, not retrieval quality.1 Vector hits catch paraphrases.
Pair with
Quote every user term before MATCH (see the query-grammar gotcha).

3Mobile vectors, browser storage (from docs, not run)

Situation
An offline phone app needs vectors without native extensions; a web app needs offline SQLite.
Why it fits
libSQL provides indexed vector columns without an extension.4 wa-sqlite runs SQLite in a browser page,7 but this chapter shows no vector search there.
Pair with
A server copy, the browser checks and sync rules below.

4Scoring last month's agent runs

Situation
A team wants sessions that ended in a tool error from rotated JSONL files.
Why it fits
DuckDB scans, joins and aggregates large tables for analysis; keep live writes elsewhere.
Pair with
Independent archives and a hot SQLite index (suggested, not measured).

5Multi-tenant memory next to existing data

Situation
A product runs MariaDB for tenants and permissions and needs per-user memory reads.
Why it fits
MariaDB's VECTOR type and index allow tenant filtering and distance sorting under existing backups and grants.6
Pair with
Measure filtered recall and check the server index plan (Chapter 11).

Numbers

No generative model needed. Probes: benchmarks/stores in the companion repository.

  • Exact search over 10,000 vectors per user evaluates 10,000 L2 distances (3.84 million float components): 15.36 MB of 384-dimension float32 vectors. The 100-user reference layout holds 1.536 GB (about 1.43 GiB); scanning all 100 users evaluates one million distances (384 million components) per query; a per-user file scans only 10,000 vectors (Chapter 00).
  • Shared CPU host, hardware unrecorded: the stores probe (SQLite 3.46.1; sqlite-vec 0.1.9, k = 10) timed 200 serial vec0 queries over 100,000 384-dimension vectors: median 138.6 ms, 95th percentile 154.4 ms. This older SQLite differs from the walkthrough pin; treat timing as order-of-magnitude only. It covers vector SQL and row fetch, not hybrid recall.
  • SQLite permits one writer. With two connections, the second used a 50 ms timeout (the walkthrough uses 5000 ms). It read the committed snapshot during the first’s uncommitted write; its write waited about 50 ms, then failed with "database is locked". This tests contention, not throughput.11
  • In one CPU-only build with a 32 MiB buffer limit, building DuckDB's graph-based vector index (HNSW, hierarchical navigable small world) over 100,000 384-dimension vectors grew process memory from about 138 MiB to 210 MiB: the limit did not cap the RAM-resident index. These measure whole-process memory.

Count embedding and prompt tokens with their respective models’ tokenizers (Chapter 03). Measure log replay, query embedding and KNN search separately. If replay dominates, checkpoint derived state and replay the tail; if KNN dominates, benchmark an indexed alternative (Chapter 11).

Setup walkthrough

Require loaded SQLite 3.51.3 or later, or backports 3.44.6/3.50.7; verify FTS5 and sqlite-vec load. Linux requires CPython 3.14, venv, curl, unzip and a C compiler. Start a separate bash shell: it uses set -e and exports LD_LIBRARY_PATH. Save named listings in lab/. Post-cutoff validation on 23 November 2026 supplements the 22 November research cutoff: CPU only, a 32-thread consumer CPU, Python 3.14.4, SQLite 3.51.3 (locally compiled) and sqlite-vec 0.1.9. Text and four-dimensional synthetic vectors test correctness, not retrieval quality, without models or datasets.

One trusted process owns the log. Never overlap events() with append or rotation: reads can repair tails and need write permission. Use a local filesystem honoring fsync. File sync makes bytes durable; parent-directory sync makes the new filename durable before truncating the old log. Choose JSONL for grep, DuckDB scans and device export despite broken SQLite schemas or extensions. Without that need, a separate SQLite events database replaces fsync, tail repair and rotation code with journaling.

  1. Install sqlite-vec in a virtual environment

    Pin sqlite-vec 0.1.9.12 CPython must allow extension loading (check: python3.14 -c "import sqlite3; sqlite3.connect(':memory:').enable_load_extension(True)") and link libsqlite3 dynamically. Fixture compiles SQLite 3.51.3 with FTS5 for the WAL fix and asserts the loaded version.13

  2. Write the memory module

    WAL allows reads during writes; busy_timeout makes another writer wait up to 5000 ms. The FTS5 table uses content='memories', indexing that table without copying text.1 quote() wraps every word in double quotes so FTS5 treats each as a literal and joins them with OR: one matching word recalls a row and BM25 ranks it (a space join would require every word). hybrid() runs both searches and the row lookups in one read transaction and fuses the lists with RRF; remove_indexed_row() removes indexed rows. User deletion appends a tombstone, then rebuilds; log keys lack row-ID mappings. A collection is one database file per embedding identity. Call add only outside an existing transaction: it can commit or roll back caller work. Initialization errors before identity checks or during schema creation can leak connections; harden connect before production.

    For substrings, replace the FTS5 declaration with fts5(content, content='memories', content_rowid='id', tokenize='trigram'); substrings under three characters match nothing. For existing databases, recreate this table, rebuild from memories and rerun the recall check.

    Builds the SQLite keyword and vector recall index.

  3. Write and reopen the database

    Separate processes test persistence. Three rows with a two-candidate pool test fusion: keywords rank A, B, vectors rank C, B, and B wins with 2/62 against 1/61. B holds one query word, so the OR join matters. Other assertions check embedding identity, empty text, invalid vectors, mid-query deletion, caller-transaction rejection and competing removals.

  4. Make the log the source of truth

    Newlines complete records. Acknowledge appends after file and directory syncs succeed; retry lost acknowledgements with identical IDs and payloads. Recovery truncates unfinished final records; malformed records and conflicting IDs raise errors. Generate IDs once (production UUIDs; demo device:counter). episodic_log.py accepts any memory kind; the fixture discards kind and indexes everything as semantic. Preserve kind if filtering by it.

    Log.append() replays all part files per append; rotation cannot bound write cost. Writers can cache events and rescan on startup. Rotation fsyncs a copy, publishes it atomically, syncs the directory, then truncates the active file. Interrupted rotation leaves duplicates; replay deduplicates by event ID.14

    pythonch12-code03 · episodic_log.py147 lines · in this PDF and the companion repositoryTested

    Durable event log with causal validation and pending corrections.

  5. Test replay, faults, sync and restore

    materialize(events, path, embed) returns an open, fresh database excluding contested keys. SQL checks all rows independently of search. Restore checkpoints, closes and syncs a fresh disk database, then publishes and reopens it. Switch stopped consumers to a never-used basename without old journals or sidecars. Only first publication is tested. Toy callback tests visibility, not quality.

    Supply a production embedding callback, cached by content hash plus embedding identity. On each write, append, rebuild a fresh file and switch stopped consumers. Measure this pause against the write-visibility budget; beyond it, implement and test incremental updates: retain keys and source event IDs, track log position, recompute affected keys including pending children and tombstones, and commit index changes with that position. Review contested keys with [k for k, v in state(events).items() if len(v) > 1]. Tests cover dependencies, supersedes, deletion, partial appends, rotation faults, corruption and restore; episode has conflicting puts.

Sync rules (not tested)

Network sync, browser persistence and browser vector search were not tested. The rules below make retries harmless and track ordered ingestion:

  • Accept: authenticate devices and authorize keys. In one transaction, insert under a unique event ID and assign a server sequence; commit durably, then acknowledge that sequence. An identical retry returns the original sequence; changed payloads are rejected.
  • Pull: devices save pulled events locally before advancing their saved last-seen server sequence number.
  • Conflicts: the server applies the same parent checks, so contested facts stay contested.
  • Tombstones: retain through exports, imports, restores and backups for the longest supported offline-device and backup period, preventing deleted facts from re-entering context; older devices require full resync (Chapter 17).

Browser storage (not tested)

For browser SQLite, start from wa-sqlite's demo/hello at revision 205eed5, which registers IDBBatchAtomicVFS, a virtual filesystem storing database pages in IndexedDB.7,15 The default demo is in-memory; AccessHandlePoolVFS allows one wa-sqlite instance and cannot directly import or export OPFS (origin-private filesystem) files.7,16 Require these checks in every supported browser:

  • Reload: commit, reload and query a memory. Restored editor SQL proves nothing: it uses separate storage. The reset parameter clears storage.
  • Export and restore: export events, including supersedes and tombstones, outside browser storage; restore a fresh database and verify deletions survive.
  • Vectors: for browser vector recall, load your vector implementation, reopen a persisted fixture offline and get the expected nearest row.
  • Multi-tab: allow one writer, or use a backend with coordinated connections; desktop WAL behavior does not carry over.
  • Storage loss: handle refused writes and eviction; browser storage is best-effort by default and users can delete even persistent storage.17

Gotchas

Gotcha: upgrade the SQLite library used by your app

SQLite documents a rare WAL-reset race that can corrupt a WAL-mode database when threads or processes write or checkpoint at once, likely present in SQLite 3.7.0 through 3.51.2; use 3.51.3 or later, or the backports 3.44.6 or 3.50.7. This book did not reproduce the race or validate the fix.11,13

Gotcha: FTS5 reads user text as a query language

MATCH has its own grammar. Local parameterized tests of OR syntax, quoted literals and unfinished quotes returned different results or parse errors. Binding stops SQL injection, not query interpretation. quote() wraps words, doubles internal quotes and joins them with OR (see Chapter 05).1

Gotcha: sqlite-vec is pre-v1, and deletes do not cascade

The README warns of pre-1.0 breaking changes.2 Keep vectors rebuildable. Locally, deleting a memories row left its row ID in both indexes. The step 2 remove_indexed_row() helper locks with BEGIN IMMEDIATE before reading old text, issues the FTS5 'delete' command with it,1 then removes the vec0 and memories rows. All removals commit together. Existing transactions are rejected without ending them; competing removals are tested.

Gotcha: silent embedding drift across model updates

Each database file stores one embedding identity (model, revision, dimensions, preprocessing), checked on every write and query. Mismatches refuse reopen, writes and queries, even for same-length vectors; rebuild into a fresh file (Chapter 03).

Verdict

Verdict: one file first, log underneath

Pick SQLite with FTS5 and sqlite-vec for one agent or desktop app needing local keyword and vector search. Durably record puts, corrections and deletes; rebuild uncontested live state; preserve event IDs and tombstones through sync and restore.

Use PostgreSQL (Chapter 08) for several writing hosts; benchmark a vector store (Chapter 11) on target hardware when exact scans exceed the latency budget. Use MariaDB vectors when tenant data already lives on that server, DuckDB for batch analysis, files for procedures, and checkpoints only for run state. Chapter 21 runs a painter's business on one SQLite file.

Part E

Frameworks and graphs

Frameworks and managed services package the read and write loop so you do not build it yourself. This part covers them, and graph-based memory with a sense of time.

Part E · Chapter 13

13

Memory frameworks

A memory framework decides how an agent saves facts, retrieves them and places them in a language model’s context.

Maturity

Shipped

Setup effort

3 of 5

Running cost

3 of 5

Best for

Agents that need persistent facts, shared recall or editable context blocks.

What it is

Memory frameworks save and retrieve facts. Choose by who selects them, a model or your code, and the saving cost.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) exposes tools; its memory server stores local entities/notes. LangGraph resumes conversations (threads) from state snapshots (checkpoints); Store shares facts across threads. Letta V1 is retired; Letta Code is current. Use LangGraph Store for keyed facts: namespace identifies whose, key identifies which. For extraction, try Mem0 (Chapter 06) or Hindsight (Step 6).1,2,3

ChooseBest fitWhat to validate
MCP reference server 2.2.1Local clients write named entities and notes to a shared file.File persistence and tool results; tested below.1
LangGraph 1.2.24Your code chooses namespace, key and timing.Store facts span threads; a checkpointer saves snapshots for resumption. Tested below.2
LettaInvestigate Code’s editable files; V1 is legacy only.Step 4 tests legacy blocks; Step 7 reports later Code outcomes. Pass it before adopting.3,4
Mem0 OSS / PlatformA model extracts user facts automatically, then relevant notes are retrieved.Tested in Chapter 06, not here. Validate corrections in fresh threads (Gotchas).5

How it works

Direct writes need no model. Extraction/agent edits add calls (Step 7); semantic indexing embeds writes/queries. Letta V1 blocks stay in prompts; keyed/semantic reads fetch on demand.1,2,5

Mem0: current retrieval design

Mem0’s April 2026 algorithm v3 (package mem0ai 2.2.1; algorithm versions are separate) makes one generative call per extraction-enabled save. ADD-only facts lack stable field keys. Your code must search user-scoped memories, identify contradictions and delete superseded IDs (Gotchas; Chapter 06’s delete call). It links entities; retrieval adds BM25 keyword scores, entity signals and time-aware ranking to semantic search. Python’s [nlp] extra and spaCy model enable entity extraction and keyword lemmatization, and Qdrant BM25 also needs fastembed. Chapter 06’s minimal installation uses semantic search only.5,6

In mem0ai==2.2.1, keyword and entity signals only re-rank semantic hits, so they cannot recover an exact match it missed. If exact identifiers matter, measure how often semantic search finds them and add a keyword branch.6

Mem0 OSS is self-run. Mem0 Platform’s proprietary optimizations, terms and published scores do not carry over (Benchmark evidence).5,7

Good for and not for

Good for

  • Notes the agent writes that must survive a session.
  • Namespaced facts shared across agent threads.
  • Preferences picked out for a small prompt budget.
  • Agent-editable context with an audit trail.

Not for

  • Fixed profile fields, which belong in a database (Chapter 08).
  • Short project instructions, which belong in a file (Chapter 01).
  • Authoritative task ownership, which needs transactional guarantees (Chapter 08).
  • Exact evidence, where you should also keep the original sources.
  • Histories that fit in context, or where plain retrieval meets your target; local extraction did not beat full context (Chapter 17).

Adoption checks for seven tools (Chapter 01 covers repository-memory upkeep):

  • Claude-Mem and AgentMemory. Both require supported capture hooks; audit capture/export/deletion separately from hook removal.22,23
  • Honcho. Workspace/session/peer scopes track knowledge of others. Keep direct evidence, label inferences, budget background reasoning. Before sharing beliefs, inspect Dream Histories (inference logs), correct sources, test scoped deletion.18,30
  • memU. Chat-model calls outside storage convert history into candidate skills; budget/log separately. Separate human instructions, candidates and reviewed skills. Test, approve and version before reuse; revoke after regression failures (Chapter 17).16
  • MemPalace and EverOS. For exact quotations, try MemPalace’s verbatim retrieval before extraction. Recall@5 (correct item among five retrieved) measures retrieval, not answer accuracy. EverOS derives indexes/reflected memories from Markdown; its answer scores cannot compare with retrieval-only Recall@5. Export both source corpora; verify deletion across sources, derived stores, exports and backups. EverOS deletes by session/user/agent; deleting one session leaves aggregates.25,26
  • Strands with MongoDB. SnapshotSessionManager resumes sessions; MemoryManager searches long-term memory within a scope, and time to live (TTL) limits how long items survive before expiry. Choose scope from authenticated application state. Closing the agent context flushes pending extraction before closing connections.27

Managed memory services

Services handle extraction and storage; applications authenticate users, select scopes and trigger ingestion. Client-supplied user ids do not establish identity.

ServiceExtraction and isolationRetention and deletion
Google Agent Platform Memory BankExtracts/consolidates session or supplied facts. Resource identity and access management (IAM) protects banks; scope key/value pairs group users’ memories.31Expiry set by default, on creation or generation; revisions retained separately. Delete memories or purge a scope; revisions can remain accessible for 48 hours after deletion.32
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore MemoryEvents feed asynchronous semantic/preference/summary/episodic strategies. Actor identifies whose events; session groups a conversation. Actor names confer no access: enforce record-namespace IAM policies.33Raw events expire within 365 days; optional strategy-record TTL, minimum 31 days. Delete events/derived records separately, or the entire resource.34
Microsoft Foundry Agent Service Memory (public preview)User profiles, chat summaries and procedural routines. Low-level APIs require explicit scope; the agent tool can resolve user identity.52Item create/read/update/list/delete; scope or store deletion. Store-default TTL in seconds, with direct remember/forget controls.53

Google generates memories when the application calls generate,31 and its scope decides which memories are consolidated and retrieved. AWS policies can restrict actor, session and normalized namespace paths such as /actors/alice/. For a stronger customer boundary, use separate projects, banks or resources. Google Cloud Logging/AWS CloudWatch record operations, not extraction correctness.32,33

  • Export. On Google, page through the memory and revision lists, and keep source sessions separately.32 On AWS, page through events per actor and session and records per namespace, and keep the actor, session and strategy metadata so records stay interpretable.34 Re-extraction from an export need not give the same facts.32,34,35
  • Foundry TTL. Default TTL covers command, extracted and direct items only in stores created after TTL support. Zero disables expiry; update/consolidation resets last-updated time. Set defaults on creation; check API-version support for later changes.53
  • Foundry identity. Validate ownership for item-id reads/edits/deletes and scoped searches. The agent tool resolves identity from the x-memory-user-id header or from Microsoft Entra. Only trusted backends should set that header.53

Managed pricing and limits

Prices (Google/AWS) and preview limits (Foundry), checked 20 November 2026. Google bills GiB; AWS’s GB is undefined. Do not compare directly.

  • Google. Storage, including revisions, costs $0.30/GiB-month. Reads cost $0.085 per 3 million reads; writes cost $0.085 per 1 million writes, both prorated. Generation and embedding tokens are charged separately.36
  • AWS. Short-term memory bills ingestion and retrieval by GB, and storage by GB-month; rates not recorded here, see the linked price list. Built-in long-term storage costs $0.75/1,000 records/month and retrieval $0.50/1,000 requests. Override and self-managed strategies are charged separately. Check region and model costs before ingesting.37
  • Foundry. Public preview needs compatible Azure OpenAI chat/embedding deployments in a supported region. Model usage is billed; memory pricing may change. Limits are 100 scopes per store, 10,000 memories per scope and 1,000 requests/minute each for search and update. Memory stores have no virtual network integration.52

Consumer chat memory is not an application store

These products store memory in provider accounts; controls vary by plan and workspace.

ProductRemembered materialAudit and deletion
ChatGPTSaved facts, past-chat context, other enabled sources.Settings → Personalization → Memory; inspect the summary and Sources. Delete memories and their chats and files, and disconnect relevant apps.38
ClaudeChat context, project memory and chat search.Settings → Your Claude (older layout: Memory); inspect and edit entries, or reset memory. Delete entries separately from chats.39
GeminiPast-chat context, response instructions, connected-app contributions.Settings → Personal Intelligence; inspect instructions and Gemini Apps Activity. Delete the relevant chats and instructions, and disconnect relevant apps.40,41

Disabling memory need not erase sources. ChatGPT summaries are incomplete inventories; Claude chat deletion may retain derived memory; Gemini chat deletion may affect personalization later. Forgetting an answer does not prove deletion.38,39,40

Numbers

Scope and scale

Server 2.2.1 reads the entire file per read. Writes lock, read, modify and atomically replace it; other processes wait. Stale locks recover, but sharing requires exclusive file creation. File size increases work and lock wait: set MEMORY_MAX_FILE_BYTES, MEMORY_MAX_ENTITIES and MEMORY_MAX_RELATIONS. They are unset by default.42

The MCP, keyed LangGraph Store and Letta V1 fixtures issue storage calls directly and use no inference tokens; their cost is process, API and disk work, with no latency promised. The Letta Code fixture also pays for the model turn that selects and issues each edit (Step 7 reports the times).1,2,4,5

These are arithmetic budgets, not measured defaults; see Chapter 00’s sizing reference.

EstimateAssumptionResult
Extraction costOne call turns 1,000 input tokens into a 100-token fact.1,000 input + 100 output tokens per write, so one million writes need 1B input + 100M output tokens.
Facts read per answerTen 100-token facts.About 1,000 extra tokens in each answer prompt.
Always-visible blockOne 2,000-token block.2,000 extra tokens on every turn.
Text storage100 facts/user × 500 bytes/fact × 10,000 users.500 MB of text before metadata and indexes.
Vector storageOne 768-dimensional float32 vector for each of 1,000,000 facts.3.072 GB before index overhead.
MCP whole-file costA 500 MB file at an assumed 100 MB/second.About 5 s per read and about 10 s per write (read plus rewrite) under an exclusive lock, so roughly six writes per minute at most.

Whole-file storage is costly at that size. The lock supports local sharing; only two small concurrent writes were tested, not crash recovery.1

Use namespaced database storage (Chapter 08) as writers, lock waits or latency grow. Replace LangGraph’s local SQLite backends before running independent workers. Monitor Letta’s per-turn context; retrieve instead of enlarging blocks. Measure extraction queue age and correction accuracy before increasing concurrency.2,4,5

Benchmark evidence

Mem0’s managed April 2026 stack claims LoCoMo 92.5 and LongMemEval 94.4 with top-200 retrieval: percent correct on long-conversation questions (Chapter 17). These vendor claims are untested here. Locally, benchmarks/longmemeval-frameworks in the companion repository tested Mem0 OSS and Graphiti with 3B extraction on LongMemEval. Ingestion per history took Mem0 19 to 58 minutes; Graphiti took two to five hours and about five times the tokens. Within the shared 14-hour wall-clock budget (Chapter 17), three histories finished, one question each; both frameworks scored zero. That cannot rank them or test vendor figures. The vendor harness defaults to GPT-4o for answering and judging; its OSS comparison uses GPT-5 for both. Record retrieval depth, extractor, answerer and judge before comparing scores.5,7

Tested locally with a 14B model (harness: benchmarks/locomo in the companion repository), Mem0 OSS scored 66/123 on LoCoMo (53.7%), between plain RAG (62/123) and full context (71/123). With extraction off (harness: benchmarks/longmemeval), it earned the same aggregate score as dense retrieval on LongMemEval: 165/300 (55.0%). Chapter 17 has the tables, intervals and ingestion times.

Letta V1 (retired) security boundary

CVE-2026-77937, published 20 October 2026, affects Letta through 0.16.8. A caller-supplied user_id header can impersonate another tenant even with LETTA_SERVER_SECURE enabled. The CVE lists no fixed V1 release; Letta’s security policy says the retired server and Docker images receive no fixes. Step 5. Forked planning: draft locally, promote explicitly

Two forks draft blue and green paint plans. After human approval, trusted code promotes blue from checkpoint state to Store. Replay reruns later tool/API nodes without reverting Store or external sends. Receivers must deduplicate stable action keys (Chapter 17’s outbox protocol).2,48

This CPU fixture sends no message: a separate SQLite table simulates atomic acceptance per action key, rejecting the second send. Production receivers must enforce this key; a local pre-call flag leaves a crash gap.

The key identifies a logical send: first fork wins. Resume only the approved fork. Relative database paths resolve under the printed scratch root.

On each managed route’s first run, check:

  • Deletion separately removes raw events or conversations and derived records. Inspect revisions and retention delays; not-found responses do not prove source, revision or backup erasure.

Gotchas

Gotcha: ADD-only stores keep contradicted facts

Mem0 keeps both “I prefer coffee” and later “I now prefer tea.” This correction test was not run here. Do not adopt Mem0 OSS for authoritative corrections until it passes. Check:

  1. The tea fact is stored.
  2. The fresh thread’s prompt identifies tea as current; coffee is absent or explicitly historical.
  3. A fresh thread answers tea.

Record the first failure. Ranking may miss current facts. Resolve per user, field and effective time; test late-arriving history. Before deletion, fetch the user’s facts for that field and confirm contradiction. Age-based deletion also loses valid old facts, such as allergies.5

Gotcha: Retrieved text is untrusted

Trusted application code chooses tenant scope, never a model-generated user id. Observations/learned skills are data, not instructions. Chapter 17 tests injection/isolation.

Gotcha: Checkpoints can retain deleted facts

Store deletion leaves earlier thread state, cached prompts, exports and backups. Test every readable copy.2

Verdict

Verdict: choose who decides what is saved

Use MCP for small local note graphs, including shared locked files. Use LangGraph Store for application-owned cross-thread facts; a separate checkpointer resumes threads. Adopt Letta Code’s CLI/Git files only after passing Step 7 within your hardware/latency budget. For custom-service edits, expose file tools (Chapter 01) or Store. Supplemental directed-edit outcomes alone were checked; /remember and CPU-only Letta Code remain unverified.

For extraction, compare Chapter 06’s Mem0 with Hindsight (Step 6) on your histories. Choose temporal graphs (Chapter 14) for changing relationships, files (Chapters 01 and 02) for small readable corpora, Chapter 08 services for concurrent writers. Managed Google/AWS/Foundry remain unrun: consider only on your existing cloud, accepting untested extraction and its deletion/retention limits.

Part E · Chapter 14

14

Knowledge-graph memory

Memory stores entities and relationships; facts can carry validity dates.

Maturity

Prototype

Setup effort

4 of 5

Running cost

4 of 5

Best for

Changing relationships across entities and questions over a whole corpus.

What it is

Knowledge-graph memory stores nodes (people or companies) and edges (their relationships), extracted by a model or written directly.

Follow entity links to answer "Who knows the person who introduced me to Bluefin?", or read community summaries. Microsoft's GraphRAG paper finds vector retrieval strong for local questions, weak for corpus-wide themes.1 Some systems also track time. Graphiti, the open-source engine behind Zep, says: "facts have validity windows. When information changes, old facts are invalidated, not deleted".2

Terms new in this chapter

Cypher
Neo4j’s language for matching node and edge patterns.
Valid time
When a claim applies in the world; in this walkthrough, the half-open interval from valid_from to invalid_at.
Recorded time
When a version was live in the store; in this walkthrough, from recorded_at to superseded_at. Also called transaction time.
Community summary
Model-written text describing a cluster of closely linked entities.
Episode
A message, note or record Graphiti ingests and retains as extracted facts' source.
Multi-hop question
A question whose answer needs two or more edges in a row.

How it works

Extract: a model emits entities and relationships from text. Resolve entities: match mentions to existing people or firms. Reconcile facts: close earlier relationships only when evidence and validity rules warrant it. Store: save nodes and edges. Retrieve: use a path query for exact relationship patterns. GraphRAG local search gathers context around relevant entities; global search reads community summaries,1 while HippoRAG 2 ranks passages with personalized PageRank (which spreads query relevance across linked nodes to score passages).

Extraction requires generation calls; queries depend on their output. If three edges are each 90% likely to be correct and errors are independent, all three are correct about 73% of the time. This is not answer accuracy. Graphiti's default fact search makes no generative LLM call.3

Two timelines

Each fact can carry a valid time and a recorded time; Graphiti describes tracking both.2 The walkthrough implements both directly in Cypher, without Graphiti.

EventValid fromRecorded at
Alice works at Acme.2024-03-012024-03-02
The application learns she joined Bluefin.2026-09-012026-09-07
A correction moves the Bluefin start date earlier.2026-08-152026-11-15

Updates close recorded intervals and append complete replacements. For 20 August 2026, current knowledge returns Bluefin; knowledge recorded on 1 November 2026 returns Acme, before the correction. Assume one employer at a time; intervals include their start, exclude their end.

Good for and not for

Good for

  • Multi-hop connections between people, companies and projects.
  • Changing relationships needing joins, history and sources. Structured updates can write edges directly; a lone attribute needs SQL.
  • Whole-corpus questions such as "what themes recur across these reports", which top-k vector search answers poorly.
  • Known entity types. Graphiti accepts Pydantic types (Python classes defining and validating fields).2
  • Teams able to afford extraction and inspect edges.

Not for

  • Single-passage lookups such as "what did I say about X on Tuesday". Use vectors (Chapter 03) or files (Chapter 01).
  • A few dozen notes. Read the files.
  • Preferences and short facts about one user need a keyed profile. For a few relations, the MCP reference memory server is the lightest graph option.
  • Local models that cannot reliably return structured output. Test one first.2
  • Write volumes that outrun extraction. If passage lookup suffices, use timestamped vectors.

Variants and tools

Graph-based memory and retrieval tools (state as of 20 November 2026)

ToolCore ideaStatus
Microsoft GraphRAGExtracts entities and relations; summarizes communities (Leiden, a graph-clustering method). Offers global, local and DRIFT (local search seeded with community context) search.1MIT license. README says the project is "largely in maintenance mode".4
LazyGraphRAGDefers model work to query time, so Microsoft reports indexing costs about the same as vector RAG.5November 2024; June 2025 note names Microsoft Discovery and Azure Local.5
LightRAGCheap indexing; local and global retrieval over an extracted graph plus vectors.6EMNLP 2025 paper. Stores in Neo4j, PostgreSQL, MongoDB or OpenSearch.6
HippoRAG 2Extracts a graph and ranks passages with personalized PageRank.7ICML 2025 paper. Code at OSU-NLP-Group/HippoRAG.7
Graphiti (Zep)Temporal graph of episodes, entities and facts with validity windows. Search mixes semantic, BM25 keyword and graph methods.2Apache-2.0. graphiti-core 0.31.2, 2026-10-20.2
Mem0 graph memoryLinks extracted entities to memories. The docs say it "does not assign typed, labeled relationships".8Platform only. OSS v3 removed graph memory and external graph drivers; Mem0 core remains open source.9
CogneeIngests text, extracts a graph and queries it with vector and graph search. Has local extraction and embeddings without a model key.10Version 1.6.10, 2026-11-18. Apache-2.0.10,11
MCP reference memory serverEntities, relations and observations (short facts on an entity) in a local file. The client model decides what to write.12README requires Node 24 or newer. It rewrites a whole-file store and serializes writes from several processes with a lock, so write cost grows with file size (Chapter 13).12

Chapter 13 covers MCP reference memory server 2.2.1 (not run): Streamable HTTP, the memory://knowledge-graph resource and filtered reads, which limit response size, not rewrite cost. It listens on loopback by default.30

Chapter 04 covers ConceptGraphs: a 3D object graph associating detections across camera views.29 Not run here; Chapter 04 distinguishes image embeddings from maps.

Graph stores

Where the graph lives (state as of 20 November 2026)

StoreNotes
KuzuArchived. Its 2025-10-10 README announces archival and says 0.11.3 bundles common extensions.13 Graphiti 0.31.2 marks its Kuzu driver deprecated.2 Start no new work on it.

Property graphs or RDF

Either model accepts extracted facts or direct writes; choose by queries and fact exchange.

ChoiceRepresentation and reasoningWhen agent memory benefits
Property graphNodes and edges have properties; Cypher matches paths. Applications define types and validity rules.16Choose for application-specific links, timestamps and path queries (walkthrough).
RDF / SPARQLSubject-predicate-object triples share identifiers. An ontology names types; an optional reasoner derives triples from its rules.17,18Combine external vocabularies or exchange facts across systems. SPARQL queries triples; separate inference provides no automatic truth checking.19

Use cases

1Who knows whom in a personal network

Situation
After recording investor meetings and introductions, a founder asks "Who knows the person who introduced me to Bluefin?" Keyword search cannot join notes.
Why it fits
Typed edges join people and firms: Bluefin, its introducer, then their contacts. HippoRAG 2 reports gains on associative recall (answers needing linked facts), also found in a reduced local run (Numbers).7
Pair with
Neo4j for the tested setup, or embedded FalkorDBLite without a server. Keep source notes for quotations.

2Changing facts that link several entities

Situation
Over a year, an assistant hears "I moved" and "I switched to Bluefin". Plain notes may preserve stale answers.
Why it fits
Each fact has a start and end date, and a change closes the old edge instead of deleting it.2 The example answers Acme or Bluefin by recorded date. One job or address needs SQL validity columns (Verdict); use graphs when facts join people and firms.
Pair with
Graphiti, or the hand-written pattern in the walkthrough. Store the source episode on every edge.

3One question over thousands of reports

Situation
An analyst asks which causes recur across thousands of incident reports. Top-k vector search returns ten reports, missing the pattern.
Why it fits
GraphRAG global search answers from community summaries built over the whole corpus.1 Microsoft reports that LazyGraphRAG avoids most up-front indexing cost,5 but LazyGraphRAG was not run locally; try RAPTOR summaries (Chapter 05) first.
Pair with
A corpus slice first, since indexing is expensive.4

4Multi-hop research across documents

Situation
A team asks which component supplier a named company owns. A bridging entity joins two documents.
Why it fits
HippoRAG 2 ranks passages over its extracted graph with personalized PageRank.7 LightRAG retrieves at a local and a global level over its graph.6
Pair with
A reranker, hybrid search (Chapter 05), and sampled edge checks.

5A small graph for one developer, no database

Situation
A developer wants Claude Desktop or Claude Code to retain people, projects and relations across sessions without a database.
Why it fits
The MCP reference memory server keeps entities, relations and observations in one local file and exposes nine tools. The client model chooses writes; the server makes no model call.12
Pair with
The file under git. Use filtered reads if only the response is too large. Measure p95 write latency at your note rate. Migrate when it exceeds your latency budget, writers regularly wait on the lock, or queries need dated relationships.

Numbers

Local runs cannot settle graphs versus vectors: Graphiti needed extraction retries with Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and finished only three LongMemEval histories (Chapter 13), too few to score.

Benchmark and cost figures with provenance (state as of 20 November 2026)

FigureMeasureEvidence
55 to 56%Graphiti and Cognee on LoCoMo (long-conversation question answering) in Wolff and Bennati's independent testbed, against 77 to 81% for Mem0, RAG and full context. The authors blame incomplete retrieval, not reasoning.20Independent paper
75.14%Graphiti on LoCoMo in Zep's counter-evaluation, quoted second-hand in the independent paper.20Vendor claim, second-hand
74.0%Letta Filesystem with gpt-4o-mini and grep-style tools on LoCoMo.21Vendor claim
94.8% vs 93.4%Zep against MemGPT on Deep Memory Retrieval, plus up to 18.5% higher accuracy and 90% lower latency on LongMemEval. Vendor figures, not run here; benchmarks are described in Chapter 17.22Vendor claim
0.1%LazyGraphRAG indexing cost as a share of full GraphRAG's; Microsoft says this equals vector RAG indexing cost.5Maintainer blog
+7%HippoRAG 2 on associative memory tasks against the best embedding model.7Paper

Neither LazyGraphRAG's 0.1% cost (Microsoft's report; cited release points to Azure integrations; not run locally) nor HippoRAG 2's +7% average across datasets was reproduced as published. A reduced run (150 2Wiki questions; Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, replacing the paper's 70B) scored answer F1 (reference-answer token overlap, out of 100) of 46.3 for HippoRAG 2 versus dense retrieval's 32.5: a 13.8-point gain (95% interval 6.6 to 21.2). Supporting-passage recall at five was 78.5% versus 53.8%. That supports the direction on one dataset, not the 7% average. See benchmarks/paper-reruns.

Zep and Mem0 dispute scores; an independent audit and the benchmark repository's issue thread both contest the LoCoMo answer key.28,31 Evaluate on your own data.

Tested on 22 November 2026 (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct Q4_K_M, 4-bit quantized; CPU MiniLM embeddings; three local judge votes per answer, majority wins; 96 GB Apple Silicon), Graphiti scored 44/123 on completed LoCoMo questions from conversations 0 through 3 (35.8%, 95% interval 27.9 to 44.6) against full context's 71/123 (57.7%, 95% interval 48.9 to 66.1). Of 320 targeted questions each, full context completed 320 (180 correct), Graphiti 123 (44), Cognee 67 (39). Retries and the deadline limited completion. Pairing requires answers and three votes from every method: 67 questions from conversations 0, 1 and 3. Graphiti scored 22/67 (32.8%, 95% Wilson interval 22.8 to 44.7); Cognee and full context each scored 39/67 (58.2%, 95% interval 46.3 to 69.3). Scores are conditional on completion.

Ingestion per conversation took Graphiti 37.6 to 148.8 minutes against vector-only Mem0 OSS's 25.8 to 39.6, including retries and waits on a shared model host, so these are observations, not controlled throughput.

On 150 LongMemEval items, a 3B local reader scored 66.7% with full context and 61.3% with dense retrieval, no clear gap. Only these two baselines ran, without graphs, Zep or MemGPT. Chapter 17 has the LoCoMo table; the harness is in the companion repository under benchmarks/locomo.

Scope and scale

Calls per operation:2,23

  • Direct edge write or lookup: zero generation or embedding calls.
  • Graphiti episode ingestion: several generation calls plus embeddings. Retries and entity matching vary the count.
  • Default Graphiti fact search: one query embedding call; add one generation call only if you turn the facts into a prose answer.

The extractor queue fills first. At the walkthrough's 57 to 115 seconds per episode on CPU with one slot, 60 writes take roughly one to two hours. Its 171.7-second timer covers index setup, two writes, checks, search and model loading, excluding installation and downloads. Time a warmed batch at your concurrency. Graphiti's default of 10 concurrent operations can exceed a local model's capacity.2

Storage estimate: at 768 dimensions in float32 (per-vector size in the Chapter 00 sizing reference), one million embedded entities plus one million embedded facts take about 6.14 GB for vectors alone, before episodes, properties and indexes. Partition users with Graphiti's group_id; measure recall and ingestion backlog as memory grows. If backlog exceeds your freshness budget, batch extraction or use Chapter 20’s synchronous SQL assistant when its narrower design fits.

The 23 November 2026 check on Linux with a 32-thread CPU postdates the research cutoff; output follows. The 20 November single-episode run passed on an 8 GB consumer GPU, without testing invalidation. You need Docker 29.1.3 (install it first on an empty machine24), Python 3.12.16 and uv 0.13.9 on PATH. Neo4j authentication is off in this disposable loopback-only lab. The temporal test uses no model; the automatic route uses local Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Ollama tag qwen2.5:7b).

Gotchas

Gotcha: one wrong edge poisons later answers

Merging two people named Smith combines their edges and contaminates later reads. Keep the source episode on each edge, as Graphiti does,2 and inspect retrieved edges. For direct writes, key nodes by a stable, user-scoped contact ID. Graphiti model resolution is not tested by this fixture. Proposed test: ingest two Smiths with different contact IDs and employers; each ID must retrieve only its own employment edge.

Gotcha: relation names drift without a schema

Free-form extraction can write works_at, employed_by and job for one fact. Graphiti lets you prescribe entity and edge types as Pydantic models;2 Mem0's Platform-only graph leaves relationships untyped.8 Constrain edge types first.

Gotcha: passing ingestion is not accuracy

A smoke-test pass measures no accuracy. Test real episodes, contradictions and empty cases against expected facts. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct passed on CPU and an 8 GB consumer GPU. Qwen3-0.6B (qwen3:0.6b) passed CPU ingestion and search in 83.2 seconds under the printed 600-second budget; a fresh read also passed. Its earlier 300-second trial timed out and returned no facts; the cause remains unknown. Extraction needs no GPU; Ollama supports CPU execution.27 Graphiti's README warns that smaller models can give wrong schemas and failed ingestion.2

Gotcha: Graphiti's bundled servers are open by default

Graphiti's bundled MCP server and REST service have no authentication or prompt-injection filter; keep them off untrusted networks.2 See Chapter 17.

Verdict

Verdict: earn the graph

Choose a graph only when all three hold: questions need multi-hop joins or corpus-wide answers beyond files and vectors; typed writes or accurate extraction are affordable; someone reviews sampled edges. Delete or correct an episode, then confirm derived edges, embeddings and summaries no longer present its old fact as current. Otherwise, treat propagation as unsupported.

One job or address needs validity and recorded-version columns in Postgres or SQLite (Chapters 08 and 12; hybrid facts and edges in Chapter 23). Start with files (Chapter 01), timestamped vectors (Chapter 03) or RAPTOR summaries (Chapter 05). Try AGE for Postgres graph queries, or GraphRAG global search on a corpus slice.
