15

Outdated approaches and how we got here

Earlier memory designs, their limits, and where each still fits.

Maturity

Outdated

Span

October 2014 to November 2026

Covers

12 older approaches, plus retired products, with evidence

Best for

Readers choosing what to build or retain.

Why look back

These predecessors still fit some small jobs. Avoid rebuilding superseded designs or over-engineering jobs they cover.

"(Reasoning.)" marks the following sentence as an inference from the design.

Terms new in this chapter

Checkpointer
Saves agent state after each step by thread_id, allowing resumption.
Parametric memory
Knowledge held in a model's weights, not in an outside text store.
create_agent
LangChain v1's agent-loop constructor with checkpoints and stores.
Store API
LangChain's cross-thread key-value store.
Middleware
Agent-step code that inspects or changes state and trims or summarizes messages.

Context window, chunk, top-k, hybrid search and reranker are defined in earlier chapters and the glossary.

Timeline, 2014 to 2026

Figure 1 covers 2014 to 2021; Figure 2, 2023 to 2026. Spacing is even, not to scale; dates follow sources.

Older approaches, one by one

Five groups roughly follow age; retired products follow. Chapter references point to current approaches.

Research roots

1Memory Networks, Neural Turing Machines, kNN-LM, RETRO

Design
Memory Networks added readable/writable long-term storage.1 Neural Turing Machines (NTMs)2 and the Differentiable Neural Computer3 learned task-time working-memory reads/writes. kNN-LM blends frozen-model predictions with distance-weighted following tokens from similar stored contexts.4 New entries need no retraining. RETRO retrieves chunks from a 2-trillion-token database during training and generation.6
Limits
(Reasoning.) Memory Networks, NTMs and RETRO require model-specific training; kNN-LM needs internal vectors unavailable through text-only APIs; prompt-time retrieval uses plain text.
Current fit
Prompt-time retrieval (Chapter 05); Part D stores (Chapters 08 to 12). Still fine for learned-memory research (Chapter 16): kNN-LM adds retrieval after training; RETRO trains with it.

2The 2020 RAG recipe as a finished system

Design
The 2020 RAG model paired a text generator with a dense retriever over Wikipedia passages.5 It combined per-passage predictions weighted by retriever scores and became the outside-knowledge template.
Limits
Its 2020 recipe used one dense retriever.5 See card 5 for retrieval limits.
Current fit
Chapter 05's pipeline over a Part D store. Still fine as a mental model.

Chat history

3Full conversation buffer and sliding window

Design
ConversationBufferMemory kept all messages; ConversationBufferWindowMemory exposed 2k messages (k exchanges); ConversationTokenBufferMemory pruned whole oldest messages to a token budget.161718
Limits
(Reasoning.) Full buffers grow unbounded; windows silently drop old turns. Deprecated for create_agent with checkpoints or Store API. In langchain-classic (legacy classes after v1), ConversationBufferMemory declares since="0.3.1" and removal="2.0.0".19 Its reference says "Since v1.5"; trust your installed warning when these disagree.20
Current fit
A thread_id-keyed checkpointer; middleware drops older messages before calls (Chapter 13).16 Still fine for short single-session chat.

4LangChain summary, vector and entity memory classes

Design
ConversationSummaryMemory, ConversationSummaryBufferMemory, VectorStoreRetrieverMemory and ConversationEntityMemory.16
Limits
Deprecated like card 3. The guide replaces summaries with checkpointing and SummarizationMiddleware.14 A secondary source maps vector and entity memory to Store API on create_agent or an outside service,16 but you must implement extraction and retrieval.
Current fit
Explicit agent state and stores (Chapter 13). Still fine for existing chains with fixed package versions; check each class's support before upgrading.

Retrieval recipes

5Fixed-size chunks with one top-k cosine search

Design
Split documents into chunks, embed them and put the top-k nearest in the prompt without reranking, for a frozen, off-the-shelf generator.
Limits
The retrieval plugin README warns embeddings "may not always be effective at capturing exact keyword matches" and recommends hybrid search.7 (Reasoning.) Fixed cuts can split a fact across chunks.
Current fit
Hybrid search, structure-aware chunks and a reranker (Chapter 05). Still fine for prototypes passing handwritten queries across real question types: required evidence must reach top-k. Cover exact names, ids or codes as well as paraphrases; a relevant-looking chunk without the required fact fails.

6Append-only message embeddings with ada-002

Design
Embed raw messages using text-embedding-ada-002; append and retrieve by similarity without updates or deletion.
Limits
(Reasoning.) Similarity cannot decide what to keep, update or forget. Mem0's paper argues for extracting and consolidating facts, not raw messages.12 OpenAI announced text-embedding-ada-002 on 15 December 2022,21 then text-embedding-3-small and -large on 25 January 2024 as successors.11
Current fit
Current embeddings (Chapter 03) with extraction and updates (Chapter 13). Still fine for immutable-message search with current embeddings. An incompatible model switch requires re-embedding corpus and queries with that model.

Agent loops and memory designs

7AutoGPT and BabyAGI memory (2023)

Design
Early, widely shared demos queried a vector store each cycle. AutoGPT22 executed goals autonomously; BabyAGI created and prioritized tasks. Both appeared in spring 2023; BabyAGI's README marks its original March 2023 version archived.23
Limits
Adoption decline is unmeasured here. (Reasoning.) Unconsolidated steps can crowd retrieval (card 6); missing task state can cause repeated work (cards 3 and 4). AutoGPT continues as a platform project.
Current fit
Checkpointed agent state and curated memory (Chapters 00 and 13). Still fine as a toy for studying how agent loops fail.

8Generative Agents memory stream with reflection

Design
Observations enter a natural-language stream. Retrieval scores recency, importance and relevance; periodic reflections add higher-level memories. The paper tested it with 25 agents in a sandbox.8
Limits
Importance scoring uses one model call per observation.8 (Reasoning.) Calls scale with observations per agent × agents; repeated reflections can compound errors, and contradictions remain active. Mem0 also calls models at write time, extracting facts and updating or deleting conflicts.12 No cited same-workload comparison exists; reflection research continues (Chapter 16).
Current fit
Fact extraction and updates (Chapter 13); consolidation (Chapter 16). Still fine for simulated characters and design research.

9MemGPT, which became Letta

Design
Context serves as RAM; outside storage as disk. Function calls page data between tiers; interrupts, including user messages, manage agent/user control flow.10 It targeted small context windows.
Limits
Only the earlier API is labelled "V1 SDK (legacy)".15
Current fit
Use the current Letta SDK or Letta Code (Chapter 13). Still fine for agent-managed memory with visible tool calls. File-based memory (Chapter 01) is simpler.

Weights, windows and compression

10Fine-tuning on user data as memory

Design
Train on user history to store knowledge in weights (parametric memory).
Limits
RAG lists knowledge updates and provenance as open problems for parametric memory.5 (Reasoning.) Shared-model weights lack per-user records for reliable fact deletion or provenance; facts go stale.
Current fit
Explicit storage (Part D) and retrieval (Chapter 05). Still fine for style, behavior or a domain skill.

11The whole history in a huge context window

Design
Put the whole history or corpus into every prompt.
Limits
(Reasoning.) Prefix caching cuts resending cost and latency; history still grows toward the window limit and competes with the question for attention. In 2023 tests, accuracy dropped for mid-context passages (Chapter 00).9 Anthropic frames the job as the smallest set of high-signal tokens.13
Current fit
Selecting what enters the prompt (Chapters 01, 02 and 05). Still fine when one document fits and is read once, after testing position sensitivity.

12Summary of summaries

Design
Hierarchical roll-ups summarize batches, then those summaries. LangChain rolled new messages into its previous summary.16 Capping the final summary bounds prompt size, not source or intermediate-summary storage; reading it needs no index.
Limits
(Reasoning.) Both can lose detail irrecoverable from their summaries alone. Plant a unique day 2 order number; require its exact recovery from both the first batch summary and final roll-up.
Current fit
Retain originals within policy and regenerate summaries (Chapters 01 and 02). Erasure: delete originals; rebuild or discard their summaries (Chapter 17). Still fine for session orientation under that policy.

Retired hosted and open-source products

OpenAI's Assistants API (threads and file search as memory) shut down on 26 August 2026. The guide maps threads to Responses API Conversations without naming a file-search replacement.24 Inventory threads and file search; test Responses' hosted file_search over your vector store on existing queries before cutover.25 For self-operated retrieval, use Chapter 05 over Part D. Zep ended self-hosted Community Edition maintenance in April 2025, directing users to Graphiti (Chapter 14) or its commercial service.26 Chapter 14 covers setup. Neither migration ran here.

Still fine today, and when to move on

Age alone does not disqualify a design.

Still fine today

  • Short single-session chat: a plain message list.
  • Small-corpus prototype, paraphrased queries: fixed chunks, top-k cosine search. Split evidence: rechunk. Inspect extra candidates: evidence below prompt cutoff means test reranking; absent evidence means change retrieval (Chapter 05).
  • Single document, one read: context window; test key passages at start, middle and end.
  • A style or a skill: fine-tuning.

Time to move on

  • Old facts exceed the prompt-token budget: store and extract (Chapter 13).
  • Missed names, ids or codes: add hybrid search (Chapter 05).
  • Position-dependent answers: select prompt content (Chapter 05).
  • Per-user updates or deletion: use a mutable store (Part D).
  • Summary detail lost: consult originals retained under policy (Chapters 01 and 02).
  • Restart recovery: checkpoints. Cross-thread facts: store. Both needs: combine (Chapter 13).

Verdict: build the smallest thing that holds

Do not start new work on deprecated classes or retired products. LangChain deprecated its memory classes, and newer OpenAI embedding models succeed ada-002. Learned memory (card 1) and reflection streams (card 8) remain research baselines. Do keep the simple answers for small jobs; follow "Time to move on" chapter pointers.

16

The research frontier

Research beyond files, vectors and graphs: maturity, evidence and what builders can use now.

Maturity

Mostly research

Evidence

Most numbers are reported by the authors.

State of

November 2026

Best for

Builders deciding what to watch, test or ignore.

Map of the frontier

Agent memory mostly uses files, vector indexes and graphs. Figure 1 maps twelve lines of research beyond them, grouped into six sections below.

Prototype in Figure 1 means open code that works in a lab, with no support promise, and Paper only means a published result with no code a team could adopt. Placement follows cited evidence; lines can occupy multiple columns.

Gotcha: results are mostly self-reported

Most figures are self-reported. An independent audit disputes LoCoMo’s reference answers (a long-conversation benchmark); its official issue thread records judge inconsistencies and acknowledged data-quality concerns (Chapter 17).74,1

Compute before the question arrives

Sleep-time compute, dreaming and offline consolidation

Sleep-time compute moves work off the query path. It anticipates questions and saves notes instead of rederiving them at query time.2 The authors report up to 2.5 times lower cost per query when several questions share one context. Tested locally (benchmarks/gap-reruns): a 7B model on 32 grade-school math contexts, 5 questions each. Arms: direct answers, notes for one question and notes shared across 5 questions, at different verbosity levels. Notes average 646 tokens per context. Weighted cost per answer = note tokens ÷ questions sharing notes + 10 × query-time generated tokens. The paper’s assumed tenfold cost for latency-optimized query tokens is a proxy here, not measured prices. Substitute your price ratio for spend estimates. Single-question notes cost 3.2 times shared notes with the tersest prompt, 1.1 with the most verbose. These ratios measure reuse, not savings over direct answering. Verbose notes lowered accuracy from 58.8% to 48.1% (difference -10.6 points, 95% interval -17.5 to -3.7). A/B consolidation against direct answers; shorten or skip notes if accuracy falls.

  • Shipped Letta. Version 0.7.0 added sleep-time agents: one talks to the user while another edits its memory blocks.3
  • Research preview Claude dreams (Managed Agents, access request needed). An asynchronous dream reads a memory store and 1 to 100 past session transcripts. It merges duplicates and replaces stale or contradicted entries in a new store. Inputs stay unchanged; outputs are discardable. A dream takes minutes to hours, is billed at standard token rates, and is not eligible for zero data retention or HIPAA.4
  • Anthropic's own measurements. A 6 November 2026 essay reports wikis built over 128 dreams lifted scores on 25 questions from 13% to 48% of graded criteria, and that wiki plus search scored 61% against 53% for search alone. On one task the wiki grew to 1.77 times the source token count with no clear accuracy gain. These are vendor measurements, not rerun here.5

Gotcha: a dream can promote a wrong note

Anthropic's essay warns that a wrong note promoted into the always-loaded layer enters every session, and that agents sharing one page overwrote each other's facts, leaving 41 of 57 facts intact until each agent got its own page.5 Review a dream's output before attaching it (write gates: Chapter 17).

Memory in weights and caches

Test-time memory: Titans and its relatives

Paper only (original release) Titans keeps attention as short-term memory and adds a small neural module that updates while the model reads.6 Google reports gains over Transformers and linear recurrent models across language, reasoning, genomics and time series, including needle-in-haystack tests beyond 2 million tokens.6 An independent reimplementation finds memory helps, but smaller chunks lose attention context and strain cross-chunk recall.7 Paper only Nested Learning studies learning processes that update at different rates, letting some learned state change while other state stays stable; its continual-learning proposal has no independent replication cited here.8

Self-updating pools, per-user edits and knowledge editing

Prototype, not run MemoryLLM adds a fixed-size memory pool inside the model's latent space that updates itself from new text. Its authors released code and a model, reporting no degradation after nearly a million updates.9

Paper only A June 2026 paper stores each user's facts as edits to a hash-keyed lookup table inside the model, with one small shared adapter that reasons over it. Its authors report that direct recall matches a separate low-rank adapter (LoRA) per user, with 5.6 times higher indirect-reasoning accuracy, and that edits from different users combine in one table; none of this was run here.10 If it shipped, per-user facts would leave the prompt and deleting one would mean editing weights.

Prototype, not run ROME edits one fact with a rank-one update to a feed-forward layer.11 This single-association edit does not establish per-user memory support; keep user facts elsewhere.

Looped transformers: compute is not stored knowledge

Shipped Inkling 2 Mini, released with open weights on 20 November 2026, runs its middle layers several times per token.72 In its variable-loop research checkpoint, Thinking Machines Lab reports better multi-step reasoning and long-context retrieval with more passes, but no gain on factual-recall tests. The maker says stored knowledge mostly tracks total parameter count.72,73 These are vendor claims, not reproduced here. Extra computation does not replace an external memory store; the maker says search and tools close the knowledge gap.72 Add retrieval when questions need facts absent from pretraining, whatever the loop count. Chapter 06 has its details and this book's one local test.

Cartridges: a trained KV cache per corpus

Prototype (run here) Train a small KV cache (attention state built from text) once instead of prompting with the corpus repeatedly. Self-study generates synthetic conversations about the corpus and trains the cache with a context-distillation loss (teaching it to reproduce the model's answers with the corpus in context); plain next-token training was not competitive with in-context learning.12 Stanford’s authors released code, reporting in-context quality with 38.6 times less memory.12 A short local training run (1.5B model, one patient’s records, 20 questions) did not match that. The cache cut stored attention state from 338.6 MiB to 5.75 MiB, but accuracy fell from 16/20 (80%) with documents in context to 6/20 (30%). The run does not test the full method. Code: benchmarks/param-reruns.

Cartridges suit stable corpora and trainable open-weight models. If new per-query cost reaches baseline cost, there is no break-even. Otherwise:

Break-even queries = preparation cost per corpus version ÷ (baseline minus new cost per query), in one currency. Preparation includes synthetic self-study and cache training. Before refresh, queries must exceed break-even and held-out quality meet your target.

Also not run: DeepSeek's Engram adds an N-gram lookup table inside the model, trained with the model, so it holds shared pretraining knowledge, not per-user memory.75 KVzip evicts low-importance KV-cache entries without knowing the query, so one compressed cache serves many questions. It needs no training, unlike Cartridges, and stores less than an uncompressed prompt cache (Chapter 10).76

Compressed context and recursion

Latent memory: MemGen

Prototype (run here) A reinforcement-learned trigger watches the model's reasoning and decides when a second module, the weaver, inserts latent tokens (internal vectors, not words). Authors report gains up to 38.22% over two external-memory systems and up to 13.44% over a baseline trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO, an RL fine-tuning method) on eight benchmarks, none reproduced here.13 Tested locally: on 150 GSM8K (grade-school math word problems) test questions (benchmarks/param-reruns), the released 1.5B checkpoint scored 68.0% against 58.0% for the same model without the memory module, a gain of 10.0 points (95% interval 1.3 to 18.7). The implementation publishes weaver/trigger training, evaluation scripts and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and SmolLM3-3B checkpoints for KodCode, GSM8K and TriviaQA, with no production support.14

Recursive language models

Prototype, not run The model inspects a long prompt variable through code and calls itself on pieces. Authors report inputs about two orders of magnitude beyond the window and, on GPT-5, median relative gains of 26% over compaction and 13% over Claude Code at comparable cost; none rerun.15 Use a code sandbox and cap recursion depth and tokens. Start with offline inputs too large for one window; measure interactive latency against your response-time budget.

Memory the agent curates or carries

Agents store, link, rewrite and retrieve memory, sometimes trained with reinforcement learning (RL). Chapter 13 covers shipped frameworks; these gains are self-reported.

ProjectWhat the agent does, and what it would change for your applicationMaturity and reported result
A-MEMWrites linked, tagged notes and rewrites old ones.16 Writes cost model calls; reads return linked notes.Prototype, not run. Open code; no result figure extracted.
ACEEdits a playbook through generate, reflect and curate steps, adding small deltas to avoid "context collapse" (rewrites that erase detail).17 The playbook consumes prompt tokens every call.Prototype (run here). Open code. Authors report +10.6 points on agent tasks. Local 7B run, 200 finance items (benchmarks/delegate-ace): 46.5% without a playbook to 57.0% with it (paired gain 10.5 points, 95% interval 3.5 to 18.0). Gains mostly reused captured formulas, not new problem-type reasoning.
ReasoningBankDistills strategies from its own judged successes and failures.18 Adds a judging call per task and retrieved strategies in the prompt.Prototype, not run. Open code. Gains over raw trajectories; no figure extracted.
MementoThe reasoner stays frozen; train and host a separate policy selecting past cases.19Prototype, not run. 87.88% Pass@3 (success within three attempts) on the GAIA agent benchmark's validation set.
AgeMemOne policy learns long-term operations (add, update, delete) and context operations (summarize, clear, retrieve).20,21 Memory calls become the model's own tool calls. Training needs GPUs managed by Ray (a distributed-computing framework) and a judge-model key.Prototype, not run. Open training code. Gains on five benchmarks; no figure extracted.
MemRLStores episodes with feedback-derived utility scores; model weights stay frozen.22,23Prototype, not run. Self-hosted; MIT code. Detailed below.
SoMemKeeps linked documents, revises them and keeps evidence links.24 Revision costs model calls; evidence links make answers checkable.Prototype, not run. Open code. +2.00 to +3.10 points over the strongest baseline on three benchmarks.

Start with an untrained playbook (ACE above; details below). Below: utility selection, hierarchical retrieval, evidence fallback, decay and learned state.

Runtime utility learning: MemRL

Prototype, not run MemRL targets repeated tasks with pass/fail checks, such as similar build failures. Two-Phase Retrieval selects similar episodes by learned utility score. Passing tests raise the retrieved episode's score, letting it outrank a similar failed attempt. Weights stay frozen. Authors report gains on HLE (hard knowledge questions), BigCodeBench (code generation), ALFWorld (household text tasks) and Lifelong Agent Bench (repeated agent tasks), none reproduced.22

  • Test it. Compare against retrieval over the raw history (RAG, Chapter 00) with the same model, task split and budget, measuring held-out repair success, tokens, latency and verifier errors.
  • Cost. Feedback needs test execution, environment interaction or a judge call on top of the reasoning and summary calls; frozen weights remove fine-tuning, not these costs.22,23
  • Risk. The paper's appendix G.4 warns that false-positive rewards can give bad episodes high utility and spread contaminated behavior. Keep the verifier independent of retrieved text, audit rewards and be able to remove poisoned episodes.22

Hierarchical retrieval: xMemory

Prototype, not run xMemory separates interaction history into events and reusable memory components, then groups related components. Retrieval selects complementary groups and expands to original messages only when needed, avoiding redundant flat top-k results and details lost in summaries. Authors report better answer quality and token efficiency on LoCoMo and PerLTQA (personal long-term question answering); official code is available. For near-duplicate support conversations, test update separation against flat retrieval.25,26

Compact notes with a route back to evidence: TierMem

Prototype, not run TierMem (COLM 2026, MIT license) keeps two linked tiers: compact summaries and extracted facts, and original interaction pages. A trained Qwen3-0.6B router checks retrieved notes for enough evidence. Otherwise, bounded retrieval follows source links to raw pages; note updates preserve those links. A lighter variant called Jev in the repository uses Markdown notes and searchable raw history, with no router training or vector database.27 Test: from a debugging session, store the timeout in a note and the failing test’s name only on its linked raw page. Ask for the timeout: require a note-only answer. Ask for the test name: require a page fetch and the correct name.

Soft forgetting without erasure

Prototype, not run Vestige’s maintainer advertises FSRS-6 (a spaced-repetition scheduling algorithm) memory decay for retrieval, a claim with no independent evidence of better answers.28 Test: toggle decay on a fixed corpus at fixed top-k. Require rare-critical-fact recall not to fall; report answer accuracy for those facts and recent trivia. Soft forgetting in Chapter 05 covers the scoring and its risk to rare facts. A low score cannot replace hard expiry or required deletion (Chapters 10 and 17).

Learned internal state: MEM1 and MemAgent

Prototype, not run MEM1 trains memory consolidation and reasoning together with RL: each turn merges new observations into a compact internal state and discards irrelevant history. Authors release training code, reporting gains on retrieval QA, web QA and shopping tasks.30 MemAgent reads document segments, overwrites working memory repeatedly and publishes RL training and inference code.31,32 Unlike playbooks, both carry state within one task and need training; neither replaces a per-user fact database.

Start with a playbook

Prototype (local attempt invalid) A playbook is a small text file the agent edits in place; ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet authors report gains without training. Dynamic Cheatsheet keeps an evolving cheatsheet for a black-box model, and its authors report GPT-4o on Game of 24 rising from 10% to 99%.33 Local 3B run on the same 100 public puzzles was invalid: most cheatsheet answers hit the output-token limit (benchmarks/small-reruns). It does not test the GPT-4o gain. A playbook costs prompt tokens on every call; a wrong rule loads every session (write gates: Chapter 17).

Learned write policies: Mem-alpha

Paper only Mem-alpha instead trains the agent by RL to decide what to store, on histories up to 30K tokens.34

Context, skills, long windows and memory systems

Context engineering, editing, compaction and the memory tool

Shipped Usable today: the memory tool is generally available. Beta Context editing and compaction are beta. Anthropic defines context engineering as curating the tokens available at inference time.35 Its memory tool needs {"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}, and your application stores the files.36 Context editing clears old tool results and thinking blocks by rule and is in beta behind the header context-management-2025-06-27.37 Server-side compaction replaces older turns with a summary Claude writes. Compaction runs on demand or at a token threshold.38 Chapter 01 shows the memory tool's file layout.

Long context versus retrieval, and context rot

Chroma tested 18 models, including GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5 and Qwen3, and found reliability falls as input grows, even on a trivial repeat-the-text task.39 A re-evaluation of long context against RAG finds long context generally scores higher on question answering, summarization-based retrieval comes close, and RAG has advantages on dialogue-based and general queries.40 A February 2026 study found that repository context files tend to lower task success compared with no context file.41 Full context is the baseline to beat when the history fits the window, accuracy on your own questions holds as history grows, and you can afford the tokens. Past that, retrieve, and keep the always-loaded layer to what every session needs.

Unverified: a 113K token cliff

Secondary blogs quote a degradation point near 113K tokens. Chroma's report does not contain it, so treat it as unconfirmed.

Net value against raw-history RAG: Memory Tax

Paper only Memory Tax (October 2026) calls gains over raw-history RAG memory benefit and losses memory tax, because reorganizing history can remove evidence. Its authors find dedicated memory systems underperform RAG in many cases, though not every workload.42 Compare against raw-history retrieval on the same history, reader and questions.

Tested locally: correct answers on LoCoMo: full context 71/123 (58%), Mem0 66/123 (54%), plain RAG 62/123 (50%), Graphiti (temporal knowledge graph, Chapter 14) 44/123 (36%); on LongMemEval (multi-session chat-history questions): BM25 (keyword ranking, Chapter 05) 191/300 (64%), dense retrieval 165/300 (55%). Intervals and limits: Chapter 17; code: benchmarks/locomo and benchmarks/longmemeval. Mem0’s 4-answer lead over RAG is inconclusive at this sample size; Graphiti trails RAG by 18, consistent with Memory Tax.

Procedural and skill memory

Shipped A skill (format in Chapter 01) is a folder with a SKILL.md file and optional scripts, loaded when relevant, so only its short description costs context until then.43 On 22 October 2026 Anthropic donated the open standard to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, saying more than 70 agent platforms had integrated it.44 Skills have three authorship models. Human-written skills are standard. Agent-written skills start with research such as Voyager, a Minecraft agent that kept a growing library of executable skills,45 ACE above, and Agent Workflow Memory, which induces reusable workflows from past trajectories.46 Reviewed skills are agent-written skills that a person approves before they load. No product read here documents that review step.

Beta memU offers automatic skill authorship in beta. It is an Apache-2.0 open-source project at version 0.11.0-beta.3 and installs scheduled tasks for Codex, Claude Code, Cursor and other hosts. They slice new session logs into jobs, and the host agent decides to do nothing, patch a skill or create one. The skill is saved as Markdown, embedded by name and description and retrieved on similar tasks.47 Its service makes no model calls, so skill writing costs your own agent sessions, and its steps include no human review.

Memory operating systems

Prototype, not run MemOS and MemoryOS manage memory as schedulable tiers. Both report state-of-the-art LoCoMo results.48,49 Mem0, the shipped library (Chapter 13), reported a 26% relative gain over OpenAI's memory in its 2025 paper.50 Neither LoCoMo headline result nor Mem0's OpenAI comparison was reproduced here; the local Mem0 run above uses different comparators. Before adoption, compare raw-history RAG and full context on your questions as above.

MemOS's research design differs from MemOS 2.0's self-hosted REST service (Neo4j and Qdrant) and local SQLite plugins (Chapter 13).51

Sharing, benchmarks and attacks

Multi-agent shared memory

Paper only A June 2026 paper names four failure modes for fleets of agents sharing memory (leakage, stale propagation, contradictions that persist, lost provenance) and proposes scoped retrieval, temporal supersession, provenance tracking and policy-governed propagation. Authors tested these in one production multi-tenant service, MemClaw, without a baseline; a direct-read scope bypass was fixed during the study.52

Portable memory between harnesses

Paper only Memoryfields proposes Markdown pages with optional YAML metadata and a rebuildable vector index.53 Universal Memory Protocol (UMP) proposes transport-neutral records with scope, provenance, validity and recording times, optional signatures, and revision and forgetting operations. Both are proposals.54

Migration to test. Export one user’s memory between agent harnesses (runtimes hosting agents, such as Claude Code) and back, keeping source ids, scope, validity times, provenance, supersession links and deletions. Check that an expired fact stays expired, a deleted fact stays absent, another user's record stays inaccessible, and vectors are rebuilt for the destination model.

New benchmarks

Prototype (full-context arm run) MemoryAgentBench tests accurate retrieval over incremental input, test-time learning, long-range understanding and selective forgetting across turns; its authors report that no method masters all four.57 Tested locally: on 150 paired questions from the five smaller histories, a local 14B model with 4-bit quantization scored 95.3% with full context (95% interval 90.7 to 97.7). No RAG comparison is reported: 111 of 150 questions exceeded the encoder’s token limit. Histories, reader and chunking also differ from the paper. Code: benchmarks/membench. Prototype (code run) BEAM has 100 conversations up to 10 million tokens and 2,000 validated questions, and reports that 1 million token models degrade as dialogues grow, with or without retrieval.55 Counts were verified and BEAM code run on 100 questions (LIGHT below); degradation was not reproduced.

Prototype (run here) LIGHT, the architecture paired with BEAM, combines an episodic index of the full conversation, recent-turn working memory and a salient-fact scratchpad. Each turn, a model extracts index keys, a summary and scratchpad notes; questions trigger dialogue retrieval and scratchpad filtering. BEAM’s authors report gains of 3.5% to 12.7% over their strongest baselines by backbone, without specifying relative or point units. Tested locally: BEAM's own code, run on 100 questions with a 3B local model, put LIGHT at 31% against 35% for plain retrieval on BEAM's rubric score (difference -4 points, 95% interval -12 to +3), so the gain did not appear at that size (benchmarks/gap-reruns). Indexing, note updates and compression cost model calls before questions arrive, and filtering adds query-time calls.55 Compare against raw logs plus recent context, counting preprocessing/query tokens, latency and accuracy.

Prototype (QA attempt invalid) HaluMem (EMNLP, October 2026) evaluates hallucinations at three stages: memory extraction, updating and memory question answering. Its authors release resources and report hallucinations accumulating during extraction and updates.58,59 Tested locally: a question-answering-only attempt on 150 questions was abandoned: the local 14B judge matched a hand check on only 28 of 41 answers and privacy masking altered ordinary words in 12 questions; validate masked questions against originals, then check a replacement judge against hand labels before scoring (benchmarks/membench). Inspect the stored record, retrieved evidence and final answer to locate failure. A task-success check shows whether it changed the outcome (Chapter 17).

Prototype, not run Chapter 04 covers embodied ConceptGraphs memory: a 3D object map and scene graph.56 WorldMemArena (May 2026) tests agents that see and act, with 400 multi-session multimodal tasks and gold evidence chains that locate a failure in writing, maintenance, retrieval or use. Authors report poor use of visual evidence. The repository (MIT license per its README) runs 19 baselines and needs a 10 GB download.60,61

Benchmarks that score actions. A recall benchmark asks the agent to reproduce a stored fact; three newer suites test whether memory changes its actions.

  • MemoryArena (arXiv February 2026, revised September 2026) gives agents interdependent multi-session tasks in web navigation, planning, information search and formal reasoning. Its authors report that agents near saturation on LoCoMo perform poorly there; this book ran no action tasks and did not reproduce that.62
  • DolphinBench (September 2026) has three knowledge-work personas of about 500K tokens of user messages each and 200 tasks per persona. Each task fails without the history and passes with it, and submissions report cost and latency. It is hosted under Mem0's GitHub organization and two authors also wrote the Mem0 paper, so weigh any Mem0 comparison accordingly.63
  • STATE-Bench (Microsoft, 19 May 2026, MIT license) has 450 customer-support, travel and shopping tasks scored against deterministic end-state checks, five runs per task, a pass^5 reliability score (a task counts only if all five runs pass) and cost per task. Microsoft reports that GPT-5.1 without memory completes fewer than half of the tasks reliably. The official protocol needs a hosted simulator and judge, so that claim was not reproduced.64

Coding memory: Hy-Memory, CMB and diff chains

Prototype, not run Hy-Memory (self-hosted SDK, Apache-2.0) stores a chat hierarchy, working facts and coding diff chains; test it when coding tasks resume across sessions or branches. Its coding pipeline links facts and reusable experiences to revision diffs, preserving changes later reverted from the working tree (Chapter 06 covers its writer model). Its model card pins retrieval and reader settings and uses fixed 20% subsamples. Its CMB (Coding Memory Benchmark) column averages two repository question-answering evaluations; do not compare it with the code-editing resolved rates below.29,65

The September 2026 CMB paper, linked by the official repository as an ICLR 2027 submission, evaluates 216 executable code-editing tasks and 750 diagnostic questions across nine repositories, replaying the same frozen histories for each memory method. Resolution requires a nonempty patch, valid test report, and passing new and regression tests. Reported by Tencent's authors, not run here: their TriLink method links facts, experiences and diffs. The public release lacks frozen tasks and grading files, preventing verification.66

Figures from the paper (results tables, source 66; DeepSeek v4-flash): TriLink resolved 35.6% of tasks against 28.2% for MemOS (tied with FullContext) and 26.9% for RAG, and scored 64.2% on QA against 62.2% for RAG. With Claude Sonnet-5, TriLink resolved 43.1% against 36.6% for Mem0.

Check both evidence recovery and repository tests. The QA score counts judge-matched reference requirements and the resolved rate counts finished edits, so on these figures RAG is within 2 points of TriLink on QA but 8.7 points (about 19 of 216 tasks) lower on resolved tasks. Limited scale and no significance test make the gap suggestive.66

Memory attacks

MINJA67 and AgentPoison68 are early papers on attacking agent memory, building on older retrieval-poisoning work, and defenses are early. Chapter 17 holds the threat model, rates and controls. Two newer attacks follow.

Prototype (run here) InjecMEM (COLM 2026) needs one chat turn and no access to the store.69 An anchor supplies topical cues for retrieval; a short adversarial command found by gradient-based search steers the answer once retrieved. The authors report reliable topic-conditioned retrieval with unrelated queries unaffected.

Tested locally: a 7B-family payload in a 3B toy store was retrieved in 0/100 trials with defenses and 0/100 without. This undiagnosed retrieval miss leaves steering unmeasurable and neither confirms nor refutes the paper (setup and limits: Chapter 17; benchmarks/security).

  • Limits. The strongest version needs white-box access to a model, a command tuned on some model families can fail on a held-out family, and systems that summarize before storing need a different attack.
  • Defense code. The repository screens text with a small judge model, a perplexity check, Llama Prompt Guard 2 or a ProtectAI classifier, at initialization, on writes or on retrieval (default: retrieval only).70 If your tests support it, screen at both write and read. In the local test the prompt write reviewer (a local model screening proposed writes) rejected all 100 benign factual writes (from ten templates), so a defended success rate of zero does not show the screening is selective.

Prototype, not run SkillJack (August 2026) attacks the step that turns experience into skills, where the agent's own extraction rewrites a poisoned experience into a skill. The authors name three properties: extraction hides malicious intent, a transient experience becomes a persistent capability, and the skill survives deletion of its source records.71

  • Reported figures. On two research systems, SkillX and Anything2Skill, with 150 trajectories, safety detection fell from 98.5% on the poisoned trajectories to 11.4% on the extracted skills in SkillX. Attack success was 56.2% on SkillX and 89.2% on Anything2Skill, and 80.0% of skill-mediated attacks persisted after the original records were deleted. These author-reported figures concern systems other than memU; nothing reproduced.71
  • What to do. Link learned skills to sources and require approval before loading. On source revocation, block dependent skills at once and restore only reviewed, reapproved versions (Chapter 17).

Usable today

Use now, safest first:

  • Memory tool (generally available), context editing and compaction (beta; expect header and field changes).
  • Agent Skills. An open, broadly supported format (Chapter 01). Agent-written skills (memU, beta) need a review step you add yourself.
  • A consolidation pass. Letta sleep-time agents ship, Claude dreams are a preview, and a home-built merge-and-prune job works too (Chapter 02; guardrails, Chapter 17).
  • Mem0 or Letta. Maintained libraries (Chapter 13), with vendor benchmark claims. Pick Letta for agent-edited memory blocks via tools; pick Mem0 for application code to extract and retrieve facts around each turn.
  • An agent-edited playbook. ACE needs no training. Gate writes, version files, prune rarely used rules, and measure token cost against accuracy.

Test in a lab only. Prototype implementations are lab candidates. Before production, compare held-out application tasks against no memory, raw-history retrieval and, where it fits, full context, within write-cost and latency budgets. MemoryArena and DolphinBench are secondary checks (weigh DolphinBench’s Mem0 ties); STATE-Bench needs its hosted simulator and judge. None was run here (Chapter 17).

Wait for production. Every Paper only artifact, including original Titans, per-user edits and Nested Learning. ROME is a single-fact-editing lab prototype, not a user-fact store. The independent Titans reimplementation has chunking limits described above.

Open problems

  1. Saturated, self-reported benchmarks. LoCoMo's reference answers are disputed (Chapter 17), few papers test MemoryAgentBench and BEAM together, and a memory vendor runs one action suite.
  2. Amortization. No published cross-workload break-even figures; see the Cartridges rule.
  3. Weight memory. No independent evidence of robustness to conflicting updates.
  4. Attacks. Authors report single-turn injection (payload tuning may need white-box model access) and poisoned skills surviving source deletion; neither was reproduced here.
  5. Deletion. Deletion propagation to weights, caches, summaries and derived skills is unsolved.

Licenses were read only where a Sources entry names one; check each LICENSE before reuse.

Part F · Chapter 17

17

Security, evaluation and operations

Memory attacks, deletion, evaluation and operating costs.

Kind

Essay

Covers

Threats, deletion, evaluation, operations

Tested here

The write protocol and benchmarks

Best for

Teams making prototype memory dependable.

Threats

Memory carries text into later prompts, making every writer a potential attacker.

OWASP calls this ASI06, Memory and Context Poisoning.1 An OWASP co-lead treats memory, hooks (automatic harness-event scripts) and configuration as trusted environment; edits give attackers standing access.2

Terms new in this chapter

Memory poisoning
False or hostile text saved for later sessions.

Where untrusted text enters and where it comes back

Rule: retrieved memory is data, never instructions

Quote retrieved text with application-controlled source/trust labels (provenance and review state). Block edits to hooks, configuration, system prompts and tool allowlists. Review tool/web content before writes; test every release, including benign writes against reviewers (Release gate).

Published attacks and reduced labs

MINJA plants memories through normal queries and outputs, without store write access.3 AgentPoison optimizes a query trigger to retrieve poisoned memory or knowledge-base entries.4

Published figures were not reproduced. Reduced poisoning labs follow; inversion is discussed below.

Reported figures (as of 20 November 2026)

FigureWhat it measuresEvidence
95.6% and 98.5%MINJA injection success (record stored) on two GPT-4 EHRAgent (clinical-records agent) datasets, with attack success (the agent then acts on it) of 57.0% and 90.0%.3,5Paper, restated
Above 80%AgentPoison attack success at a poison rate below 0.1%, with less than 1% effect on normal task performance.4Authors' paper
92%Exact recovery of 32-token passages (Natural Questions dataset) from the open GTR-base embedding model; a commercial embedding API, not run here, reached 60.9% on MSMARCO.6Authors' paper

Local MINJA and AgentPoison labs used Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct Q4_K_M, 100 trials per arm (companion repository, benchmarks/security; revision pinned in manifest). Defenses ran together: the same model reviewing writes, a recall filter accepting only records the application labels trusted/reviewed, and retrieved text quoted with source labels. MINJA exposed shopping actions without reasoning traces; 0/100 searches redirected with or without defenses, measuring only defense costs. AgentPoison used arithmetic and a weaker trigger search: attack success was 99/100 undefended and 0/100 defended, but review rejected 100/100 harmless writes. These rates are not comparable with the papers'. This unusable reviewer needs calibration on private benign/hostile writes.

Combined defenses cannot reveal which blocked attacks or reduced accuracy. Separate costs were measured: harmless-write rejection and ordinary-answer accuracy on existing records. MINJA answer accuracy fell from 100/100 to 71/100 with defenses. AgentPoison accuracy was 91/100 clean, 90/100 poisoned and 77/100 under attack with defenses. Poisoning cost one percentage point (95% interval 0.0 to 3.0 percentage points), too imprecise to confirm or refute the paper's less-than-1% claim. High recall can coexist with poison; include poisoning regression probes.

A single interaction can persist

InjecMEM crafts a message the agent stores and retrieves for a targeted topic, without store access. Released write/retrieval classifiers offer no guarantees. Test targeted topics and unrelated benign queries.7

A reduced lab directly inserted the released 7B-family-optimized payload, skipping extraction, compaction, fresh optimization and full MemoryOS tiered memory management. Payload retrieval and attack success were each 0/100; conditional success is undefined without retrievals. This cannot assess the paper's attack.

Persistent injections have reached ChatGPT memory through untrusted content and Claude Code memory and hooks through a cloned repository; both were fixed.89

Poisoned learned skills

SkillJack disguises malicious experiences as durable skills surviving source deletion.10 Controls to try:

  • Link skills to source experiences.
  • Require review plus benign and hostile activation tests before promotion.
  • Revoke skills with their sources; test deletion across layers.

Detecting direct store tampering

A September 2026 preprint tested store edits in LangGraph's SQLite checkpointer 3.1.1, Letta 0.16.8 and Mem0 2.0.20. All 15 edits reportedly passed silently, including forged insertions. The attacker has storage access; results cover only these pinned versions.11

Locally, the five edit classes, forged insertions included, were accepted in all 1,500 trials on those three releases (15 edit and release cells, 100 repeats each). Per-store keyed hash chains, keys/latest hashes held externally, caught all 1,500 storage-only attacks. Key management, concurrent writers and performance were not tested. Controls to try:

  • An append-only audit log whose entries hash the previous entry.
  • Signed writes, with signing keys kept outside the store.
  • An independently retained signed log head detecting truncation.
  • Check chains/signatures on every read/restore; audit access/failures. On failure, quarantine, stop serving and alert; recover from an independently verified log head. Never re-sign suspect state.

OWASP recommends tamper detection, read-only log copies and monitored log access.12

Cross-user leakage

Shared vector databases can leak memories across users. OWASP's LLM08 entry recommends permission-aware stores, logical partitioning, source validation and immutable retrieval logs.13 Use store-enforced row policies or credentials restricted to a tenant partition. With shared credentials spanning partitions, isolation depends on the trusted retrieval service.14 Bind namespaces to authenticated identity; probe cross-user IDs in vector/keyword search, graph expansion, summaries, caches and restored indexes.

Gotcha: checkpoint stores have had real CVEs

Check installed langgraph-checkpoint and langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite. The SQLite checkpointer saves per-step thread state; langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite 3.0.1 fixes CVE-2025-67644, a SQL injection in its metadata filter.15 CVE-2025-64439, a deserialization flaw, is fixed in langgraph-checkpoint 3.0.0. Check Point reports the two chain to reach code execution.16 Never let end users control checkpoint history filters, and delete checkpoints with the thread as personal data.

Inversion, secrets and personal data

Embeddings can reveal source text, so a vector index is not anonymized.6 A reduced local attack on 4-bit GTR-base and Vec2Text models (five correction rounds, where the paper uses 50 plus a wider search) exactly recovered 0/100 synthetic 32-token texts, though the output shared most of its words with the original (word overlap 0.724); it does not match the published 92%. Exclude secrets at write time; reference them by ID. The lab embedded bare opaque references and vaulted text separately, removing semantic matching for those records; retrieval utility was unmeasured.

Privacy and deletion

Delete across the source records and everything derived from them. Engines differ: PostgreSQL retains dead rows until vacuum makes space reusable, usually without returning it to the operating system.17 Check logical invisibility, disk reclamation and backup erasure separately.

What "delete" leaves behind, by store type

StoreCopies to account forAction and check
Files (Markdown, JSON)Version history, editor backups and sync copies.Rewrite files; purge history and backups.
Vector indexDerived vectors, index files, replicas and snapshots. Graph indexes such as HNSW usually mark deletes and reclaim only at vacuum, compaction or rebuild (Chapters 08 and 11).Remove searchable records and verify with queries. Follow the engine's reclamation policy; expire affected backups.
GraphDerived edges, summaries and community nodes.Link every derived item to its source; delete both, then query by source ID: expect nothing.
CachesEmbeddings of summaries, cached answers, saved model KV-cache files (attention state for resuming prompts) and prompt caches.Invalidate every cache keyed to the source. Persisted KV state is sensitive derived data.
Model weightsLearned parameters are unaffected by a source-row delete.Do not promise erasure from weights through a database delete. Exclude personal memory from training by default.
Backups and logsFull copies of all the above, plus logs that name the memory.Schedule backup expiry, or use per-tenant keys so destroying the key makes the copies unreadable.

Crypto-shredding destroys encryption keys to make data unreadable. Every copy must use that key, without recoverable key copies. Volume encryption cannot selectively erase one tenant while preserving others. Inventory plaintext exports/logs and derived data surviving key destruction.

Inventory source/derived copies, erasure/retention deadlines and completion records. Scope retention exceptions, restrict access, set expiry and test absence across layers. Agree requirements with your privacy team; this is no legal-compliance determination.18

Evaluation

Public benchmarks compare ideas; private tests check your data. Separate reported scores from replications.

Public benchmarks and their limits

Six benchmarks used for memory systems

BenchmarkWhat it testsKnown limit
LoCoMo (2024)Ten long conversations test answers, event summaries and dialogue.19It tests neither deletion nor poisoning. An independent audit found incorrect answers; the official issue thread records inconsistent judging and maintainers' acknowledgment of data-quality concerns.20
LongMemEval (ICLR 2025)500 chat-history questions test extraction, multi-session and temporal reasoning, updates and abstention.21It tests chat answers, not poisoning or deletion.
MemoryAgentBench (2025, v4 June 2026)Multi-turn tasks test retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding and selective forgetting.22Selective forgetting, not erasure or poisoning.
MemoryArena (2026)Interdependent tasks across sessions: navigation, planning, search and reasoning.23Covers only its designed environments.
DolphinBench (2026)600 knowledge-work tasks, scored on completion, total cost and latency.24Three personas; no poisoning or erasure test.
HaluMem (EMNLP 2026)It tests hallucinations during extraction, updates and answers.25Its dialogue datasets still need security tests.

MemoryAgentBench, MemoryArena and HaluMem descriptions use public releases, without published scores. Using a local Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct Q4_K_M reader, 150 paired questions per method, MemoryAgentBench's EventQA split scored 95.3% with full context, 86.0% with BM25 RAG (keyword ranking, Chapter 05) and 76.7% with dense RAG. HaluMem QA scored 41.3%, 41.3% and 32.7%, respectively. A five-step MemoryArena pilot showed only that the pipeline runs. These do not measure all four MemoryAgentBench competencies, HaluMem extraction/updates or MemoryArena action completion (intervals: benchmarks/membench).

Local LoCoMo, 22 November 2026: 123 matched questions, four of ten conversations, Qwen2.5-14B on an Apple M3 Ultra, 96 GB, CPU MiniLM embeddings, up to 20 retrieved items, and the same model judging by three-vote majority (harness: benchmarks/locomo). Mem0's LoCoMo scores are vendor results;26 the published column is Wolff and Bennati's, with different settings, unreproduced here; graph shortfalls were attributed to incomplete retrieval.27

Full context led four complete local runs (71/123); Mem0 led those four published results (81.08%). Among those four, Graphiti scored lowest in both columns (44/123 here). These 123 questions do not establish between-system differences. Cognee's incomparable 67-question result is unranked. Different settings and Graphiti extraction retries preclude graph/vector ranking.

On a seeded 300-question LongMemEval sample, retrieving up to ten chunks, BM25 scored 191/300 (63.7%, 95% interval 58.1% to 68.9%) against MiniLM dense retrieval (Chapter 03) at 165/300 (55.0%, 49.3% to 60.5%), a paired difference of 8.7 points (95% interval 2.7 to 14.7 percentage points). The reader and three-vote judge were Gemma 2 9B at 4-bit on an Apple M1 Ultra, 64 GB (harness: benchmarks/longmemeval). Full context could not run: every history exceeded the 8,192-token window. BM25 was strong on user facts and knowledge updates, weak on multi-session reasoning and preferences.

An implementation agent checked 40 random judgments per benchmark against questions, answers and references, blinded to machine labels: agreement was 32/40 on LoCoMo, 37/40 on LongMemEval. Without independent human validation, treat small LoCoMo gaps cautiously.

A private regression set

Test scrubbed interactions on every change.

  • Contents: labeled questions on expected facts, supporting IDs, updates and abstentions, plus poisoning cases, cross-tenant probes and correction and deletion races.
  • Versioning: store the model, extractor, chunking and judge settings with the dataset.
  • Metrics: recall@k (fraction of expected supporting IDs in the top k, averaged over questions with at least one; score abstentions separately), answer accuracy, stale answers, conflicting facts, durable write precision (accepted writes still correct once built) and invalid outputs. Report poisoning and tenant leaks separately, check judge decisions by hand and keep every failure.

Periodically sample records per tenant; label accurate, stale or junk, and delete or re-extract stale/junk items. One user judged 9,911 of 10,134 entries junk; that self-report was not checked here and is not an expected rate.29

Cost, consistent writes and operations

Calls and tokens per write and per read

Flat files need no embeddings. Vector retrieval embeds writes and queries (Chapter 03). Extraction adds fact/update decisions; graphs add entity resolution/invalidation.3031 Count retries and added prompt tokens.

Mem0 reports 91% lower p95 latency and over 90% fewer tokens than full context for one workload.26 Wolff and Bennati report plain RAG with comparable accuracy at 8.4 times lower total cost than Mem0; not reproduced here.27 On 123 matched LoCoMo questions across four histories, Mem0 used 97.8% fewer read-path input and output tokens combined than full context but only 27.2% fewer on the same basis including ingestion. Its p95 answer latency was higher (11.41 versus 5.82 seconds). Possible explanations include short histories, local 4-bit inference and uncontrolled prefix-cache reuse speeding full context. Measure locally. Counting LLM input/output tokens (extraction included, embedding omitted), Mem0 cost 11.6 to 20.8 times as much as dense RAG across the four histories.

Break-even between full context and memory

One study reports Mem0-style memory cheaper after about ten turns at 100,000 cached tokens; long context was more accurate on LongMemEval and LoCoMo.32 At $0.15, $0.075 and $0.60 per million uncached input, cached input and output tokens (GPT-4o mini list rates checked 22 November 2026; full-context prefix cached after the first question), one 34-question history cost $0.1010 to ingest, saving $0.00435 on question one (uncached input) and $0.002125 thereafter. Projected payback is 1 + ceil((0.10095 − 0.00435) / 0.002125) = 47 questions. Pooled payback projects 49 questions for Mem0 and 51 for Graphiti, beyond the observed 24 to 34. Their 95% bootstrap intervals, resampling four whole histories, were 48 to 51 and 45 to 63, respectively; Mem0 per-history estimates ranged from 47 to 52. These extrapolations assume read-only questions after ingestion. Per-turn writes delay break-even. Ignoring price and caching, Mem0 uses 27.2% fewer tokens at the observed mean of about 31 questions per history; cheaper cached input delays dollar payback. Uncosted storage, embedding and maintenance must also be repaid by repeated reads. If full context cannot fit or suffice, compare the cheapest capable baseline.

A consistency protocol for asynchronous writes

Protocol terms

Outbox
Work committed atomically with source changes; a worker builds the projection later.
Projection
The searchable copy built from a source record.
Tombstone
A deletion record (Chapter 12) preventing resurrection during rebuilds.

The store commits saves/deletes before workers build projections. Figure 2 includes idempotent retries/dead letters. The worker checkpoint, separate from thread state, advances after every event through its sequence finishes or dead-letters. Gaps block advancement; restarted workers resume after it.33 This proposed protocol is not standardized.

  1. Accept. Authenticate the tenant; atomically commit the new source version and outbox entry. Store an HMAC of tenant, memory ID, operation and payload under each tenant-scoped event ID. Retries return the original receipt; changed payloads are rejected.
  2. Materialize. Publish only current source versions so slow jobs cannot overwrite newer data. Tag derived items with tenant, extractor revision and all contributing source IDs/versions. Hide items with deleted, superseded or unauthorized dependencies; rebuild from authorized sources before serving. Commit the projection update and its delivery row (in the delivery table) together if possible.
  3. Retry. Retry with bounded backoff/jitter; then flag a dead letter for an operator: terminal for checkpointing but unsuccessful, automatic delivery stopped. Record attempts/redacted errors, alert on queue age/dead letters, and retry the same event ID after repair.
  4. Checkpoint. Advance only past terminal events, including dead letters; never skip gaps.
  5. Delete. Commit a versioned tombstone, remove source text, hide stale reads immediately and delete derived items. Use a new memory ID for replacements to prevent stale-write resurrection.
  6. Rebuild. Rebuild from authorized sources and tombstones. Erasure-safe restores need a separately recoverable tombstone ledger covering every restorable snapshot. Current-state restores also replay committed updates to a verified position before serving. If later updates are lost, declare the recovery-point objective (maximum tolerable data loss). Probe a corrected, never-deleted record after restore.

Remote indexes retain text-free versioned tombstones until workers finish and retention expires. Write only newer versions before recording delivery locally; crash redelivery safely repeats writes. Without conditional writes, process one memory ID at a time and compare index against source. Retrieve candidate IDs, then hydrate/filter against current authorized sources before prompting. Version equality hides the entire record during lag, indefinitely on dead letters. For read-after-write, await materialization or read source. See also Chapter 13, Forked planning: draft locally, promote explicitly.

Runnable consistency check

Post-cutoff lab verification: 23 November 2026 (research cutoff: 22 November 2026), CPU only, containers capped at two CPUs; Docker 29.1.3, CPython 3.14.4, SQLite 3.51.3. The demo checks local conflict, tenant isolation, retries, reordering, dead letters, deletion and rebuilds; remote indexes/power loss are excluded.34

A fresh process checks durability; rebuild needs no replay. Purging outbox rows loses receipts: retain a separate tenant-scoped receipt table through the retry window; test an original retry after correction/rebuild of a live record. Post-delete redelivery only checks the duplicate guard. Reset memory.db before reruns. HMACs use owner-only request.key outside SQLite; use a production secret store. Purge HMACs with tombstones. WAL/backups may retain deleted bytes; this tests logical non-resurrection, not physical erasure.

Remove this exercise's directory and image:

bashTested
rm -r /var/tmp/memlab-17
docker image rm memlab-17-sqlite

Harden the lab network

Docker publishes to all host interfaces by default; in the book's database and model-server labs, bind ports to 127.0.0.1, or publish none and use a private network.36 Before LAN access, authenticate databases/model-server proxies; Ollama's API defaults to unauthenticated loopback access.37,38 Before Docker 28.0.0, localhost-published ports may be segment-reachable; upgrade or enforce firewall isolation.36

Operate the memory path

Log tenant, source version, retrieval score and opaque record-version ID under access/retention controls. Correlate text via tenant-scoped HMACs, external keys and defined retention; never log plaintext. Back up sources/tombstones; test restores in quarantine. For embedding migration, build a shadow index (serving no reads), pin model revision and dual-write via outbox. Record the last committed sequence. Switch after its worker checkpoint reaches that sequence without dead letters, tenant/deletion probes pass, and private-regression recall@k and accuracy match the live index. Dual-write deletes while rollback remains possible. Consolidation (merging/summarizing memories) needs live-write version/deletion checks against resurrection.39

Release gate

Check writes before launch and after model/prompt changes. Record release margins/budgets against current controls and workload requirements.

  • Test cross-tenant retrieval, poisoning, correction races, delete, replay, restore (including corrected, never-deleted records) and source/tombstone rebuilds; require latest authorized versions on reads.
  • Compare representative private tasks with no-memory/current-release controls; report completion, cost and latency. Add task-matched MemoryArena or DolphinBench comparisons. Fail on confirmed cross-tenant retrieval, action-changing poison, completion below the control by a preset margin, or cost/p95 latency over preset budgets.
  • Commit labeled harmless facts/corrections, await materialization, query in a fresh session; require a preset share correct. Report hostile-write acceptance and benign-write rejection as counts/denominators; fail above either preset budget or the answer-accuracy-loss budget.
  • Monitor queue age, retries, dead letters, stale-version skips and delete completion in every derived store.

Forward example. Chapter 22 applies these controls to a doctor's office: per-patient scoping, an append-only audit trail, tombstones that survive a restore.

Part F · Chapter 18

18

Choosing an architecture

Pick the smallest memory that fixes a failure you can see, then grow it by measured signals.

Compared

14 designs/components (Chapters 01 to 14), ten criteria; 3 further families, five criteria; 2 tools unrated.

Answered

12 head-to-head selection questions.

Routed

2 flowcharts from the kind of memory to a store.

Built

7 reference stacks, 4-step scale path, regional rule and nearest case study (Chapters 21 to 23).

The ratings are editorial judgments, not benchmarks. Start with “Start small” for capability gaps and the scale path for capacity limits; consult comparisons and stacks as needed.

Verdict: begin with files, and let evidence move you

Single-user tools and prototypes start with flat files and git history, then keyword search and embeddings in one SQLite file. Use Postgres for cross-host writes, tenant isolation or excessive contention. Trial a note-taking model when verified chat facts repeatedly go missing from notes; keep it only if omissions fall without more false writes. Use a task graph for blocked, claimed or ready work; notes suffice for simple hand-offs. Managed services trade operation for payment. If stable material fits the window, see “Long context or any memory”.

Comparison matrices

Dots run from one to five; fewer means less effort/cost. Running cost is memory’s added expense; Write cost counts model calls per save. Matrix 1 setups work disconnected with models/services inside the deployment; Matrix 3 varies. Exact terms, Meaning and Changing facts rate retrieving literal strings, paraphrases and current facts after replacement. Scale ceiling rates data/load before replacing the design. Postgres + pgvector means PostgreSQL with the extension. Store rows include local embedding calls per vector write; note-taking models are small memory LLMs. Component rows (Chapters 03, 04, 05, 06, 07 and 10) include their tested stores. Read the reasons before deciding on one-dot differences.
