One line of reason for each row

ArchitectureWhy it is rated this way
Flat filesReadable, no service/model calls. Claude Code loads a partial MEMORY.md index each session (Chapter 01).1
LLM wikiIngest calls a model, which can flag conflicts; rewrites can damage unrelated pages.2,3
Text embeddingsOne embedding call per item; unreadable, strong on paraphrase. Memory size and the write queue break first (Chapter 03).4
Multimodal embeddingsIndexes slides and photos directly, but needs larger models; a text embedder scores higher on text.5
Hybrid + rerankOne embedding call per written chunk; keyword indexing and fusion need no model, and the reranker runs on read. It changes retrieval, not storage; add only after measured misses. Chapter 05's 24-note test showed none: embeddings alone found the right note in every top-three result (recall@3 1.00), against 0.95 for hybrid. Test your set.
Note-taking modelsEvery write calls a model; slow on CPU, offline-capable (Chapter 06). In Chapter 06's one-input test a 2B model saved one fact and dropped the other.
Uncensored LLMsCosts match a stock note-taking model. Chapter 07's small test: the uncensored (weight-edited) model reversed one correction (two reversed facts); the stock model did not.
Postgres + pgvectorTransactions, joins, row security and hybrid SQL in one store. Tuning is yours.6
Redis, ValkeyFast expiring state, all in RAM (about 16 GB per million 1,536-dimension vectors, hash plus index, versus about 6 GB raw float32, Chapter 09). Crashes can lose the last second with AOF fsync every second, more with snapshots.7
Memcached, cachesA disposable key-value cache. It stores answers, not memory.
Vector storesBest vector features and scale. In many, tenant isolation needs your metadata filter; check native namespaces (Chapter 11).8
SQLite, othersOne local keywords/vector file; serialized writes. Pin pre-v1 sqlite-vec. SQLite 3.51.3 or later fixes concurrent-write/checkpoint WAL corruption (Chapter 12).9
Memory frameworksQuick extraction/search costs extra model calls. Scores are vendor claims; Chapter 17 compares independently.10
Knowledge graphsTracks sourced facts’ true/learned dates. Highest write cost, estimated: several calls/episode, varying with matching/retries. Chapter 14 ran offline on CPU. Setup: graph database, JSON-capable 7B note-taking model.11
Task graph, BeadsTasks, dependencies and claims; no write-time model call or knowledge-retrieval rating. Embedded mode: one writer/database.12
Context databaseBrowsable files, model summaries, scoped vector search; one model call/directory imported. Gains are maintainer claims.13,14
Managed servicesExtraction/storage/retrieval billed per use; enforce scopes. No servers, no offline use. Chapter 13 surveys, not runs: Google/AWS memory generally available (checked 2026-11-20), Microsoft Foundry memory in public preview.15,16,30
MemPalace 3.12.0Verbatim conversations: wings scope people/projects, rooms topics, drawers content. Local-first, MIT. Recall@5: fraction of relevant items in five results; with one, hit rate, not answer accuracy. Not run (Chapter 13).17
EverOSReadable Markdown source, SQLite/LanceDB indexes. Self-run, Apache-2.0. Scores are not comparable; session/user/agent deletion scopes differ. Not run (Chapter 13).18

Decision flowcharts

Head-to-head answers

Flat files or an LLM wiki

  • Pick files when facts are short, stable and person-written. Keep them within the Chapter 01 limits.1
  • Pick a wiki when one agent maintains a few hundred pages on one topic, with diff review. Long rewrites corrupted 25% of content on average with three frontier models; this book's 7B run lost 71% in four edits.2,3
  • Combine: store notes in the wiki; point a short file to its index. Retain raw sources.

Keyword search or embeddings

  • Pick keyword search when question and note share words: identifiers, error codes, names. Anthropic illustrates an embedding miss with error code TS-999, found by keyword ranking;4 Chapter 05's 24-note embedder test found it. Test your corpus.
  • Pick embeddings when labeled questions miss relevant notes because wording differs. For a pile too large to scan, try indexed keyword search first.4
  • Combine: index text with FTS5 and sqlite-vec in one SQLite database; fuse rankings (tested with sqlite-vec 0.1.9 on SQLite 3.51.3).9

Text or multimodal embeddings

  • Pick text when the corpus is text. Qwen reports its 8B vision embedder averaging 67.88 on text, versus 70.58 for its 8B text model (not run here).5
  • Pick multimodal when you search screenshots, slides or photos directly. ViDoRe V3 reports visual retrievers beat textual ones on document pages.19
  • Combine: for a readable trail, embed image captions beside image vectors.

An embedding model or a note-taking model

  • Different jobs. Embedders index unchanged chunks by meaning; note-taking models extract facts from raw chat. Search unchanged chat when passages suffice.
  • Pick the note-taking model when you need discrete facts and the baseline repeatedly misses them. Each write calls a model; false facts stick. In Chapter 06's CPU test, thinking mode raised one schema-checked extraction from 3.4 s to 96.9 s. Queue the write, turn thinking off and review it. Use a stock model unless it fails: Chapter 07's ten-prompt test retained every fact with a stock small model; an uncensored model reversed one correction.
  • Combine: put a note-taking model before an embedder for semantic fact lookup. Mem0 packages this (see "A framework or building it yourself").

Redis, Memcached or Postgres

  • Pick Redis (or Valkey) when the data is the working layer (sessions, semantic cache, expiring keys, streams). It must fit RAM; crashes can lose the last second (AOF fsync every second, more with snapshots).7
  • Pick Memcached when you need a shared, disposable exact-key cache.
  • Pick Postgres when the record must commit with business data and row security separates tenants.6
  • Combine: Postgres with Redis as a hot tier that rebuilds from it, or with Memcached as a versioned answer cache (Chapter 20).

An embedded file, pgvector or a dedicated vector store

  • Pick one SQLite file when writes stay on one host, contention meets your latency budget, and you want keywords and vectors without a server (Chapter 12).9
  • Pick Postgres + pgvector when you run Postgres and want joins, transactions and row security. pgvector defaults to exact nearest-neighbor search. Measure approximate versus exact results (index recall), then labeled fact retrieval (retrieval recall). The pgvector README gives no approximate-index row cutoff.6
  • Pick a dedicated vector store or managed service when a tuned index cannot meet recall at the required p95 latency (step 4 of the scale path below), or you search page images with several vectors per page (late interaction, Chapter 11).
  • Combine: Postgres holds truth; rebuild the vector copy, recording each vector's model name/revision.

A framework or building it yourself

  • Pick a framework when you want extraction and search in few calls. Mem0 runs with Ollama and Qdrant.20 It needs a separate keyword branch when exact identifiers matter (Chapter 13).
  • Build it yourself when the schema is narrow, memory sits in your database, or you must audit writes. A plain retrieval baseline matched Mem0 at 8.4 times lower cost in one published comparison;10 this book's local run found about 16 times lower generation-token cost (Chapter 17).
  • Combine: a framework extracts and your store keeps the result. LangGraph has Postgres storage.21
  • Tested routes (Chapter 13): Hindsight, a self-hosted memory server, retained/recalled across restart; Letta Code passed scripted retention of explicitly saved information. Neither proves unprompted fact selection or minimum model/GPU requirements; measure yours.
  • For the surveyed tools in Matrix 3, preserve source exports and verify deletion from source and derived stores.17,18

Self-run memory or a managed cloud service

  • Pick a managed service when you prefer per-use billing to operating extraction/storage and can enforce user scopes. Prices checked 2026-11-20; recheck: Google Memory Bank bills $0.30 per GiB-month plus model tokens. AWS AgentCore bills $0.75 per 1K records-month and $0.50 per 1K reads, so 100,000 records and 1M monthly reads cost about $575 ($75 storage plus $500 reads); at an assumed 2 KiB per record, Google storage alone is about 0.19 GiB, or $0.06 monthly. These subtotals are not comparable: price identical saves, reads and model-token volumes.22,23 Microsoft Foundry Agent Service Memory, public preview, has quotas, no virtual network integration and changing model-usage bills (Chapter 13).30 AWS raw events expire within 365 days; delete derived records separately.24
  • Pick self-run when memory must stay on your hardware or every record must be inspectable.
  • Combine: the service extracts/serves memories; export source conversations separately, since derived records are not backups (Chapter 13).

Vectors or a knowledge graph

  • Pick vectors when questions are local lookups and facts are short. An independent LoCoMo long-conversation test scored Mem0/retrieval/full context at 77 to 81% answer accuracy, Graphiti/Cognee at 55 to 56% (Chapter 17 reruns locally with different settings).10
  • Pick a graph when facts have dates and links. Graphiti invalidates a replaced fact instead of deleting it,11 and keeps two timelines (Chapter 14).
  • Check the note-taking model: use a model that returns valid JSON (7B and 0.6B passed ingestion/search smoke tests; an earlier 0.6B trial timed out); Chapter 14 has the gotchas and the acceptance test.11
  • Combine: lookups and dated links: vectors as the base, the graph on top.

A task graph or notes

  • Pick a task graph when sessions or agents must track blocked, claimed or ready work. Beads bd ready lists unblocked items; claims are atomic within one database. Across replicas, route claims through one writer (stack 7).12
  • Pick notes when the content is facts and conventions that stay true. An issue tracker suffices with ready-work selection and atomic claims (Chapter 01).
  • Combine: Beads holds the plan and notes hold the conventions. A framework checkpoint (such as LangGraph's) resumes one run, replacing neither; rewind does not undo cross-thread store writes (see Chapter 13, Forked planning).

A context database, a wiki, a summary tree or plain search

  • Pick a context database when a folder has thousands of files and grep finds words but not the right directory. OpenViking generates per-directory L0 abstracts/L1 overviews for scoped vector search.13,14
  • Pick a wiki when one person reviews every page, or plain search (SQLite FTS5 or the qmd markdown search tool) for ranked passages only (Chapter 02).
  • Pick a summary tree when questions span themes across manuals/research corpora rather than passages or dated links. RAPTOR clusters chunks and summarizes them upward, at extra model calls per write (Chapter 05).25
  • Combine: the files stay your own and the database is a rebuildable index. Treat an abstract as a pointer: it is generated text.

Long context or any memory

  • Pick long context when stable material is small. Anthropic advises it under about 200K tokens with caching.4 Long-context GPT-5-mini beat a Mem0-style system on accuracy in one study.26
  • Pick memory when history outgrows the window. The same study found memory cheaper after about ten turns at 100K context;26 on this book's shorter local histories the break-even was about 49 questions, not turns (Chapter 17). Chapter 20 measures each addition's prompt tokens and correctness on 24 fixed questions.
  • Combine: memory picks what enters the window.

Seven reference stacks

Stacks are untested exactly as listed; Chapters 20 to 23 are nearest. Chapter 20 stages a community Qwen3.8-2B, Q4_K_M assistant. Build dependencies first; review writes. CPU-only runs from November 2026 (Chapters 05, 06, 07, 12, 14 and 20) show functionality, not retrieval quality at scale.

1Solo developer's coding agent

Situation
One developer, one or two repositories, Claude Code or Cursor; commands, naming rules and decisions disappear between sessions.
Why it fits
Files load without retrieval, grep finds the rest, and git reviews changes.1,27 Keep them short.
Build order
  1. Chapter 01: CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, scoped rules and notes with a dated index. Check past-decision answers in a fresh session.
  2. Chapters 02 and 17: dated decision notes, pruned monthly.
  3. Chapters 05 and 12: SQLite FTS5 only if grep stops finding things.

2Private assistant, fully local

Situation
One person, one small machine, nothing leaving it; Chapter 21 is closest, with different hardware and model size.
Why it fits
One SQLite file holds text, keywords and vectors. Pin pre-v1 sqlite-vec; use SQLite 3.51.3 or later (Chapter 12).9 Tests used Ubuntu CPU, and Chapter 21 a Mac mini; re-measure.
Build order
  1. Chapters 12 and 01: a short profile file and JSONL message log: one object per event with id, timestamp, role and text; a delete event names its target id so rebuilds omit deleted messages.
  2. Chapters 03, 05 and 12: FTS5 first; add Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and sqlite-vec in that file after a paraphrase miss.
  3. Chapter 06: a note-taking model after each session, writes reviewed (Chapter 21 uses 9B versus Chapter 06’s 2B test), or Chapter 13 (Hindsight, tested locally).

3Social-media reply agent in its owner's voice

Situation
Drafts use the owner’s published voice and account context. A person approves every post.
Why it fits
Embed the fixed archive with each post’s URL and date. A note-taking model tracks changing, dated, sourced facts by account and marks superseded notes. Voice rules fit a flat file. Untrusted replies can poison memory: MINJA plants false memories through ordinary-looking queries (Chapter 17),28 so approval gates both publishing and writing.
Build order
  1. Chapters 01, 03 and 12: a voice file, and the archive embedded in one SQLite file with sources shown beside each draft.
  2. Chapter 06: one approved row per fact: note_id, account_id, fact, date, source_exchange_id, supersedes_note_id. Exclude superseded rows from current replies; keep extraction only if omissions fall without more false writes.
  3. Chapter 17: approval queue, trust labels, and a test requiring drafts to cite real posts and exclude superseded facts.

4Customer-support bot with many tenants

Situation
Hundreds of customers need isolated, changing facts and answer-time audits. Chapter 22 (per-patient isolation, audit) is closest.
Why it fits
Postgres + pgvector commits facts, embeddings, tenant and audit rows together, with row security.6 Many vector stores rely on your tenant filter; bugs leak data;8 check for native namespaces or per-tenant collections (Chapter 11). Valid and recorded times (Chapter 14) show which fact applied; log the version IDs cited.
Build order
  1. Chapter 08: tenant_id with row security; append-only fact versions with valid_from, recorded_at and supersedes_id. For past answers, select versions recorded by that date, excluding those superseded within that set; log cited IDs.
  2. Chapters 05 and 08: per-tenant search. Filtering approximate-scan candidates can leave fewer than k matches despite enough tenant records. Iterative scans probe within configured limits; raise limits or use exact search if needed. Test per-tenant recall against exact search.6
  3. Chapter 17: an outbox (change events written in the same transaction as the data) with event ids, and a tombstone per delete, so replay never restores a deleted record; trust labels, write gating, a cross-tenant test in CI returning zero foreign rows.
  4. Chapters 09 and 10: Scope Redis sessions by tenant/user/purpose. Answer keys add query and fact-set revision; advance it transactionally with corrections/deletes. Test that the next identical query misses the old answer. A managed service (Chapter 13, not run) can replace the store, with scope checks still in your code.

5Companion or role-play app

Situation
Months of character conversations need plot continuity and user memory.
Why it fits
SillyTavern layers hand-written lorebooks, generated summaries and optional vector retrieval of past messages, matching this stack’s files, log and summaries. Summaries can lose details or hallucinate.29
Build order
  1. Chapter 01: character card and lorebook files.
  2. Chapters 12 and 06: a JSONL log with FTS5; a local note-taking model appends one dated summary per session (Chapter 02).
  3. Chapters 03 and 07: vectors as a supplement; an uncensored model only if the stock note-taking model refuses legitimate role-play and the replacement passes the Chapter 07 correction test.
  4. Chapter 17: sample summary claims against the log. Regenerate summaries unsupported by the log; if they still lose or invent fixed plot facts, discard them and rely on the log.

6Team of cooperating agents

Situation
Researcher, writer and reviewer agents share facts and must not overwrite one another.
Why it fits
Shared Postgres with a version-checked pointer prevents stale overwrites. Shared-file writes can lose data.27 The MCP reference memory server locks writes but rewrites its growing file (Chapter 13). Ordered writes alone permit stale overwrites. LangGraph namespaces separate private notes; shared facts need version checks.21 Graphiti shares dated facts but needs structured model output (Chapter 14).11
Build order
  1. Chapter 08: shared Postgres with source_agent, recorded_at and supersedes columns. Use compare-and-set: append a version linked to its predecessor. Transactionally advance the current pointer only if that predecessor remains current. Otherwise roll back, re-read and retry; queue contradictory claims for human review.
  2. Chapters 13 and 09: a namespace per agent, and Redis streams for hand-offs, never as the record.
  3. Chapter 01: a task graph (Beads), so two agents cannot take the same task. Use the Chapter 01 multi-writer mode or route claims through one process; embedded mode allows one writer per database.
  4. Chapter 17: gate poisoned writes; test that two edits from one predecessor yield one commit and one conflict.

7Coding agent that resumes work across machines

Situation
Machine or agent hand-offs need completed, blocked and next work.
Why it fits
A task graph keeps the plan outside any session. Beads lists unblocked work and syncs through the git remote with bd dolt push and pull.12 Push before leaving; pull on arrival. Concurrent workers route claims through one writer: local claims do not reserve tasks elsewhere. Embedded mode allows one writer per database (Chapter 01 ran this against a local remote).
Build order
  1. Chapter 01: CLAUDE.md and the notes folder, committed; Beads 1.3.4 on both machines, bd ready first each session.
  2. Chapters 12 and 17: for offline search, commit only history-safe Markdown/JSONL; rebuild SQLite per machine. Tombstones suppress replay, not old commits or clones. For erasure, keep sources out of Git and choose a store and replica-retention policy supporting it. For offline edits, deduplicate event ids; send edits and base versions to one authoritative writer. It versions writes, rejects stale edits and retains versioned tombstones (delete markers) until every replica acknowledges deletion. Re-creation needs a new record ID.
  3. Alternatively, Chapter 13: one shared Hindsight server (tested on one host only; cross-machine use is untested), a per-repository bank, writes reviewed.

Start small

Add one piece at a time to flat files (Chapter 01), each when its signal appears.1 Start with 20 to 30 failure cases; with traffic, test 100 to 300 scrubbed real interactions for recall, updates and forgetting (Chapter 17). Drop pieces that do not improve results.

Signal and the piece to add

SignalAdd
You retype facts each sessionWrite them to notes (Chapter 01)
CLAUDE.md exceeds 200 linesIndex and split, append-only topic notes (Chapter 02); avoid full-page model rewrites
Grep returns too many hits to read, or misses word variants and you need ranked resultsKeyword search (Chapters 05 and 12)4
The note exists in different wordsEmbeddings (Chapter 03)
The right chunk is in the top 50, not the top 5Reranking (Chapter 05)
Sessions or agents must track blocked, claimed or ready workA task graph12
Grep finds words but not the directoryA context database13
A verified fact is in the source chat but repeatedly omitted from notesA note-taking model (Chapter 06); keep it only if omissions fall without more false writes
Answers cite replaced facts, or must say what was known on a dateDated facts or a graph (Chapter 14)11

Scale path and the closest case study

This path adds capacity for users, writers or regions; “Start small” adds capabilities. Enter step 1 for keyword search or embeddings. Signals come from Chapters 01 to 14’s Scope and scale blocks and the case studies.

Deployment changes and their triggers

StepTake this step whenRead
1. One writer host: SQLite with FTS5 and sqlite-vecOne writer host; exact-scan and append time fit your latency budget. No universal user cutoff.Chapters 12 and 21.
2. Shared writes/tenants: Postgres + pgvector; Redis hot readsTenants need row security, another host needs direct writes, or local contention, exact-scan or append time exceeds your latency budget. Add Redis when repeated recall, embedding or session reads dominate. Set p95 and minimum recall targets on your test set (Chapter 17). Stay on exact search until p95 misses; then use approximate index scans (iterative for filtered queries), and go to step 4 when a tuned index still misses either target.Chapters 08, 09 and 22. Chapter 20 stage 4 is the narrower single-user Postgres comparison.
3. Several workers and inference serversThe write queue grows older than your freshness budget, or a long image or document job blocks live replies. Mem0 saves search existing memories; remeasure with growth (Chapter 06). Split model hosts from the application host.Chapters 06, 14 and 22 (two GPU lanes).
4. Dedicated vector store or managed serviceOn labeled queries a tuned index misses recall at the required latency while exact top-k over the same eligible rows finds the fact (if both miss, revisit chunking, embeddings or keyword search first), or measured I/O on the working set (sizing in Chapter 00) makes the tuned deployment miss its latency or cost budget. Choose managed operation separately, when you would rather pay than operate.Chapters 11 and 13.
Any step: regional deploymentsWhen personal data must not cross a border: one database, cache, inference endpoint, key set and backup per region, with no personal-data federation.Chapter 23 (five regions).

Part F · Chapter 19

19

Field report: four memory systems

One operator runs four memory systems side by side: timings, three traps, two search findings.

Kind

Field report

Systems

Four, in daily use by one operator

Evidence

First-party, not independently verified: one operator's own counts, 2026

Best for

Engineers choosing memory systems for different workloads.

The setup in one picture

Assistants are A and B; hosts and products are unnamed.1

SystemJob in this setup
Flat filesHold hand-editable coding-agent rules, procedures and project notes without a service.
WikiPublishes dated, sourced pages: one answer per fact.
Framework + local note-takerExtracts chat facts for two assistants locally (Chapter 13).
PostgreSQL searchRuns lexical and semantic search over a fixed document corpus.

Terms new in this chapter

Retain, recall, reflect
Retain saves a note; recall fetches related notes; reflect reasons over them. Wide recall fetches notes with a high budget; its unit and value were not logged.

You will need: HNSW and IVFFlat, approximate nearest-neighbor indexes (Chapters 08 and 11); rank fusion and rerankers (Chapter 05).

System 1: flat files with an index

Projects have Markdown notes with one-line index entries; counts and arrival rates are unknown. A global file loads hard rules at session start; procedures load when needed; facts go to the wiki.1 Chapter 01 covers mechanics. No service runs; curation depends on System 2.

System 2: a wiki compiled from the files

Agents maintain Git-tracked Markdown pages under a schema, with an index, append-only log, types, dates and sources.1 Chapter 02 describes the pattern. A script lists changed or new notes. An agent compiles their facts into pages and marks each note handled in a separate ledger, leaving the source untouched. A checker validates metadata and links.1 At the last read, 1,177 of 1,424 source notes awaited compilation; read date, accumulation period and cause are unknown.1

Unverified: the counts do not reconcile

The operator reports 257 compiled entries; 1,424 minus 1,177 is 247. The unexplained gap of 10 leaves roughly five sixths pending.1

System 3: a framework with a local note-taker

Each assistant’s framework starts PostgreSQL and maintains its memory bank (store). A local LLM extracts chat facts on an Apple Silicon Mac. Model: about 9 billion parameters, about 5 GB quantized, reasoning off; valid-JSON fact-extraction test passed.1

B replaced reflect’s synthesis with wide recall’s notes, shifting reasoning into its context. A recall and B wide recall are not proven equivalent. Compare note overlap and answer quality on identical banks and prompts.

Timings, 19 to 20 November 2026 (not comparable)

OperationTimeWhat it means
Recall, assistant Aabout 2 sCalled before each answer.
Retain, assistant A, warmabout 25 sRuns in the background after the answer.
Cold daemon start, assistant Aabout 2 minStarts the stopped service once per restart.
Reflect, assistant B40 to 50 sReturned prose with note ids.

B’s memory daemon stays running; A’s idle policy is unknown. Bank sizes, trials, statistics and acceptability are unreported; extrapolation needs scale data.1

Three traps

Gotcha: ids that collide within one second

Parallel saves collided on framework-generated clock-second note ids. Check omitted-id generation. Persist unique ids per logical save; reuse on retries. Verify retries leave one note: replacement, ignored retry or conflict (Chapter 17, queued writes). Corrections need new ids; recommendation: link predecessors, exclude superseded notes from current-fact recall.1

Gotcha: the gateway dropped system messages

B’s gateway removed system messages before the model, including memory instructions. Those moved to a preserved field; compare sent and model-bound requests. Unprompted saves and fresh-session readback confirmed storage and retrieval, without proving instruction delivery.1

Gotcha: a changed prefix loses the cache

The note-taker’s server caches identical tokenized prefixes (first token: cold 0.776 s, repeat 0.165 to 0.232 s). Its client keeps the system message unchanged and first.1

System 4: PostgreSQL search

PostgreSQL with pgvector searches a fixed corpus. Queries filter by the pinned hosted embedding model and size (1,536 dimensions), excluding other models even at equal size. Changing models requires re-embedding all rows.1 Chapter 08 covers this stack.

One SQL statement filters both branches by model, dimensions and kind (record category). Semantic search keeps the nearest 40 passages by cosine distance; lexical search ranks by full-text score, cutoff unrecorded. Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines them with constant 60. The final limit defaults to 6, configurable from 1 to 20.1 Chapter 05 explains the technique. A 26 September 2026 count found 3,245 active documents and 7,668 passages.1

Finding one: the semantic branch had no approximate index

The 26 September 2026 audit rated missing approximate indexes "Severe": three tables used bare vector columns without HNSW or IVFFlat, computing distances exactly. Exact search loses no recall through approximation. Without measured query cost, the rating establishes no current bottleneck.1

The proposed migration adds partial HNSW expression indexes to two tables (cosine, m=16, ef_construction=64). For 1,536 dimensions, use a dimensioned cast in index and query ordering, or constrain the column dimensions. A partial index holds filtered rows; PostgreSQL must prove the query requests only those rows. Match its predicate and dimensioned expression in the query. The third table stays intentionally unindexed, reason unknown. The migration was unrun on 27 September 2026; later deployment is unconfirmed.1

Finding two: a miss with incomplete diagnostics

One query missed its correct passage: rank 159 of 1,905 lexically and 1,063 of 7,668 semantically. Its lexical-only fusion score, at most 1/219, trails all 40 semantic hits (at least 1/100 each), excluding it from the final results regardless of lexical cutoff. That cutoff decides whether a reranker could see it. A replay’s 30-fold widening and rank 240 lack branch labels. Log both ranks and cutoffs, fusion rank and final limit to distinguish pool exclusion from low final rank. An untested proposal reserves merged-pool space for unique headings in document front matter.1

What to do differently

  1. Track the inbox as a metric. Schedule compiles from day one. Set a publication freshness target; alert on oldest pending age and compare arrivals with completions.
  2. Inspect, then test end to end. Check model-bound instructions and roles, then test unprompted retention and fresh-session recall.
  3. Record cold start and idle behavior next to recall time.
  4. Audit the vector index. Inspect the deployed index and EXPLAIN the real query, including partial-predicate implication. Time representative searches. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) executes the statement; use it on read-only searches. A scan may mean a missing or skipped index, or the planner’s correct choice for a small table. Keep exact search if it meets the budget.
  5. Measure candidate rank before adding a reranker. It cannot reach a passage outside the pool.

Verdict: start with one system

Start with flat files. Add a scheduled wiki for curation backlog, a framework for extracting chat facts, or PostgreSQL search for a fixed corpus. Only the wiki builds on the files. Measure backlog age, answer latency and candidate misses before adding systems (Chapter 18).

Sources

  1. First-party measurements by the operator, 2026, published with permission; not independently verified (first-party)

One assistant, six memory stages

Build a personal assistant layer by layer, testing the same questions after each addition.

Best for

Choosing which memory layer an assistant needs.

The scenario and its limits

Ivo describes a new home, job and pottery class. Six weeks later the assistant must recall current and older facts while withholding a forgotten locker code.

The invented history spans September 1 through October 13, 2026. All stages face the same 24 questions; stage 0 sees no history, while later stages change storage and context.

Scope: one user, synchronous writes and a tiny fixture, not general quality. Isolate records before serving multiple users (Chapter 08).

Stages 1 and 2 add layers; stage 3 replaces file loading with search; stage 4 changes input, filters and retrieval together. Stage 5 compares 2B, 4B and 9B writers with fixed 2B answers.

What changes at each stage

AdditionWhat it can buyNew failure to check
0. BaselineNo history is loaded.Abstention can pass without recall.
1. MarkdownFacts survive a fresh chat.Recent chatter displaces older facts; no deletion.
2. Memcached 1.6.45A repeat skips answer generation.A missing data version serves stale answers.
3. BGE + pgvectorOld sessions can reach the prompt.Similarity can retrieve obsolete or forgotten text.
4. Authoritative SQLValid dates and deletion filter recall.Correctness depends on the supplied fact records.
5. Qwen fact writerThe model writes fact bodies; keys stay supplied.Valid JSON can still contain wrong facts.

Fix the questions before building

Four questions per category test stable (S), updated (U), temporal (T), multi-session (M), unknown (N, never said) and forgotten (F). Correct answers earn one point each, at most 24.

The scorer lowercases answers, collapses whitespace, requires every required string and excludes every forbidden string. Unknown and forgotten answers must also contain one of: I do not know, I don't know, not provided, not mentioned, not specified or no information. Literal checks miss paraphrases: quoting an old value ("instead of coffee") fails; day numbers match inside larger numbers.

Prepare a private CPU lab

The model is Empero's community Qwen3.8-2B-Distill-GGUF, not an official Qwen release. Its Apache-2.0 card describes a Qwen3.5-2B base trained on Qwen3.8 teacher traces. File: Qwen3.8-2B-Q4_K_M.gguf at revision f4f73582d0b149595450c719b9a7521a03894f9c. See Chapter 06 for naming.1

Tested: llama.cpp b12464 with --jinja --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":false}' returned direct answers; the harness rejects nonempty reasoning fields or think tags. Requests use temperature 0, seed 7 and disabled prompt reuse, with a 4,096-token context. Answers allow 96 output tokens; extraction allows 768.2

Measurements: stages 0–3 and the 2B writer, 21 November 2026; stage 4, cache checks and larger-writer results, 23 November 2026. These reruns extend the book’s 22 November cutoff. Hardware: a 32-thread x86 laptop-class CPU, 28 GiB RAM, Linux, Python 3.13.18 and Docker. The chat container has four CPUs and 4 GiB RAM; the embedding container has two CPUs and 2 GiB. The front matter’s reference 8 GB GPU and 16 GB Mac were not timed.

Requires Docker, curl, uv 0.13.9, host Python 3.11+, Linux and non-symlinked /var/tmp. Save fixture.py, start.py, lab.py, stale.py, writers.py and cleanup.py together outside /var/tmp/memlab-20. Setup verifies checksums, isolates Python, guards owned resources and allows 180 seconds for readiness, logging failures. Cleanup handles partial setup but refuses missing metadata or mismatched owners. Budget 9.3 GiB of downloads plus images and 14 GiB of container memory limits during writer runs.

Startup runs once and is excluded from timings. The 2B file occupies 1.22 GiB (1,312,164,224 bytes); the BGE cache occupies 127.6 MiB (133,806,795 bytes). Both are excluded from Stored data. Setup binds ports 39200 through 39203 to localhost; writers.py later binds 39204 for the larger writer.

How to read the stage tables

Tables score the first 24-question sweep. Grounded passes have loaded evidence; literal passes can be guesses. First ask is median retrieval-plus-generation latency after startup. Repeat ask is the median of two later sweeps, cached from stage 2 onward. Tokens are first-sweep mean prompt tokens; read calls are per first ask. Hits make no model calls. Stages 1 and 2 send identical prompts on misses. Their 1.06 s median difference establishes no cold-request speedup.

Calls R/W: R counts model-server calls per first ask: one chat call, plus one query embedding in stages 3 to 5. SQL search makes no model call. W is amortized per question: extraction and embedding calls for the scored ingestion divided by 24 (the script misleadingly prints write_calls_per24): stage 3 embeds 12 sessions, so 12 / 24 = 0.50. Tokenization requests are excluded. Stage 5 checks stability across three fresh ingestions with matching insert counts; code always scores the third, preventing score-based selection. Stored data (KiB) includes stages 1–3 Markdown, allocated SQL tables/indexes (including free space) and live cache bytes; excludes weights, runtimes, fixed input, logs and backups. Stage 3 includes 3.9 KiB of unread Markdown.

Stage 2: reuse a finished answer

Memcached returns stored answers before loading files or calling Qwen. Misses follow stage 1 and store results for an hour. Chapter 10 covers exact-response caching. The get/set operations wait for replies; lab.py sets default_noreply=False to acknowledge stores.3

Keys hash stage, data version, model/generation settings, system message, complete question record, embedding revision and retrieval settings. A check outside the six scripts confirmed unchanged inputs hit; changing either embedding revision or retrieval settings missed. Shared deployments need authenticated user/policy scope. File-backed stages version by session count; editable files need content revisions. Cache workers must preserve committed changes and handle duplicate changes safely (Chapter 17).

Stage 3: retrieve old sessions by meaning

Search now covers all twelve sessions. Hugging Face Text Embeddings Inference (TEI), image tag cpu-1.9, serves BGE-small-en-v1.5 at revision 5c38ec7c405ec4b44b94cc5a9bb96e735b38267a and returns normalized 384-dimensional vectors. Only queries get the model card's retrieval prefix. See Chapter 03.4

load() embeds each raw session once. recall() embeds a cache-miss question and asks pgvector 0.8.7 for the closest sessions by cosine distance, breaking ties by row ID. It takes four hits and fits them into the same 600-token memory budget. There is no approximate index. PostgreSQL 18.7 holds the search copy (Chapter 08). Stage 4: make dated SQL rows authoritative

Hand-written fact rows record source session, key, body, since/until dates and deleted flag. Sessions arrive in effective-date order. A correction closes the open row at the session date; the new row is valid from that date, inclusive. This date-only rule cannot reconstruct backdated corrections or two states within a day. Untested alternative: store effective and recorded times separately, selecting effective-date state among rows recorded before the query. The session write and version increment commit together. The lab flushes cache before commit; the transactional version change prevents old-key reuse.

A current question selects rows valid on October 13. Question q10 selects the September 21 view. Every read, even a historical one, excludes deleted rows. The forget event names the locker key and source session s04. The application redacts that session and its facts, clears their vectors and flushes the response cache, independent of the answer model.

recall() now combines six exact vector candidates with up to six keyword candidates from PostgreSQL’s text search. Reciprocal-rank fusion (RRF, Chapter 05) adds 1 / (60 + rank) per list and keeps six rows within the same budget. Cache keys read the data version from SQL before reuse.

Stage 5: let Qwen write the facts

The 2B answer model first serves as writer. load() requests a JSON object with a key/text facts array, with schema-constrained decoding (Chapter 06). Python checks types, allowed keys, nonempty text and duplicates before SQL insertion. Failed validation rejects the whole session without retry; incomplete/refused responses stop execution. The schema lacks a key enum. Adding one and validating facts individually are untested remedies; neither detects plausible facts assigned to wrong keys.

Writers select supplied keys; reusing one supersedes its current row. The explicit forget event bypasses extraction and targets application-supplied source s04.

The 2B writer scored 8/24. Duplicate locker keys and an unsupported date key voided whole sessions. Valid chatter extractions invented facts that superseded correct ones. q03 (oatmeal) passed without supporting context: a lucky match. q24 defined locker contents generically rather than abstaining, so it failed.

Keep the answer model fixed and enlarge only the writer

Only extraction changes writers; answers remain 2B. The extraction prompt, key vocabulary, JSON schema, validator, session order, supersede rules, retrieval, question set, temperature 0 and seed 7 stay unchanged. Each larger writer ingests twelve sessions three times, with eleven extraction calls each: forgetting bypasses extraction.

The larger writers are Empero's community Qwen3.8 distills at Q4_K_M, both Apache-2.0. They are not official small Qwen releases. The 4B file is Qwen3.8-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf at revision 391fc7d103e3942a408def3e4f51c2f85d464417.6 The 9B file is Qwen3.8-9B-Q4_K_M.gguf at revision 760121cd70bb4c36b2b5ec58eb765e0df5987efe.7

Tested: all writers used the same 32-thread x86 CPU class, with four inference threads. Each larger writer had an 8 GiB memory limit and a 4,096-token context on llama.cpp b12464, with thinking disabled by the same server flag. The answer server retained its four-CPU configuration.

The measured 4B and 9B weight files occupy 2.59 GiB and 5.38 GiB. Both are excluded from Stored data.

Assistant needsStop atCost to accept

Verdict: pay for the missing behavior

Stage 4: 24/24 with all valid hand-written facts; 23/24 with default hybrid. On 16 recall questions (S, U, T, M), Markdown passed 9 (7 grounded); default writers 1, 4 and 4. The 2B total, 8, equals no memory. These local writers underperformed files under unkeyed retrieval. Pick the smallest passing stage; retest corrections/deletion after model/retrieval changes.

Part G · Chapter 21 · Local models only

21

A painter replaces CRM and billing

One owner keeps customer history and the books in SQLite, while local models turn the right records into useful drafts.

Maturity

Prototype

People

One owner, perhaps one helper

Local models

9B assistant, 2B vision, 0.6B embeddings

Tested boundary

Dated recall and guard fallbacks with the 2B model

The business being replaced

“What colour and sheen did we use in the Hendersons' dining room?” The assistant answers with a signed completion-card link. Cedar Brush Painting is invented: one owner, an occasional helper. The assistant retrieves house-specific evidence and drafts actions. Owner-controlled hardware runs every model; no hosted model API receives prompts, photographs or customer memory.

SQLite (Chapter 12) holds room colours, estimate lines and payments. Chapter 20's bounded memory-to-prompt loop runs here with separate code, invented data and the 2B on a Linux CPU. The recommended 9B, vision, voice and Mac paths are unrun. This engineer's build specification is no tested accounting package or practitioner deployment.

At a site visit, the owner records rooms, surface areas, prep, access and photographs. An estimate specifies surfaces, coats, product, sheen, materials, labour and exclusions. Acceptance triggers a deposit request and a job date; added trim or repairs need a separately approved change order. Completion photos and leftover-paint notes lead to a final invoice, payment, review request, warranty record and repaint date. The paid tools sell the same steps: PaintScout lists production rates and materials lists, Joist lists photos and change orders.12

External boundaries remain: a processor handles card payments and confirms settlement; a provider delivers messages; the accountant supplies sales-tax rules. Adapters send only approved amounts, contacts and message text. This reference design supplies no legal, compliance or tax advice.

What this leaves out

  • A full CRM. Its administration exceeds the owner's need for dependable tools.
  • A voice receptionist. Truck notes need transcription, not live telephony.
  • Autonomous estimating from photos. An image gives no reliable dimensions or prep difficulty.

The subscriptions it replaces

Compare one chosen subscription with annual hardware depreciation, electricity and maintenance hours at the owner's rate. Never stack alternative subscriptions' savings. Payment fees and setup reduce savings; maintenance may exceed Joist's price. Data ownership and property recall justify the design.

Architecture decisions, November 2026

Hardware and local models

Start with owner-controlled hardware. Apple lists a candidate Mac mini M6 with 32 GB unified memory and 1 TB storage. CPU and GPU share memory; 16 GB leaves little room for model, context, application, uploads and another model.5 The 32 GB price is unverified. Get a quote; run acceptance gates on borrowed or returnable hardware before purchase. Any passing machine suffices.

Use Qwen3.5-9B as the main local assistant, served by Ollama 0.40.16. Its card lists 9 billion language-model parameters, Apache-2.0 and 262,144 native tokens; the Ollama package adds a vision projector and is labelled for tool support. The qwen3.5:9b download is about 6.6 GB with its vision part, and download size is not runtime memory (Chapter 06 covers the packaging).67

Set 8,192 working tokens. Budget roughly 12 to 16 GB for package, context cache, embedder and headroom; this is unmeasured. Queue vision and transcription behind chat; verify peak memory at installation.

The 9B card defaults to thinking, so send think: false to Ollama for record extraction and routine drafts, and check that the installed package returns no thinking trace (Chapter 06). If a trace appears, treat the package as mislabelled and pin a different build. Ollama supplies tool-call messages and JSON-schema constraints, but neither makes an argument true or a write authorised.89

Qwen3.5-2B Q8_0 uses 8-bit weights; Q4 uses smaller 4-bit weights (Chapter 06). Normal role: read photos, receipts and can labels at 4,096 tokens. Fallback role: after a 9B load failure or speed regression on accepted hardware, reload the 2B at 8,192 tokens (fallback_context in config.json). Suspend vision; render SQL templates until the 2B passes each task's draft gate. When the 9B resumes chat, return the 2B to vision. Its card lists image input, Apache-2.0 and the same native context maximum; thinking defaults off, unlike the 9B. Keep it off. Treat a label transcription as unapproved until the owner compares it with the image: OCR misreads colour codes, and a photograph never fixes a paint colour. The inspected Ollama 2B package is Q8_0 (about 2.0 GB plus a 671 MB projector), not a Q4 build.1011

Local roleDecisionReason and limit
Text embeddingQwen3-Embedding-0.6B; 1,024 float32 dimensions; Ollama.Apache-2.0, 32K maximum; cap notes at 512 tokens. No remote embedding API.12
Photo caption / OCRQwen3.5-2B, one image at a time; 4,096 context.Describe surfaces and extract labels. Store path and source, then the owner verifies.
Truck voice notesWhisper large-v3-turbo, local whisper.cpp worker.MIT weights; local transcription queue. Recognition of colour codes needs review.13
Expected interactive speedUnmeasured on this M6 configuration. Planning allowance: 10 to 30 output tokens/s.Engineering estimate, not a benchmark. A 300-token draft implies 10 to 30 seconds of decoding plus prompt/load time.

Exclude a 27B or 70B assistant unless the smaller model fails a task that templates and typed records cannot handle.

Give every kind of memory a home

Join on property_id, identifying a customer's tenure at an address: two houses need two IDs; a sale creates a new ID, preventing buyers from inheriting sellers' notes. Attach dining-room completion evidence to its room and job. Gate codes are current access facts; expired warranties are history, never free-repaint promises.

Chapter 00 defines semantic facts, episodic history, procedures and working context. The separate business ledger stores ordinary money and customer rows accessed through tools; models never rebuild balances from memory.

LayerStored materialWhat reaches the LLM
System of recordOne SQLite file: customers, properties, rooms, surfaces, estimates and lines, jobs, invoices, payments, events.Typed tool results with row IDs and revisions. Chapter 12 supplies the SQLite store pattern; Chapter 20 compares memory layers using Postgres.
Semantic memoryDated facts with source and validity: room finish, preferred contact, gate code, dog/access warning.Only active facts for the property. Chapters 00, 03 and 05.
Episodic memoryJob diary, call/text summaries, original photos and completion evidence.Relevant excerpts or captions with links to originals. Chapters 00 and 04.
Procedural memoryOwner-edited pricing rules, exclusions, estimate template, reminder cadence in Markdown.Only the procedure for this task, with its version. Chapter 01.
RetrievalFTS5 exact words plus sqlite-vec cosine search of caption/note embeddings.Fused top hits, scoped before either search. Chapter 05.
Working memoryCurrent question, chosen records, relevant procedure and draft.A bounded fresh prompt, discarded at task end. Chapter 00.

Keep “north bedroom: Benjamin Moore HC-172 eggshell” in an authoritative approved surface revision and a dated search fact linked to that revision. Retrieve sensitive gate codes only for authorised job preparation, never customer-facing drafts. “Prefers texts” records a preference; “Dog was in the garden on Tuesday” stays episodic until confirmed as an ongoing access rule.

Keep raw voice files and photograph hashes. The owner accepts or corrects locally proposed transcripts, captions and facts. Commit accepted rows and events atomically, marking embeddings stale until refreshed; meanwhile, use FTS5 rather than older vectors.

A background queue embeds approved notes within minutes. Nightly work retries failures, finds duplicates and proposes diary summaries. The nightly job may rebuild derived FTS5/vector indexes, even from empty, using approved notes and the pinned model digest without owner approval. It cannot change a colour, contact, price, tax code, warranty promise, consent flag or payment state.

A replacement names its superseded note. Acceptance atomically publishes the surface revision, closes the old fact interval, writes its replacement and queues its embedding. Test recall/fallback agreement and retained historical evidence. The original event stays as evidence, subject to Chapter 17's erasure policy.

Search two ways: exact words find “HC-172” and invoice IDs, and embeddings find paraphrases such as “the cream room we did two summers ago.” Filter by customer, property and validity in both branches before selecting candidates. Fuse the rankings with reciprocal rank fusion, 1/(60+rank), using each branch's 1-based rank to avoid raw-score dominance (Chapter 05). The smoke test scans ordinary BLOB rows with sqlite-vec cosine functions, without a vector server.14

Photo search embeds approved captions with a small text embedder. Missing/wrong captions hide photos; allow job-thumbnail browsing. Chapter 04 covers direct image embeddings for visual similarity.

Working context has a budget

Count tokens with the serving tokenizer before submission; caps are planning figures. Tools, instructions and message overhead share 1,200 tokens. Separate image processing returns a short caption. Each total fits under 8,192.

TaskInstructions / questionRecords / procedureOutputTotal cap
Estimate1,200 / 3003,000 / 1,2001,2006,900
Historic colour1,200 / 1501,200 / 2003003,050
Estimate/invoice chase1,200 / 2002,000 / 5006004,500
Tomorrow1,200 / 2002,400 / 6008005,200
Repaint candidates1,200 / 2002,400 / 6008005,200

For 200 overdue accounts, SQL lists candidates; draft one eligible account per prompt. For overflow, cut lower-ranked notes; retain identity, approved financial rows and citations. If evidence still exceeds the cap, split tasks and label each property.

Acceptance gates: speed and correctness

Test synthetic prompts at all five input budgets before accepting hardware. Time loading, prompt processing, decoding and the owner's end-to-end wait separately; the speed gate permits 30 seconds to decode a fixed 300-token draft. Before testing, set the longest acceptable Estimate wait and, per task, the fraction of answerable cases whose unedited drafts must be complete and source-supported. Require abstention on flagged conflicts. Score raw drafts, sent messages, template fallbacks and review fallbacks separately on fixed colour/reminder cases, including superseded colours and disputed accounts. A task missing its draft threshold stays template-only. Reject a purchase if the 9B misses the speed gate. Require zero incorrect releases: unsupported amounts, attachments, promises or access disclosures fail installation.

Files, tools and daily operations

This production layout specifies an uninstalled service. painter.sqlite owns financial truth; files hold photos. Local vision reads one original at a time; retrieval embeds approved captions, which alone reach drafting. Chapter 17 covers the request, outbox and change-delivery protocol.

textch21-code01 · layout.txt11 lines · in this PDF and the companion repositoryFrom docs, not run

Authoritative rows: fixture and production

Only the append-only trigger, inline price comparison and backup read-back were tested. Test production controls before retiring paid software.

The tested schema.sql permits fractional quantities despite INTEGER affinity. Integer-cent totals require integer units: square feet, quarter-hours or line items. Production needs STRICT tables or typeof checks for quantities/cents; test half-unit rejection and two-quarter-hour acceptance. Approved rules supply whole-line tax_cents, added once after qty*unit_cents in both totals; models never predict tax. Issued lines copy prices/descriptions, immune to estimate edits. The fixture has 11 completed, invoiced jobs; Vale has a sent estimate but no job, invoice or payment. Vale's jobless completion card is simplified; production follows the acceptance workflow.

What production must add to this tested schema

  • Issued invoices are immutable. Corrections use credit notes: separate linked records reducing the original amount owed, requiring an additional invoice kind and balance logic absent from schema.sql.
  • Payments are allocated once. Record deposits against jobs as unallocated receipts. Invoice issue atomically allocates them: payment_allocations stores payment_id, invoice_id and cents; UNIQUE(payment_id) enforces one invoice per payment. Unique provider event IDs prevent duplicate receipts. schema.sql subtracts all positive payments, so refunds there would wrongly reduce debt. Production needs positive kind=refund rows linked by refund_of; balances subtract payments minus refunds. A $100 refund of a $400 deposit leaves $700 due on $1,000; cumulative refunds above $400 fail.
  • A job, its estimate, each change order and the invoice's source lines share one tenure. Enforce it with composite keys or transactional checks, and test that a valid estimate ID from another property is rejected.
  • Store unique request IDs, payload hashes (fingerprints) and payload-bound approvals. Make posting safe to retry after timeouts or double taps: identical ID/hash retries return prior results; changed hashes under an existing ID fail. New IDs require approval and base-revision checks.
  • Production adds append-only surface_revisions with valid_from/valid_to and source IDs, plus the columns schema.sql lacks: tenure end on properties, contact hold and dispute flag on customers, an access class on notes (bound per task), a stale flag on vectors (set on an accepted edit, filtered in the dense branch), job_id on notes and a revision on every mutable table. Both reminder lists require current tenure, no contact hold and no open dispute. Invoice reminders also require an issued invoice, positive balance and due date before today. Repaint reminders require repaint_on on or before today and marketing consent. Exclude a successful reminder for that surface and repaint_on; recheck before dispatch and test that rerunning sends no duplicate.

Pin the runtime and declare policy

The configuration pins packages by manifest digest: the hash Ollama reports after a pull, recorded in the lock file at install. Model contexts differ from task caps. JSON keys and test prompts retain American color: Historic colour maps to color, Estimate/invoice chase to invoice; Tomorrow/repaint use the remaining named caps. If a tag changes, fail and review the new artifact. The smoke test uses a smaller model and its own lock file. Whisper and the whisper.cpp checkout are pinned by revision, but transcription still needs a validated binary build at installation.15

Give the model narrow tools

Expose no arbitrary SQL or shell. Bind customer/property from the authenticated screen, never model arguments. Each proposal carries a base revision; single-use approval binds target, parameters and current revision hash. Changes during review require a refreshed preview.

Owner-edited pricing rules specify units, rates, rounding and effective date. Tools resolve approved rates; captions cannot supply them. Follow-up rules block disputes and contact holds. Version accepted changes; show versions in estimate previews.

Delimiters separate instructions from evidence without enforcing authorisation (Chapter 17). Exclude access facts from message prompts; block drafts containing stored access codes before approval. Verify body and recipient against the approved preview before sending.

Backups protect future reads and the books

Before deployment, pin a backup tool's version; keep its recovery secret off-machine. Run this every night at 02:00:

  1. Complete SQLite's online backup API snapshot: recent commits may remain in the separate write-ahead log (WAL), outside the main file.
  2. Back up that snapshot, the original media, procedures, config and model lock to an encrypted repository on a second disk.
  3. Make a second encrypted off-site copy.

Only SQLite online backup and read-back were tested; encryption, remote repositories and scheduling remain unrun.

Once a month, restore into a new directory on spare storage and check it:

  1. Open it with the fixed SQLite runtime, run integrity and foreign-key checks, and count customers and invoices.
  2. Recompute balances.
  3. Retrieve a known paint record and its photo.
  4. Compare an expected manifest of accepted event IDs and media hashes.
  5. Practice restoring from the off-site copy, using the recovery secret.

An upload alone does not prove Henderson's colour is recoverable.

Reach it from the truck, privately

A private VPN such as Tailscale reaches the app from the truck. The plan must permit business use; this design does not assume a free personal plan applies.16

  • Bind the application to its private interface and deny public access.
  • Require an app login as well as device access, and revoke lost phones.
  • Keep the gate code out of notifications.
  • Let the phone upload directly to the private app. A public messaging bot would route customer inputs through a third party before the local model sees them.

Five days in one owner's work

These invented days use the caps and one property per fresh prompt; measured prompts are separate fixtures.

1. Draft the estimate after a site visit

The owner uploads a voice note and four Vale room photos: “Dining walls, two coats; repair the crack; keep existing trim.” The phone carries property ID 2. Local Whisper transcribes; 2B captions photos and flags a partly readable can label. Unaccepted episodes link to originals; the owner corrects a misheard dimension before pricing.

Budget: the Estimate row above (6,900 tokens in total). get_property, recall_notes and read_procedure supply the transcript, captions, surfaces, prior work, pricing rules, template and exclusions. propose_estimate returns surface IDs, measured units and a scope description; the price tool, application code the model cannot call, turns them into line rows and totals.

The owner approves dimensions, prep, coats, product, exclusions and exact lines. Commit the estimate, lines and one event; sending needs separate approval. Later changes require change orders.

2. Find an old colour without guessing

“What colour and sheen did we use in the Hendersons' dining room in 2024?” get_property reads the surface record and recall_notes brings the signed completion-card excerpt. Use the 2024 job despite newer notes. Authorise against today's tenure, then select scoped evidence by job ID or validity at the requested date. Historical evidence never grants present access. The fixture checks different cited answers for 2024 and now.

Budget: the Historic colour row of the budget table. It reads semantic and episodic notes plus the surface record, and writes nothing. The expected answer is “Benjamin Moore HC-172, eggshell, from the dining-room completion card dated 12 June 2024,” with the source ID.

Internal answers need no approval. For conflicting cards and receipts, show both for owner review; vector rank cannot decide truth. Corrections follow the surface-revision transaction above; original job evidence stays.

3. Chase unpaid invoices and unanswered estimates

A morning query lists invoices past due and sent estimates unanswered for the owner-set interval. SQL finds the candidates; a semantic search for “still owes” would not. For Henderson invoice 1, line rows total $1,000, a recorded deposit is $400 and the balance is $600. The fixture returns Vale's estimate sent on 1 November and asserts that Vale has no job, invoice or payment.

Budget per account: the Estimate/invoice chase row. read_ledger supplies amounts and dates, read_procedure chooses the cadence and propose_message drafts only a non-financial note slot, rejected for digits or currency terms. Code renders invoice numbers, dates and balances into the template. Recall can miss disputes, so SQL decides eligibility using the rules above; recall_notes only personalises qualifying accounts.

The owner reviews each recipient, amount and tone. The adapter records send results; failures stay pending. Recheck eligibility before sending; later payments or contact holds suppress reminders.

4. Prepare tomorrow's schedule and materials

“Prepare tomorrow's jobs and what to pick up.” read_schedule finds booked jobs and accepted change orders, then get_property reads access and surface rows. recall_notes adds the recent diary about leftover paint. read_procedure supplies the rounding and pickup checklist.

Budget per job: the Tomorrow row. Make one property-scoped call per job; code concatenates results. Calculate quantities from approved lines and coverage rules, rounding purchase units up before model formatting. The draft separates planned purchases, confirmed stock and uncertain leftovers.

Purchases and schedule changes need approval; listing writes nothing. Accepted material updates write revised requirements and an event. An empty can creates an episode, then a reviewed stock correction. Route optimisation and travel-time promises are excluded; helpers see access data only for assigned jobs.

5. Ask about repaint work at the right time

“Prepare this month's repaint reminders.” The owner assigns surface-specific repaint_on dates; these business choices do not assert model-predicted paint lifetimes. The eligibility query selects dates due, current ownership, marketing consent and no contact hold or dispute, so a sold house never triggers a message to the previous owner.

Budget per candidate: the Repaint candidates row. get_property, read_ledger, recall_notes and read_procedure supply surface, last-job, contact and consent context, and propose_message may say “Would you like us to inspect the finish?” It cannot claim a warranty has expired or paint has failed unless an approved record says so.

The owner approves list and messages. Successful sends record the surface and repaint_on in last-contact events and episodes. Marketing opt-outs clear marketing consent, suppressing repaint reminders; a contact hold stops all contact, including invoice reminders.

A real CPU smoke test

Later lab run, 23 November 2026, after the book's 22 November research cutoff: consumer CPU, with Ollama limited to four CPU threads and a 6 GB container, no GPU, Python 3.14.4, SQLite 3.51.3 compiled locally, sqlite-vec 0.1.9 and Ollama 0.40.16. It is an anecdotal correctness test: 12 invented customers, properties and rooms, 11 completed jobs, invoices and deposits, and 38 notes with real embedding vectors.

The chat model uses Qwen3.5-2B Q8_0 at 4,096 tokens with a shortened prompt, not fallback_context or prompt.txt. It replaces the earlier Qwen3.5-0.8B fixture model.17 The 9B, photo and voice paths remain unrun; the 9B needs the proposed 32 GB class or validated equivalent. The embedder is the recommended Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, not hand-made vectors.

Use Linux or a Linux VM, not native macOS; Python needs SQLite loadable-extension support. This fixture cannot accept the Mac. Save schema.sql and the following files in empty /var/tmp/memlab-21/. Prerequisites: Docker, curl, unzip, C compiler, Python 3.14.4 and venv. Failed digest assertions indicate changed registry tags: review and repin, never disable the check.

Start an isolated runtime

Save setup.sh and run bash setup.sh. It compiles SQLite 3.51.3 with the WAL-reset fix (Chapter 12); lab.py asserts that exact version. Production backup and restore may use 3.51.3 or later.18

Observed output and limits

Real output, wrapped for print; wording/timings vary with load, but digests, scope, source IDs and SQL totals must hold. PASS separates replaced drafts from guard success; production templates render SQL amounts. Recall wall time includes embedding; chat wall time includes reload/prompt processing; decode time measures output generation. The first two recalls use the resident embedder; recalls after chat reload it, and each generation reloads chat.

textch21-code10 · results.txt44 lines · in this PDF and the companion repositoryTested

Real seed and fresh-process output, including package digests, token counts, timings, price rejection and restore result.

Embedding 38 notes took 3.398 seconds. The three colour drafts took 8.471, 6.071 and 7.112 seconds; the invoice draft took 16.578 seconds. These are 2B fixture results, not 9B planning figures.

The 2B model returned only “Matte” for the current finish; the guard substituted the scoped OC-17 matte record. The reminder cited invoice ID 1 as a note rather than retrieved note 11; the citation guard replaced it with a plain template. With note 11 cited, the reminder would pass while disclosing internal “no warranty disputes” prose. Production therefore restricts the note slot and retains owner review.

The injected price tests the guard, not model invention. SQL comparison blocks schema-valid but wrong totals; code renders line-item totals. This fixture checks dollar/cent strings; production rejects digits and currency terms in model notes.

The test checks scope, dated citations and task evidence in the top 2 of at least three eligible notes, including distractors. PASS covers that cap; configured 6-row recall remains untested. It proves neither injection resistance, photo reading, safe reminders nor years-long recall. The substring guard accepts “not HC-172 eggshell”; production needs typed brand/code/sheen/source validation against approved revisions, code-rendered answers and a contradictory-finish probe.

Fallback hard-codes the repaint date, accepts expected note IDs and takes the first property surface. Production must resolve tenure/room/surface kind/date and return source IDs; test two differently finished surfaces per property and review overlapping revisions. Deployment must also test disputed-colour review, sold-tenure isolation, withdrawn-consent suppression, provider_ref deduplication and rejection of competing revision writes.

Scope and scale

Estimated capacity for checked drafts, not a SQLite limit: one owner, one occasional helper, 1,000 customers, 2,000 properties, 100,000 short notes and 50,000 photos, with one active generation and a background queue.

Stored itemArithmeticPlanning size
Original photographs50,000 × 4 MB average200 GB decimal
Note text and metadata100,000 × 2 KB average200 MB before indexes
Float32 note vectors100,000 × 1,024 × 4 bytes409.6 MB before row/index overhead
FTS, rows and headroomAllow 3 × the text-plus-vector subtotal in totalAbout 1.83 GB in total, text and vectors included; estimate
Model packages and snapshotsReserve 30 GB model files; media dominates backups.1 TB internal plus a separately sized backup disk.

At 12 MB/photo, originals reach 600 GB; at 4 MB, budget three 202 GB copies, roughly 606 GB across three locations, plus models, retention and growth. Deduplicating backups send originals once, then new photos. Encryption cannot protect an unlocked original disk from theft.

Unrestricted scans over 100,000 1,024-dimensional vectors touch about 410 MB before SQL overhead; 50 property-scoped notes occupy about 205 KB. Measure both. Repaint campaigns select by indexed date/consent, then search per property. Profile due-date/owner queries before adding indexes.

Nightly consolidationBatch embeddings; optional one chat call per capped episode group.Cap at 20 groups × 2,000 input + 400 output = 48,000 tokens/night; estimate.

At the planning allowance of 10 to 30 output tokens/s, a 600-token reminder takes 20 to 60 seconds to decode, plus input processing, model loading and retrieval. Prefer templates without personalisation. At 40 seconds each, 100 reminders occupy about 67 minutes before review: serial generation and owner approval limit throughput before database capacity.

Costs cover electricity, depreciation, downloads and owner labour, without hosted token fees. At an assumed 30 W average extra draw for eight hours a day, annual energy is 0.030 × 8 × 365 = 87.6 kWh; multiply by the owner's tariff. This unmeasured Mac power assumption cannot establish maintenance savings against a $17 plan.

Before scaling for customer growth, measure queue wait, prompt length, peak memory, writer wait and retried writes:

  • If two simultaneous staff sessions regularly wait over 30 seconds for a free model slot, try a second inference machine before changing the database.
  • If workers need continuous concurrent writes, or writer wait repeatedly exceeds the five-second timeout, adopt the Postgres and Redis patterns in Chapters 08 and 09: Postgres owns transactions; Redis holds disposable sessions and caches. Chapter 18 explains the wider choice.

Risks and what the owner still owns

Bookkeeping correctness. SQL computes totals, the model drafts and the owner approves. Commit approved rows and events atomically; enforce the request ID/payload retry protocol above (Chapter 17). Reconcile processor settlements, fees, refunds and bank receipts, and export for the accountant. Import customers/properties with distinct tenure IDs, reconcile opening invoices and balances to the old books, and leave imported colours unapproved until source-matched. Keep both systems until a parallel billing period agrees and a restore passes.

Customer privacy. Local inference still needs access controls on the operating system, phone, backups and adapters. Exclude card numbers from this database and third-party health or family details from job notes. Chapter 17 covers deletion and rebuilding derived indexes; an append-only log is no reason to keep personal data forever.

Losing the machine. Independent backups preserve context and books together. Approved notes can rebuild embeddings; summaries cannot reconstruct missing signed completion cards. Restore authoritative data before model caches; keep recovery credentials accessible without the failed machine.

Mistakes in customer-facing prose. A model can sound certain about an unsourced finish, offer a discount or repeat an access code. Show the owner citations and a deterministic money panel, reject unsupported claims, extra recipients and unapproved promises, and fall back to a template or “needs review.”

Professional boundaries. Accountants determine treatment, tax rules and reconciliation; processors or banks move and verify money. Local models only assemble evidence and explanations. Start with sourced colour answers and correct reviewed estimates, then migrate records under control.

Part G · Chapter 22 · Local models only

22

A doctor's office

Replace contact, billing, scheduling and phone interfaces with local agents that remember only what each task needs.

Maturity

Reference design; isolated text smoke test

Practice

3 clinicians, 10 staff, 4,000 patients

Capacity target

4 calls and 6 staff sessions

Model boundary

Open weights; practice-controlled hardware

The practice and the boundary

Phone calls, reminders, insurance cards and billing questions occupy much of a doctor's office day.

This engineering design is not legal, compliance, tax or clinical advice; the practice owns risk analysis. Regulatory references are US federal; elsewhere, remap the legal gates. People and events are invented.

Meadow Lane Primary Care has three clinicians, ten staff and about four thousand patients. Agents handle contact, scheduling, billing support and phones; clinical questions and urgent requests go to a human. The phone system has a hard-coded emergency path outside the language model.

Full deployment requires engineering maintenance capacity; otherwise retain existing interfaces or adopt SQL memory/gates without phones.

All models, including speech, vision and embeddings, use practice-controlled hardware. Block inference-server outbound traffic; copy weights in. No patient data reaches providers through inference, telemetry, crash uploads or remote support.

Replace four interfaces: patient-contact customer relationship management (CRM), billing support, scheduling and automated attendant. The practice-management and electronic health record (EHR) system remains authoritative for clinical records and the ledger. OpenEMR offers records, practice management, scheduling and electronic billing, but is not required. Certification and security depend on installation.1

That system owns demographics, appointments, encounters and ledger postings. PostgreSQL holds administrative memory and versioned read models. An adapter imports authoritative changes with source IDs and revision numbers. The scheduler’s transaction API prevents conflicting reservations through the LLM screen; this design supplies authorization and context assembly.

Staff still approve codes, correct charges and release claims; the adapter handles eligibility inquiries and responses, claims and remittances without the LLM. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) lists adopted electronic transaction standards, including X12 5010: 270/271 for eligibility, 837 for claims and 835 for payment and remittance. Billing reads posted rows; models never invent claims or interpret insurance contracts from memory.2

The American Medical Association (AMA) requires permission or licensing for Current Procedural Terminology (CPT). Keep licensed tables and versions in billing; never train on or distribute the code set with this example.3

Local models do not make the office local-only

External services include the carrier or Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) trunk, emergency calling, claims clearinghouse, payer networks, card payments, e-prescribing and messaging providers. Allowlist each destination at its adapter. Send the agent a payment token, never card details. E-prescribing stays entirely in the clinical workflow.

The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) requires written assurances from business associates, outside parties providing covered functions/services involving protected health information (PHI). Assess flows and obtain applicable business associate agreements for clearinghouses, messaging and PHI support. Payment and payer classifications differ.4

The conduit exception excludes transmission-only services with transient storage from business-associate status; voicemail and transcript stores retain PHI and fall outside it. An outside encrypted-PHI backup custodian remains a business associate without the key, requiring contract and risk review. This design uses a second practice-controlled appliance off-site.5

Architecture decisions, November 2026

The two language-model lanes

Main: Qwen3.8-27B, a dense Apache-2.0 native vision-language model (VLM), 27B parameters, 262,144 native context tokens; operational cap 16,384. Its card documents tools and per-request non-thinking mode. Use it for drafts, reconciled balance explanations, summaries, background note-taking and card extraction. The four-bit Q4_K_M GGUF size estimates weight memory only; production uses a different vLLM artifact, and the smoke test uses Ollama. Pin the serving artifact, hash and quantization in the release manifest.6

Phone: Apache-2.0 Qwen3.5-9B, with vision, documented tools and 262,144 native context tokens; use Q4-class at 8,192. Chapter 06’s Ollama llama.cpp Q4_K_M (4-bit GGUF) has 5.6 GB weights, 6.6 GB with projector, within the 7 GB allowance. Its size reserves speech capacity and shortens prefill (prompt processing before output). Main-lane failure pauses drafts and card extraction; staff use existing interfaces. Reserve the phone lane until mixed-load replay passes; its fallback is a deterministic menu and human transfer, never an untested model.7

Both cards document thinking on by default. For administrative turns, the gateway sends chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking=false on every request (Chapter 06). Verify that no hidden reasoning consumes the output budget.

Use one continuously batched serving lane per GPU with separate admission queues. Serve with vLLM on a pinned, supported native 4-bit artifact, such as AWQ if supported for the exact model and cards; otherwise re-budget a higher-precision build. Re-measure either choice; GGUF sizes are planning proxies. Constrain tool arguments and extraction results with a JSON schema, then validate patient ID, field types, policy version and authority in application code. vLLM supports structured output constraints; the model can still select the wrong action.8

At four calls, target useful text within 350 ms and about 50 output tokens/s per stream. Measure complete tool calls separately; tool tokens and filler are not spoken answers. Four 2,500-token prefills in 350 ms need about 29,000 prompt tokens/s uncached: put stable policy first, enable prefix caching and measure cold and cached turns separately. Missed targets reduce admission or trigger transfer, never clinical small talk.

Three options are rejected:

  • A 120B model for the phone loop, because its larger allocation and prefill compete with speech for a task that usually selects one tool.
  • A single 64 GB Apple-silicon Mac: both lanes and speech share memory and one accelerator, so card images can delay speech. A one-call office could validate it.
  • Hosted inference, which violates the premise.
